text: Karma was off to a good start. I found myself in a very cool street with a nice evening vibe and I immediately liked the bistro-style of the restaurant as I walked through the door. The welcome and service by the waiting staff was really good and very friendly. Unfortunately, it all fell apart when the food came, which I guess is the most important bit. The samosa appetizer just wasn't - a samosa, that is. The thick, doughy deep fried pastry was just wrong in every way and while samosas are meant to only be lightly spiced, the filling was almost devoid of any flavor except for the tang of not quite cooked potato left on the palate. To me, it's always a bad sign when they ask how hot you want a curry sauce. Particular dishes in Indian cooking are defined by specific flavors and spicing, there are no varieties of heat for any dish. I have never been asked this question in India. So, it didn't bode well for the butter chicken and, sadly, it lived down to my expectations. This dish is all about luxurious, smooth flavors and nothing to do with heat. This one was all about heat and was just wrong from its dark brown colour to muddy texture. On a positive note the rice was light and fluffy and the naan bread was fabulous but that's not enough to warrant a $35 bill for two dishes and a bottle of sparkling water. So very disappointing.

text: There are two types of Italian restaurants. Those that are effortlessly and properly Italian. And those that are laboriously wearily Italian. Of the latter you'll find some stereotypical Italian-American name such as Mario, Vito or...Tony. The menu, speckled with "authentic" things such as lasagna, spaghetti and meatball sandwiches, will mostly be covered in so much sauce and cheese that one plate is indistinguishable from the next. Welcome to Tony's Restaurant in Carpinteria where all the aforementioned missteps abound. I've been there twice--the first time, for a sandwich that my tastebuds have forcefully ejected from its memory. Too much cheese and too much sauce can do that to you. Most recently, I went there for a pitcher of beer and frings. The beer, from down the way at a place called Island Brewing Company, was the avocado honey ale. A good beer overall but nothing especially notable. The frings, for somewhere between $6-7, is a joke. There were literally only about 5 onion rings and 10 steak fries. Both were overcooked by about a minute and a half. I have no words that can fully convey my disappointment so I'll stop really soon. Tony's is like that Italian friend you have that is very proud of his heritage even though the only knowledge of Italian culture he has is from the Godfather trilogy and that some guy named Domino makes good pizza. If that's your idea of Italian then fine. It's just not mine.

text: The IMA's collection rests on its chief benefactors, namely the Clowes, Lilly, Marmon and Pantzer families and their differing collecting tastes. While Indianapolis is a relatively old Midwestern city, the IMA's history is recent; it was known as the "Art Association" until 1969. The recent multi-year renovation, redevelopment and expansion of the Museum and grounds created an entirely new experience for art patrons. Let's all say our condolences to the Krannert Pavilion's Brutalist architecture of the 1970s and hello to a somewhat uninspired series of camera-ready atria that will no doubt allow some very impressive parties. The collection itself is conservative and unprovoking. Highlights include Robert Indiana's iconic masterwork (and trademark-infringed) "LOVE" painting and sculpture, a beautifully painted though incredibly ill-placed Rembrandt, a decent Hopper, an encyclopedic Asian art collection that is one of the best in the country, and the largest collection of JMW Turner drawings outside of Great Britain (although quantity does not trump quality). I thought the gift shop was as poorly stocked as the previous one. Not a single postcard of the new museum's exterior, yet there were plenty of old postcards showing the now-demolished Krannert Pavilion. And for an artwork that's been copied, dubiously appropriated and downright stolen, why was there not one postcard available of Robert Indiana's outdoor "LOVE" sculpture? And what about museum merchandise based off its own artwork: scarves with motif from the museum's Tiffany piece, jewelry pieces mimicking something from the Asian galleries or pop-up note cards laser-cut with the new museum facade? Sure, all the "LOVE" stuff is nice, but capitalize on other museum strengths. This is a wonderful museum that has a decent collection. The parking is free, the new eating options are terrific, and there are other fun attractions on the museum grounds, most notably the Lilly estate, Oldfields.

text: The Produce Place manages to pack an incredible amount of quality stuff into its tiny interior. It has saved me several times from having to buy yucky grocery store preservative laden bread and it's handy to pick up some fresh locally grown vegetables, of which (space allowing) they have a decent selection. If you want to cook dinner, this is not the place to go in searching for recipe ingredients, rather, go with an open mind and create something from what they have. They have a nice selection of quality organic cheese, local milk in a glass bottle (you can take it back for a refund) and a limited selection of rather pricey organic deli meats and bacon. The back wall is lined with bulk bins of various legumes and grains, which are probably the Produce Place's best value items. They are not open on Sunday, and they close at 6:30 on weekdays, which makes it difficult sometimes to catch them when they're open, but I'm always happy when I do and I can indulge my cravings for San Pellegrino Aranciata or a nice Virgil's root beer, and pick up some Provence or Great Harvest Bread, and a block of yummy cheese.

text: If you're 20-something, live in Levittown or Langhorne or thereabouts, and you're too lazy to drive to Philly, then the Hulmeville is the place to be on a weekend night. In my case, I date a guy from Levittown, and he and his friends love this place. So I tagged along when he and I started dating, and the place really has grown on me over the past year. This place is historic, as well as fun. Located on Trenton Road in historic Hulmeville, PA, the Hulmeville Inn has been in business for over two hundred years. Originally, it was a hotel and stage coach stop for those traveling between Trenton and Philadelphia. There is still a hitching post and a stone step that was used to board the carriages located on the property. During Prohibition, the Inn operated as an ice cream parlor. Now it's a great place to grab a beer and watch some sports. I like this place because it's spacious (yet tough to get a table if you get there late on a weekend night), has pool tables, and has a pretty good beer selection for a place in the 'burbs. In fact, I can always count on them offering Dirty Hoes because they always have Hoegaarden and Framboise on tap (and I like Dirty Hoes... no, not that kind, the drink, silly!). They change their beer selection to keep things fresh every once in a while, so check out what they have on tap on their website before you go. They've also got bar food - fries and such. Their wings are pretty good. Usually, this place is pretty much a townie bar during the week, but it becomes 20-something central on the weekends, with a fun crowd and good juke box music. You can always find the random sketchy old dudes at the bar on the weekend, though, which reminds you that you're still near Levittown. They just add local flavor to the place and keep it from becoming too much of a hipster hang-out. The Hulmeville bartenders are always really nice, and the ID-checker guys at the front door get to know the regulars after a while. I like having people know me at businesses that I frequent. I just don't like getting hit on by the sketchy old dudes at the bar (some have said some really GROSS things to me while I tried to order a drink...). If you're a cute girl, be sure to order your beer at the other end of the bar from them. The prices are pretty reasonable, and you can also catch the Phillies game or whatever sports game on their really nice tv's. I also noticed that the owners constantly upgrade the place to keep it fresh. The decor has changed little by little since I started going there a year ago. Oh, and the pitchers have a compartment in the middle where the bartender puts some ice, so your beer stays cold until you finish the pitcher. That's always appreciated. They are open seven days a week from 11 a.m. until 2 a.m. My only complaint is that the Hulmeville is outside the Philly city limits, so the smoking ban is not in effect there. Thus, I've had difficulty breathing and leave smelling like an ash tray. Since the place isn't huge and it gets really crowded on the weekends, and since I don't think they have a state-of-the-art ventilation system, it gets WAY more smoky in there than your average bar that still allows smoking. In fact, it's so bad that I've been avoiding going there very often since the Philly bars went smoke-free. If the entire state ever institutes a ban, though, I'll be back in the Hulmeville at least once a week, like when I first started hanging there. In the meantime, I'll still go, just not as often as I'd like because I value my asthmatic lungs. If you can take the smoke, though, check it out. This place rocks.

text: My bf and I adopted two adorable kittens through ACCT/PSPCA over Labor Day weekend, and while we went to the ACCT headquarters for the paperwork, I have now been to the PSPCA headquarters multiple times due to one of our kittens. We decided to adopt a brother and sister who were being fostered by an amazing foster mom, and we wanted to pick them up ASAP after their surgery. I got a call the evening of their scheduled visit from the foster mom telling me that the boy was unable to get his surgery due to an undescended testicle. And so the epic saga began. I was able to 'adopt' him temporarily as a foster myself (since PSPCA doesn't allow you to adopt animals that aren't fixed), and told I had to reschedule his surgery for when he's big enough to handle the surgery. Over a week ago I brought him in at the ungodly hour of 7am to be neutered, and when I arrived that evening to pick him up they told me they COULDN'T FIND the undescended testicle. FML. They explained what they did, that its possible he doesn't have another one but we won't know until I bring him BACK in a month to check if he's developing sexually. They gave me some painkillers for him since he had two major incisions on his belly and he had a plastic collar on so he couldn't reach his incisions (one held together with stitches, the other with glue). The collar ended up being too small and we realized a few days into his recovery that he COULD reach his incisions and was licking them, possibly causing some minor bleeding and maybe beginning to infect himself. We called Jessie, who had left her number in case we had any questions, and made an appointment with her the next morning. She saw me immediately, took a look at his belly herself, then showed it to a surgeon who had operated on him and also one of their primary doctors who had also operated on him. They all agreed it didn't look bad (and that the collar was WAY too small for him), but while the glued incision was healing well the stitched one looked a little infected. They put a larger collar on him, gave me both oral and topical antibiotics, and told me to bring him back in a week to remove the stitches. The best part of all of this treatment is that not only was it all free as part of his neutering surgery (since its technically not done - YET), but both Jessie and Dr. Howard talked to me about him and what they saw and what I could do, answered all my questions, and handled him like he was their pet. These people are wonderful and they do not get enough credit for all the hard work they do, and the GOOD they do on a daily basis. They are an extremely organized place, and CLEAN and MODERN facilities from what I saw. Go and adopt one of the many wonderful animals in need of good homes, and help support the PSPCA's efforts!

My least favorite were the chicken options because the chicken wrapped in bacon was really dry and unimpressive, and a chicken leg is just a chicken leg no matter how you prepare it. I couldn't do this every month, or even every other month for that matter; I swear my lower intestines have come to a complete stop (TMI, I know) after that meal, which can only be described as gourmandizing (yes, gourmandizing). text: My husband and I are just moving to Tucson. My parents lived here 40 years ago and they ate at Mama Louisa's all the time back then. For as long as I can remember, my mom has talked about Mama Louisa's linguine with clam sauce and how great it is. As a treat and thank you for helping us move, my husband and I decided to take my mom to see if it was still as she remembered it. According to my mom, it's still the best linguine with clam sauce she's ever had. She's been eating her way across the globe for the last 40 years so that's saying something. Neither my husband nor I are big Italian food lovers - at least the food called Italian that's served in the US (we both love Italian Italian food - sorry folks but alfredo is NOT from Italy). So, the dinner was for my mom. However, my husband and I both enjoyed our meals as did our kids. We got our kids the pasta with meatballs and there was not a piece of food left on their plates. They aren't picky eaters but they also never clean their plates. I had the linguine with garlic and olive oil. It was good but could have used a little more spice. My husband had Joe's Special and he said he would go back for it. That's a huge compliment from him. They make their own pasta and you can tell, it's very good. The bread was reminicent of some of the chains and most of it stayed in the basket. According to my mom, the decor hasn't changed one little bit in 40 years except that they added the salad bar. I'll leave it up to the reader to decide if that's a good thing or not. Our service was excellent. Our waiter checked back quite frequently to make sure we had everything we needed. Our food arrived without much of a wait. We'll definitely be back.

text: So there are lots of places to get sandwiches in town, and I have compared Bread and Company to the Food Company in my review of that place. I may have sounded unnecessarily harsh since I do enjoy the food at Bread and Company. This store on Hillsboro was the first one I came across. I used to live right down the street, and I worked down the street as well. I think the thing that amazes me is how crowded this location is. It is always packed. In fact, all of the Bread and Company locations are in great spots. There development/real estate team deserves a pat on the back. There are a somewhat dizzying array of sandwiches and salads to choose from. I would recommend studying the menu before getting in line. That's just me talking; I don't enjoy being behind people who are still reading through the menu when they (finally) get to the sandwich counter to give their order. Some of my favorites are the balsamic turkey with (pulled, not sliced) turkey, goat cheese, and balsamic vinegar. All of the toppings for the sandwiches are fresh, and the people making the sandwich (at this store, at least) are right there so you can give any special requests. Soups rotate daily. You can get them in a nice bread bowl or 'boule,' I suppose I should say. Their fruit tea is delicious. You can get gallons of it to go. There are other items in the deli cases as well to get on the run...pre-made sandwiches and salads. I love the salads with fresh fruit; a strawberry salad deserves special mention. Summer is the time for fresh strawberries. A salmon fillet salad and the cobb are keepers. Sandwiches are served with kettle chips. The chips might not be made in store, but they are delicious. There is brunch on the weekends with omelets made to order. Like some other people have pointed out, this lunch can set you back some $$$. I would say this is to be expected. Bread and Company is going after a certain clientele, and they are succeeding. I imagine their demographic can afford to drop $8 or $9 on a sandwich, no problem. (See also the comment about their store locations.) I don't mind doing it every now and then. This was the first location I came across, but it is no longer the closest one to me. I'm also growing increasingly wary of going in to Green Hills (damn you, Hill Center!). Be careful trying to get in and out of this store since Hillsboro is so busy. I almost got rear-ended one day. He said it was my fault. Whatever, he made a left-hand turn in front of me when I had the right of way. I believe this is also the favored location for Nicole and Keith so tell them hello when you stop in!

text: If you've read my other reviews, you know that I'm not one to full out hate someplace, or give vague reasons why I don't like something. SO...I do not hate The Delachaise, but I do have several specific reasons why I did not have a good experience there. 1. It is small and not well equipped to being a restaurant, staff-wise. 2. There was smoking allowed indoors, and no ventilation. 3. We had to literally argue with another party to get a table outside, when we had been waiting for over an hour. *4. The service. If you're interested in hearing about the service, please read below. We sat down at our table (finally) and had to go up to the bar to order food - there was a waiter, but it looked like he was just there to deliver the meals. And talk on his phone. Our food finally came! Yay! It was 10:00 or so, and we were all really hungry. So, anyway, our food came. No - wait - everyone else's food came and my stomach continued to growl. I waited for about ten minutes before going up to the bar to inquire about my missing grilled cheese sandwich, and when I did, bartender A told me he'd check on it. I stood there watching him not check on it for ten more minutes, before asking the other bartender. I was told by bartender B, that because so many people order the grilled cheese, the oven was backed up. "It'll be out in a few minutes." Mmm Hmm... So I waited for another fifteen minutes and went back in again. Me: "Hi, I still haven't gotten my sandwich." Bartender B: "You still haven't gotten it? Hang on..." When he came back, he told me that it was on it's way out. I was almost in tears at this point I was so hungry and frustrated (I know, silly, but true) and said that I thought it made sense if the sandwich was on the house. He had no idea what I was talking about, and asked me if I had changed my mind about the sandwich. "No, I still want it - the rest of my table has already had their food for over a half and hour. I think it should be free." I went back outside and waited for an addition ten minutes, before going in again with my fightin' words ready to go. Still no sandwich, but bartender B went and found it (piping hot) in the kitchen and gave it to me. I settled my tab at the bar with bartender A, who had no problem taking my sandwich off the bill, and everything was - ehem - fiinnne after that. Not the end of the world, but I expect better from people who earn their wages in tips and work six feet from the place where the food is cooked. The wine was good - I had the Malbec, and people I was with had beers and scotches, all of which seemed to satisfy them. Alcohol is definitely this place's forte - they should probably leave the restaurant business to people who know what they're doing.
label: NEG

The burger and fries had the savory taste I was craving, and in the 40 minutes we were here, there were another 10 walk up orders, all of them for an Awful Awful (or 2). text: Can I get a whaaaa? Alicia F and I went to live our '80's fantasy and were treated to a real educational experience, all for just $10 (it was Thanksgiving Eve, so I don't know if that's the regular cover or if they were bringing in a few more bucks like every other club in town was last night). First of all, if you plan on getting in with a wristband (21+), your ID better be real or real good, because those dudes do not mess around. I almost didn't get in because they didn't believe that the pic on my license was really me. OK, for the record, I did have blonde hair but really...if I was gonna fake it would I fake being born in the '70's? I'd say no. When you walk upstairs there is a ginormous room that seemed to be the playground for all the goths in the tri-state area. W.O.W. I thought I had seen it all, so I wasn't quite prepared for dudes walking around in gas masks, women with shaved eyebrows and a scantily clad senior citizen who made bedroom eyes at many of the underage boys who came to par-tay. Besides almost having an epileptic seizure because of the damn strobe lights, though, it was really interesting to hang out in there for a bit, mostly because this community seems to have a trait that is seriously missing in the other counter-culture groups out there: there seems to be no judgements, no rules about how thin or rich (or poor) you have to be, nobody cares how much money you spent on your outfit or where it came from, etc. From what I observed everyone came to dance (and maybe a little more, but what do I know?) and be themselves. I thought that was awesome. When we had finally had our fill of scary music telling you to "kill your babies," the '80s room started seeing some action. We danced our faces off and sang along to every song. We found ourselves not giving a rip what anyone saw when they looked at us being completely goofy and carefree. In that moment I felt totally free. It was lovely. Finally around 1 am we were danced out and decided to split. We walked the short distance to the car (I totally got a princess parking spot right up front) and drove off, leaving the kids (and yes, most of them are kids) inside to do their thing. Leash and I were in total agreement: we were very pleasantly surprised with how much fun we had. Then, as a perfect ending to a wonderful night, we hit up the Taco Bell drive through and stuffed ourselves with cheap food. This is the stuff memories are made of.

text: Going to New Orleans to find a quiet place to sleep? That's potentially a hard task close to the French Quarter, but Baronne Plaza Hotel pulled it off. My first impression of the hotel from the outside was that it was sort of run-down, but the inside is far nicer. There's an ornate lobby with some small side rooms with fireplaces and a sushi restaurant adjacent. The desk staff was friendly and when I arrived early for my room (it wasn't ready yet), they were able to stow my bags and let me roam around the city. There's also parking at the basement of the hotel (Careful! It's fairly narrow there.): you need to notify the front staff because they have a small gate blocking the entrance. The rooms are small but well furnished and clean. You can tell it's an older hotel, but has aged gracefully. Bathrooms are reasonably sized and come with a coffeemaker. One note from my room was that the shower did tend to change pressures: there would be a small squeek as if from a dying animal and the pressure would drop. Another squeek and the pressure would increase again. I liked to think that there was a small animal on a treadmill running the shower who would get momentarily tired and give a little squeek of fatigue. In case you were wondering, I was far more entertained by this than anyone has a right to be from a shower. Overall pricing is fair for a center city hotel and was a little bit cheaper than some of the other options along Canal Street. The location is hard to beat as well: a few blocks from the French Quarter and a short walk to the Riverfront and Convention Center.

text: OK, I'm going to be honest, after reading such great reviews about this place, I had high expectations, but this place didn't even come close. I'm sure this one review won't change your mind about going to this place when compared to the rest of the raving reviews. He gave us a couple of complimentary bottles of champagne and invited us to hang out as long as we liked. They are a tight knit group of people, who are laid back and easy going... they made me a loyal customer ever since. In fact, most of the servers were standing in a semi-circle about 20 feet from our table just yapping it up and laughing. Then finally - as we were leaving with very disgusted looks on our faces the manager came over and asked how everything was for us. I told him I couldn't really tell him because we hadn't even been able to get a glass of water after waiting at our table for over 45 minutes. He then offered to buy us a drink or do something to 'make it better' - which was nice. I told him at this point - there was nothing they could do to make my experience 'better'. So, we left - went across the street to 'Bricktops' and had a wonderful dinner. My friend was obviously embarrassed as he had talked up Rumba so much. He is trying to get me to go back again some other time - but I doubt I will. I can deal with mediocre food and maybe try again some other time. text: The only reason this place still exists is that West Philly is dying for more restaurants and is desperate enough to patrionize what we can get. With any modicum of competition they would be driven out of business. BEER: Overly hopped. Instead of brewing up a well rounded beer they toss in an extrondinary amount of hops to impress us. I appreciate that they contracted a good deal on hops prior to the hop shortage and skyrocketing prices, but NOT enough to want it to be the primary flavor in every beer offered. They had, and ran off, atleast 2 decent brewmasters that I know of. If you want a good, local microbrew try the Philadelphia Brewing Company, Manayunk Brewery or Riverhorse Brewery. All three are amazing. PIZZA: Cutting corners seems to be their primary motivation. Times are tough but I still want a decent pizza when I am paying for one. Sparse toppings, often hastily made. Trio fries=burnt leeks. Allegro pizza doesn't have a wood fired oven and will still knock the socks off a Dock street pizza anyday. WARNING: The "VEGAN" pesto is a lie. Some of the prep-cooks put parmesan cheese in it to "make it taste better." Some of them don't, but most vegans I know aren't willing to take the chance. CUSTOMER SERVICE: I live in West Philly and am friends with several cooks and servers who used to work here. There's a reason the owner declared bankruptcy and ran atleast one other restaurant to the ground. They treat their workers like poop and the good ones leave. I can't speak for those still there. Maybe if they were paid fair wages, treated better by management, and allowed to make and serve quality food (not forced to cut every corner possible) this place would be decent. And the acoustics are AWFUL. It is hard to hear the person sitting next to you. Throw rug anyone? It could help with the cafeteria style sound. I'm just looking for a good slice and beer to wash it down. But I live 2 blocks from the place and get take-out from other places or go downtown for my pizza and beer. Its a shame, I wish they were good.

text: So I totally didn't know what baba ganoush was, or at least every time I had had it before it was a gelatinous mess of eggplant seeds and greyish, whitish, palish.....yuck. Marhaba is LEGIT. That's what I say when something captures exactly what it's supposed to in terms of....well, that depends. In this case in terms of culture. Middle eastern food is all about style -- Lebanese is separate from Greek is separate from Turkish is separate from Israeli. They all use fundamentally the same ingredients, but have different spice blends and preparation techniques. So, Marhaba is a Lebanese restaurant because they have things like zattar (it's like lebanese oregano) or baba ganoush and hummus (these transcend cultural boundaries, oh because they're amazing!) The weird thing is....no one seems to go in there. Every time I go, it's empty except for mine and my boyfriend's table, and another table that looks like it's one of those 6 hour long lunch tables. There's one server, and she's about 17 years old, and then two cooks. One guy just makes pita. The other guy makes everything else, or at least that's what it looks like. Oh, did I mention they make the pita THERE?!?! Unheard of. UNheard of!! Except for the fact that the smoke dries out my eyes, I love it. It comes to the table all inflated like a big doughy balloon, and then you dip it in perfectly blended hummus topped with bright green olive oil and one single, small green olive, and then you eat it. With your face. I also love the schwarma, and the beef kabob pita. I don't eat lamb, because babies taste weird, but I'm sure it's delicious...if you like that sort of thing. Not sold yet? Eat this: it's a BYOB. With awesomely cheap prices.

Atmosphere - the atmosphere was bad. Bright lighting, loud room (made worse by the acoustics), boring people, old carpeting. When I say this place had no character, I mean it. Service - perfectly pleasant. The woman who waited on us knew the menu, served the food promptly and quickly opened the BYOB bottle of wine we had brought with us. Price/value - The place wasn't cheap. It wasn't expensive either, but for the quality of food they are serving, it ought to be really cheap. In fact, maybe they should have paid us. At the end of the day, I have to believe there are better places in Lambertville. This comes highly acclaimed from some (NYMag, you let me down), but I would caution anyone looking for Thai food in Lambertville, NJ and expecting to be pleasantly surprised.

But, if you only make it a destination at Christmas time, you are missing out. It's a fun place to check out at any time of the year, and if you have out of town friends you should definitely take them here to see the Soldiers & Sailors Monument and for a treat at the South Bend Chocolate Company's Chocolate Cafe. I hadn't been to the top of the monument since I was just a wee tot, so was mildly excited to go back up to the top earlier this summer. Sorry Sarah A, but I didn't actually climb the stairs to the top. I'm sure it would have been great exercise, but it was a really hot day and I didn't have it in me. So, for $1 a person I went up to the top with my mom and brother. We had fun looking through the dirty windows out to the various parts of the city, and spotting a few rooftop hot tubs. However, it ended up being really crowded up there in a really small space... and making our way back to the elevator on the short but narrow staircase was really frustrating. Being in that close of proximity to sweaty people, however many feet in the air, made me a little claustrophobic and really annoyed. If you want to go to the top, I would HIGHLY recommend going on a random weekday -- not a Saturday or Sunday afternoon like I did. Big mistake on my part, and I paid for it by smelly stinky strangers who climbed the stairs!
label: POS

text: Hank Y - The utensils and napkins are conveniently located in a beer mug on the side of your table. I'm not sure why your waitress didn't bring that to your attention. And $90 for a table of 4 including beer, is really not that bad. I don't see how any of you left hungry, you must have unusually large appetites. I disagree completely with all of your review. I'm considering budgeting Brauhaus into my weekly income, granted if I did that, I may not be able to fit into the door due to the over consumption of brats, potatoes and beers. Each dining experience has been excellent, better than the last. I've only had to wait once for a seating, and it's expected on a Friday night. Any other day, I've never had to wait. I was told 45 min, although it was more like an hour.( No biggie, I had a beer to savor and finish anyway, although I wouldn't take my Oma on a Friday, given the wait and the noise). After being told how long we'd wait, me and my party of 3 hastily made our way to the crowded bar, and the bartender was very attentive. Afterwords, we found a cozy area in the back to enjoy our ice-y brews. The waitresses are very friendly, patient and informative. The rotating oom-fah music makes you want to bounce in your seat. After being seated, we were promptly offered water by our kind waitress which we turned down, yet she returned with a basket of breads and some dill butter. Yum, a good start! I typically order the Nurmberg Wurst with the potato pancake and braised cabbage. Some of the best wursts my friends and I have had. Pancakes were crisp at the edges and lightly browned in the middle. The cabbage is tart and tender, mmm. Some may say this place is expensive, but the portions are huge, especially when you have a beer to help it go down... so I'm always bringing home leftovers. The braised cuts of meat are quality as well. I also like the very diverse, happy crowd. I like that they show Bundesliga. I love that they offer 20 draught, ice cold beers, as well as an extensive bottle list. I like that you may choose to order the inexpensive tapas for something light, or a hearty meal. My only complaint would be the bathrooms. The walls around the toilet could be wiped down. I think someone had too many drinks he couldn't aim for the toilet. All in all, it's a great place to gather friends for some good cheers!

text: After all of the glowing reviews here on Yelp, I thought Lacroix would be the perfect place to enjoy some Philadelphia French gastronomy. And while my dining experience had a few hits, unfortunately, the misses will stand out most prominently. First, the hits. The service is great. The waitstaff perfectly balance the high-brow service you expect in a place like this with a smiling, down-to-earth helpfulness that makes you feel welcome. The service is graceful and efficient and encourages you to savor each bite. I began with a dinner salad with a "chocolate" dressing. Which, although it sounded gimmicky, was very good. The only trace of chocolate taste was kind of a darker flavor that complemented the bitterness of the frisee salad beautifully. For an entree, I had the Muscovy Duck Breast which was spectacular. The skin was beautifully browned and crisp, the inside was juicy and flavorful, and the parsnip coconut sauce was creative combination of old and new world flavors that was smooth and rich. Unfortunately, though, there were misses. And they were big ones. My companion had the butter lettuce salad to start, which offered an Asian twist on the traditional butter lettuce salad. And the flavors just didn't work. The chef put sesame oil in the dressing to Asian-it-up a bit, and the pungent flavor of the sesame oil melded with the stinky flavor of the gorgonzola cheese and resulted in completely palate-offending combination. My companion also ordered a side dish of enoki mushrooms with chili sauce which was not only palate-offending, but pretty much inedible. The enokis were soggy and wet (after all they're enoki mushrooms--that's why the Japanese use them in soup) and no amount of thai chili flavor could redeem their sorry state of affairs. And finally our dessert, 5 phases of pumpkin, was disappointing. In the chef's quest for uniqueness and creativity, he forgot that pumpkin is comfort food. And unforch, there was nothing comforting about the 5 measly pieces of odd-flavored pumpkin-oriented minutiae that dotted the dessert plate. Ultimately, the food here tells me that the chef here is very impressed with himself. I also think that if he read this review, he would disdainfully proclaim that "she knows no-ting about zee French cuisine". However, I am too classy to name drop my French gastronomy street cred here. So suffice it to say "zat was zee last time zat I will dine at Lacroix."
label: NEG

text: You must be kidding! As a former rider who was exclusively dependent upon public transit my first couple of years out of school, I must say, without a doubt, that IndyGo is the absolute, unequivocal WORST public transportation system in existence. From schedules that are far from convenient, to busses that break down for no reason, to drivers who could care less about you or your situation (plus some with attitude to boot) because none of the drivers have to ride the bus, to an incompetent administration who embezzles public money and makes a hell of pension for just five years of service, I am horrifically embarrassed by our public transit when guests come from out of town. The first problem are the waaaaayyyy overpaid drivers. I am not anti-union because I believe there are some industries (automakers) that have to have them because the execs and shareholders try to screw the employees out of benefits. However, the unionized workers at IndyGo do not give good service because they know that they cannot lose their jobs for treating people like crap. The union will always defend the bus driver no matter how egregious the claim against them and the union fought to keep cameras off of the busses for years (they still don't have microphones or any sound to hear how foul mouthed they are.) I have personally witnessed bus drivers intentionally pass people who are standing at the bus stop (usually for a racist reason), put public lives in danger (usually by driving too close to the curb, break way too late and too hard as if they were driving a Honda and not a 40 ton bus, and I personally have been struck by a bus while waiting at the stop because there was no sidewalk and the driver WAS ON HIS CELL PHONE!!!! I was not hurt, nor knocked down, but do you think the driver bothered to call it in to his supervisor or fill out an incident report. Of course he did not because he knew he'd get in trouble but the most that would happen is he would be suspended (with pay) but not fired. The other problem is that the busses only go to one location for transfer. That is all the way downtown. It takes over an hour to get downtown on the bus system (longer from some locations still within the city) and that is once you are on the bus! If you have to get to a place on the north side that directly driving would take you about twenty minutes (let's say from St. Vincent Hospital to Castleton Square Mall) it would take you two hours and 15 minutes to get there! Are you serious????? Crosstown routes would get more ridership from IndyGo (and not cancelled) if they would advertise them and make them run more often. Instead IndyGo relies on a stupid, outdated, 1950's kind of thinking of demand determines how they operate. Question: How would you know if there was any demand if the route never existed on a schedule that people would find convenient? I've never heard of IndyGo doing door to door neighborhood surveys to find which residents would favor an alternative transportation to the car. It is really because Indianapolis and IndyGo do not care about public transportation as a real asset to a city. Instead they give lip service to the media and treat the poor, disabled, and elderly who are dependent upon their horrendous service as second class citizens. Once I had the means to buy a reliable car, I got a 2nd job so that I could keep the car and insurance payments up. But it is the sad state of affairs that is IndyGo that forced me to abandon Indianapolis' public transportation forever. Update: For Neal P.'s review from 02/03/09: I think you have a great theory of the current state of IndyGo with your "Institutional Inertia" theory. Although race played into it, also socio-economic status, which encompasses race as a factor, is even a more determining factor. How else would you explain the equally poor south side with a mostly white and poor population? You are right in that Hamilton County did not want bus service to keep certain elements out, but they also did not want to pay for any kind of public transportation. Greenwood discontinued their bus service because, much to the lament of Greenwood Park Mall shop managers, because the city did not want to pay Marion County for the service. Instead they started their own, even more inconvenient, transit service which consisted of "on demand" vans. The mall managers wanted the bus service so that they could have a reliable source of transit for employees (who are not highly paid.) I think you should write some more and expand upon your ideas, but use socio-economic status to show how IndyGo does not care for the marginalized and helps maintain marginalization.

text: The Masonic Temple is a gloriously kitschy attraction that rivals the Mütter and Eastern State in weirdness, and it's hiding in plain sight, right across the street from City Hall. Built in the 1860s as the grand lodge for the state of Pennsylvania's many masonic lodges, the Temple is filled with a repetitive series of meeting rooms that each pay homage to the stonemason's craft: there's a Morrocan Room, a Renaissance Room, a Corinthian Room, an Ionic Room, and a positively psychedelic Egyptian Room. Some of these rooms have stone and tile details, and the main hallway is mainly marble,though many of the theme rooms feature painted plaster. The Masonic Temple is an architectural candyland, offering a bizarro tour of how elite 19th-century Americans viewed other cultures, and a peek into the mysterious, kinda-creepy, kinda-laughable world of the Masons. You do have to take a tour (I think full admission is $8), as they won't let you wander. My guide was a funny and likeable mason who seemed more interested in chatting up one of the women on the tour than telling us about the building. But he was refreshingly frank when asked about the Masons and their history, and he had some good one-liners. I'm not sure I'd join his club, but it was fun to visit.

Everything on the menu looked great, but if you're going to eat here, get the seafood. You can see the fleet of fishing boats from the back windows. The three-way ceviche sampler was great. Lobster bisque was excellent, but gigantic. I could have done with 25% of it. Based on the previous Yelp reviews, I had to try the king crab claws. I have never had sweeter, easier-to-eat crab meat. I'll definitely get that again next time I go back. The restaurant itself is really interesting. The see-through floor to the wine cellar is a great touch and all of the fixtures and hardware are very elegant. It's fun to watch the chefs grill the fish, steaks, and chops right out on the giant wood-fired grill. If you catch it at the right time, you can watch them feed more of the deliciously aromatic wood into the grill. I would fly back to St. Pete just to eat here. text: i have to preface this by saying that i used to work there, so I'm obviously biased, but then again, being biased is what this is all about. I've loved the pneumatic diner for years; through different owners, through being an omnivore to being a strict vegetarian, to dabbling into moderate veganism, all of it. and i know that being on customer side of things it can seem a little daunting and unaccommodating. it's a tiny place that's hard to find with only seven little tables to sit at. and sometimes, you even have to wait to sit at one of those seven little tables. but it is worth every inconvenience that we have grown accustomed to expecting from other larger restaurants. first things first, and this should not be overlooked because it's strikingly rare in a city like Reno. everything is made in house. the hummus, the rojo sauce, the tahini sauce, the falafel, the ratatouille, the soups, the lasagna, the pesto, the buckwheat waffle batter, everything is made with loving care and dedication by the exemplary staff at pneumatic diner who put in far more work than they get paid for because the place is worth the effort. i've moved on to bigger and better things; studying and now practicing architecture in San Diego, and still to this day, the Pneumatic Diner is the first place i go when i get off the plane coming home. my favorite dishes are the theban wrap with added falafel, the vegan bayard, the falafel plate and of course the slab tacos. but for the uninducted, i have to recommend the infamous cookie bomb and the beanie dip. you haven't had good eating until you have had the beanie dip. so yeah, the odd location and all vegetarian / vegan / sometimes raw menu will turn some people off, and i say: that's great, because there are only seven tables, but otherwise, in my opinion, you don't really know *R*E*N*O* until you know pneumtaic diner.

text: Switching hair salons is always a terrifying experience. I recently had to find a new hair salon because my girl had a baby and decided to retire (The audacity, I know!) Finally, I relented when one day I finally gave my hair a good long look in the mirror and realized, I was in trouble. This, seriously, might be the best my hair has ever looked. Keep in mind, I do not have easy hair to deal with. My hair is incredibly curly, and not in that pretty Keri Russell kind of way, in that bad, Julia Roberts in My Best Friend's Wedding kind of way. Whatever Clare did to me, it worked. My hair is shiny, my curls are bouncy and not frizzy at all, and it straightens out with little to no struggle from me and my round brush. Also my high lights...I can't brag enough about my high lights! It has never looked so real. If you put my hair next to that of my 19 month old niece, you couldn't tell the difference. It's amazing! In terms of personality, Clare is the nicest, funniest person to speak to as well. It was a completely pleasant experience having my hair done. She even squeezed me in at the end of her day knowing I was in desperate shape. Also, the price was a lot cheaper than a lot of places around Clayton. For a whole head of high lights and a massive clean up on my hair, it only cost me $140 bucks and that included tip! If you are looking for a new hair salon, go here. The meal began with two appetizers - ceviche trio and "Cuatro" (chips + three salsas and guacamole). The ceviche left something to be desired, especially if you've had it anywhere else. Instead of chunks of high-quality seafood in citrus juices, each sample was, at most, two small pieces of a single type of fish in a bath of watery fruit. The guacamole with the "Cuatro" was very good, but I've had better chips and salsa at Baja Fresh. For our meals we selected the Adobado Shrimp and Baja Fish and Chips. The shrimp were TERRIBLY overcooked. By overcooked I mean like six or seven pieces of shrimp-flavored rubber. The accompanying coconut rice was moist and tasty. The green beans "sambol" were essentially just sautéed green beans like what I've had anywhere else. The Baja Fish and Chips were excellent for something that typically qualifies as bar food. We finished the meal with creme brulee. I'm sure that Lime prides itself on the unique twist of topping this traditional dessert with bananas and serving it with a side of sugar cookie. However, in this case it was simply a high-priced banana pudding + Nilla wafer. In sum, I would recommend Lime to anyone looking to over pay significantly for very substandard fare.

text: As someone who prefers power vinyasa in a heated room, I'm fine with doing the occasional Bikram class and I actually got into hot yoga by doing their 2-weeks for $39 intro special when visiting my parents during the holidays last year. I've actually decided to attend a couple of classes this year, too, even though the constant 26-pose Bikram routine always bores me (Hey, I like variety.), but St. Louis is sadly deficient in studios offering hot yoga. It's Bikram Yoga, so the instructors are naturally hollier-than-thou and spit out the same spiel you've heard before if you've ever done Bikram (Eagle = pearl necklace, for example). The Chesterfield studio is newer than Clayton, so the carpet doesn't smell as rancid. I actually preferred the instructors at Clayton rather than the ones in Chesterfield although there is some crossover. I wish the website would provide instructor bios, alas they do not. Chesterfield also seems to have more well-preserved soccer moms in SUVs than the Clayton studio. Down the street from my parents house, I attended classes here more than the other and there is definitely a cadre of Bikram devotees of this variety.

text: Okay, so a few nights ago, my parents ask "Hey Jim, why don't you take us to one of those good spots in the city for dinner? Maybe Aunt Carolyn would like to come along too". It was a Wednesday night, and I had nothing better to do, so I figured why not? They wanted to go to the usual places they go down here...either Soho pizza or Campo's. They're both great, but they get old after a dozen or two times. Also, if I was going to be dining with my parents & slightly-less-than-normal aunt, I would need a place capable of continuously supplying me with beer....lots of beer. Finally, I had a chance to try the Race St. Cafe! I've been wanting to get there for a while...seemed like such a cool place. Well, it was the perfect idea. From the minute I walked into this place, I knew I was going to like it. Easy going, nice people, cool atmosphere, and...lots & lots of beer. Dad & I quickly ordered...Oktoberfest for me, and I think a #9 for him (at first he was thinking Coors light...but after a seriously disappointing grin from me, he changed his mind). The menu was adequately sized...not huge, but very good, with great variety, and well-priced. Perfect for this place! All in all, the meal was great. I'll definitely go back soon, hopefully without the parents. This is one of the few bars in the city that I know of that are perfectly fine to go to alone (if necessary). Being that many of my friends are reluctant to go out in the city (or even leave their damn house)....this is a big plus. It's nice to escape the ridiculousness that Old City can be sometimes. Race Street Cafe does a nice job of being different, and different is always GOOD.

text: My boyfriend took me here for my birthday last year and it was an experience. Morimoto was a little hard to find and we were surprised the cab driver didn't know what we were talking about. I usually don't do fruity drinks, but this one was perfectly mixed. We both enjoyed the Chef's Choice Omasake Menu. It was about 10 courses if I remember. It was expensive, but worth every penny. It included oysters, scallops, sushi, lobster tail, kobe beef, and many more. The sushi was top grade and melted in my mouth. I tend not to eat scallops, but the scallops here were so fresh and had a nice crunch to it. I am not sure if I would come here to have a regular menu item, but defiantly come for sushi and the tasting menu again since it changes frequently. It was the perfect way to celebrate my birthday!

text: The Second Mile Center is a series of second hand stores on one block. They sell everything under the sun, and they have the space to do it. I'm sure there's an interesting story here as to how they acquired so many properties, but that's a story I have yet to learn. Today, they are well-organized and very reasonably priced. Here you can buy electronics, furniture, luggage, housewares, and of course clothing. The clothing store is especially huge, but it's not so overwhelming because all the offerings are spaced out in aisles and aisles of racks. The property is a big square with a very high ceiling, so it feels spacious, which is nice. When it comes to quantity, Second Mile takes first prize. When it comes to quality, Second Mile is much lower on the thrift store list. They have a lot of junk in my humble opinion; however, as the owner of Toviah Thrift told me last year, just because I wouldn't buy something doesn't mean that nobody would. There certainly do exist thrifters who aren't concerned with trends, and I'm sure Second Mile gets plenty of those shoppers. While Second Mile has a lot of low quality items, it also has its share of gems. The ratio of crap to gems here is the same ratio as at Toviah Thrift; Second Mile is just a much larger, more organized property. Like TT, SM also had some religious affiliation. Definitely stop by--they have everything under the sun and it's all oh-so-wallet-friendly. Racks and racks of shoes, dresses, blazers, handbags, AND this place has sales from time to time. A thrift store holding a clearance sale? Yes, they do. Once my mom and I came here on Xmas eve and they entire inventory was being sold at half off. Pretty crazy. This block is positively magical when the weather is warm. Tons of trees, lovely Victorians in the area, not too much traffic. With the SM folks on the block, it's the type of place where you'd want to sit down and just chill for a while. There's just something about South 45th Street. When you visit, cross the street to visit the used furniture store with furniture that talks to you. Someone here tags the items with papers that - well, talk to you! Sometimes it's a story, sometimes it's general commentary, sometimes it's a snazzy one-liner. Even if you have no need for gorgeous vintage items that could never fit in your apt, come visit them to see what they have to say.

text: I live locally and visit this food store at least once a week. If there aren't crowds, it can make for a fairly pleasant shopping experience - provided that you yourself are pleasant. Although I'm not the most social person, I often find myself chatting and joking with the cashiers, especially the older women who work most frequently. (Sure, sometimes they're grumpy, but they deal with a lot of crap from customers; I was there one evening when a woman threw a piece of fruit at one of them.) The deli is crummy and closes early, and I wouldn't trust anything in the fish section. But I appreciate the selection of ethnic food and can almost always find what I'm looking for. I'm with everyone else - the yogurt selection and sales are terrific. The meat is reliable; even if it appears a little sketchy, I've never had a problem. Last night, I went in to buy a Purdue Oven Roaster to make for dinner tonight. I use reusable shopping bags, but the cashier suggested putting the chicken in a plastic bag so as not to contaminate my other groceries. I lugged my groceries home, and it didn't occur to me until 5 a.m. when I was feeding my cat that the chicken was not, in fact, in my fridge since I had not, in fact, remembered to take the plastic bag home with me. To make things worse, my receipt was at the bottom of the trash bag I'd used to clean my fridge last night and was covered in leftover bean and bacon soup. I called this morning, pretty sure I was s.o.l. and would have to buy my chicken again. The woman on the phone somehow kept herself from laughing at me and asked me to call back in ten minutes so she could check the book where left-behind purchases are recorded. I dutifully called back and was put on hold for a bit. The hold music was "Don't Wanna Miss a Thing," which I appreciated since I was so desperately trying to find my lost chicken: "'Cause even when I dream of you The sweetest dream will never do I'd still miss you, babe And I don't wanna miss a thing" And dontcha know - they had my chicken. The woman on the phone sounded honestly about as excited for me as I am to be reunited with my chicken. (Hey, we grad students don't have lots of money to buy duplicate chickens.) I would have given the market three stars for all of the reasons everyone else has listed, but they definitely earn an extra for reuniting me with my Purdue.

text: After my fifth visit to Citizens Bank Park, I decided it was time to stop procrastinating and write a review. Citizens Bank Park is yet another new ballpark built to resemble old brick ballparks. As one of the yelpers said, "thank G-d for the Baltimore Orioles" who started the tradition of building beautiful new ballparks. What an upgrade over Veterans Stadium! Then again, what isn't, right? I was in Philly when they tore down The Vet and I was happy to see it go. Citizens Bank Park is a great place to watch a ballgame. You're guaranteed a homerun experience, since the ballpark is a proverbial bandbox. Balls fly out of the park at an alarming rate due to the short porches in left and right and a ridiculously low wall in center. My seats were directly behind home plate, 31 rows from the field. The view was truly spectacular. The scoreboards provided all the information, allowing even sophisticated baseball fans to thoroughly enjoy the game. The loudspeaker, however, was located above my seats and a few rows in front of my seats. As a result, I had a hard time hearing the PA announcements. Maybe I am just getting older and my hearing is slowly going, who knows. Also, there must have been a smoking section nearby, because I could definitely smell cigarette smoke from my seats. GROSS. I really enjoyed the walkways on the field level. The aisles were clear and spacious, with plenty of room to walk and ponder various food options available to you. The area behind centerfield wall is a bit convoluted and confusing, in my opinion. If you're not interested in crowds, chaos and clutter, I would recommend staying away from there. If you find yourself in the bleachers, walk down to the front row and check out the flower pots just behind the outfield walls. They're truly a part of baseball history, as they are partially responsible for the introduction of instant replay into our national pastime. And finally, I would be remiss if I didn't say anything about the fans. Remember, Philly fans are the ones who booed Mike Schmidt and Santa Claus, and they will do it again. Don't provoke them. Most fans in the nice seats are the corporate, fair-weather, bandwagon type fans who care more about the beer than the game. Sadly, it's the case at many ballparks these days. While those fans are too busy to appreciate the game, they're quick to boo anything that moves. When their struggling outfielder, who we shall call, umm, Rat Squirrel, to protect his identity, misplayed a ball of the wall, the fans booed like it was going out of style. Never mind the fact that he had hit over 30 homeruns in 2008 . . . Some things never change, new stadium or not. Overall, very nice stadium catering primarily to the casual fan. Plenty of parking options around the stadium. Nice monuments around the ballpark, too.
label: POS

text: When I moved to the Hendersonville, TN area in January 2007, Banfield was a pretty great veterinary clinic for simple care. Their insurance plan was wonderful and came in handy with our dog and cat. HOWEVER in the past year and a half, their quality of care has plummeted. Whenever I go in, there are different veterinarians and vet-techs. My first bad experience was when my 2-year-old cat was sick. They examined her and determined it was an infection and sent me home with antibiotics. Two days later (a Saturday evening), I was at the all-night emergency vet with a dying cat in my arms... and they were unable to save her. Banfield had basically patted me on the head and said it was nothing to worry about and sent me on my way. Going back through the papers from that last visit, they hadn't even bothered to do bloodwork on her -- the only notation was that they listened to her stomach and it was "gurgling". I felt partially responsible that I hadn't DEMANDED a more thorough examination - but at the same time, I expected the vet knew what he was doing and when they were confident she'd be OK, I felt like I could trust them. After she died, I tried to cancel the pet insurance I had through them for my dog and my now-deceased cat. They wouldn't let me cancel EITHER insurance plan! The dog, I understand. However, I was told I'd either have to let the insurance I'd carried on the (dead!) cat run out for the year contract or I'd have to back-pay all the discounted services I'd received already that year. (Which would have been several hundred dollars more than continuing to pay for insurance on a dead cat for 4 more months!) I found that just plain SICK. However -- this reflects on Banfield CORPORATE, not this specific branch. Finally, as I said, my dog still has insurance through them (it runs out in December and clearly I will NOT be renewing). She was due for a checkup and teeth cleaning. Had she been SICK I'd have rushed her to our NEW vet, but I thought that for a simple check up and teeth-cleaning I may as well take advantage of the insurance that I'm stuck paying $24/mo for. I took the dog in and get a call a few hours later saying that they can't get a catheter in her and that she keeps ripping it out (which she's never done before) so they'll be unable to clean her teeth. Ok, FINE. I don't really care. I go pick her up, and the poor dog is TERRIFIED. She's never had a bad vet-experience before but she's just not herself. ... Needless to say, I'm NEVER taking her back there for so much as a toenail clipping. I don't care if I had to pay insurance for the rest of forever, I'd never USE it ever again. Truly if you love your pets, don't take them here.
label: NEG

text: Excellent Romantic Ambiance! Just be sure to ask for one of the three dining tables found directly facing the bay towards the back of the restaurant. You will need a light sweater-ladies or sports coat/light jacket-men,... since the dining tables in the rear facing the bay have the air conditioning a bit cooler than the rest of the restaurant. On weekends they have a one-man band playing your "classic" top hits! He really added to the romantic ambiance/dining experience. Drinks: Try the rasberry lemonade martini - def winner! The calamari appetizer is unbelievably fresh and comes with two wonderfully mixed sauces. The barbecue jumbo shrimp appetizer is a "must try" if you like a zesty smoked flavor-Note: Shrimp is wraped in a very thin slice of bacon that gives the shrimp a nice punch-of-a-taste-great presentation as well! The house salads were very good but take a rain check on the salad dressing and just ask for balsamic vin. or olive oil. Oh my goodness, if you like scallops then you don't want to forego ordering from the "light entree" section of the menu the scallop meal - trust me - you will not be disappointed - the sauce is very light and buttery. Under the same "light entree" section of the menu you will also want to order the jumbo shrimp dinner meal. This dish has an amazing taste - with the red roasted peppers, asparagus and light cream sauce as the bed of the shrimp,... the dish is divine! If your palate is savoring for sweets, then you don't want to pass on the Key Lime Pie! I've tasted many a Key Lime and theirs is by far the best - extremely light airy texture with a perfect balance of "tart and sweetness" to it! Very nice selection of wines and mixed drinks....I would highly recommend this place! Our server, Jason, was excellent as well! I will def be back to this hidden gem located inside of the Marriott Suites in Clearwater/Sand Key in the near future!

text: A few years ago I embarked on a tour of St. Louis pizzerias. I've been to The Good Pie, Pi, Dewey's, and many others, but the one that I keep coming back to is Katie's Pizzeria Cafe. I like the boho chic ambiance with the mismatched furniture and grad student artwork on the wall. I even like how all of the staff is super hot and super friendly, but kind of clueless. But, most of all, I really like their Neapolitan style crust and their endless array of topping combinations. On my most recent visit, we enjoyed a squash blossom pizza with goat cheese and fresh cherry tomatoes. The squash blossoms were lightly pan seared and added a crunchy element to the creamy goat cheese and juicy tomatoes. We also enjoyed an artichoke, prosciutto, fresh mozzarella and fennel pizza that was deliciously chewy and salty in all the right ways. Other memorable pizzas were the egg pizza (goat cheese, speck, rosemary and sunny side up fried eggs on top), the fig pizza (fresh figs, gorgonzola, and rosemary), and the tres amici (salami, sausage, and pancetta). You have to start your meal off, though, with some fresh prosciutto spring rolls and artichoke toasted ravioli. Both are homemade and uniquely prepared. To be quite honest, I'm usually in a drooling quandary whenever I sit down for a meal at Katie's. Everything on the menu sounds so darn good and I just can't make up my mind. My husband got the spicy filet and langoustine salad and loved it, though he switched up the dressing, choosing citrus vinaigrette instead of the menu-listed soy vinaigrette. I got the mixed green salad minus the gorgonzola. Little did I know that the gorgonzola was the only thing that gave the salad flavor. The dressing, a roasted garlic vinaigrette, tasted like nothing more than oil. The menu-listed balsamic onions and roasted red peppers were flavorless. After my husband had nearly finished his salad and mine remained nearly untouched, waiting for the server to return, we finally stopped another server to ask for more dressing. When ours returned with more citrus dressing (assuming it was for my husband), I asked if they had a balsamic vinaigrette dressing, she said yes then brought out plain balsamic vinegar. Our table lacked a pepper grinder, so we grabbed the one off the nearest table (since our server never bothered to ask if we needed anything). It didn't actually grind the pepper, just spewing out near whole peppercorns. We borrowed one from the neighbor's table but had the same result. In spite of our experience, I actually might return. Their pastas look pretty good, and I wouldn't mind giving them a try. text: CAN YOU SAY HALIBUT TACOS?! Oh boy, whenever I'm craving sushi I'm making the trek across town to get my fix from Fujiyama, which is in the same complex as Fresh Off The Hook. A few days ago, I was craving fish, but not raw fish, so Tay and I poked our heads into Fresh Off The Hook and I am SO glad we did! The exterior is inconclusive and almost unassuming, one would not think a Seattle "harbor" style interior would be hiding underneath a strip mall exterior! When you get in, head straight for the front counter where you can browse at a menu held in a menu box to the right, or browse at the menu actually on the top of the counter. The service was a little slower than I hoped for and since I only had an hour for lunch and had driven from Eagle, we had to hurry which is never ideal. The fresh and delicious food made up for it though! I had one halibut taco (I debated on whether I should get two or not) with a generous portion of battered halibut mixed with a fresh concoction of what seemed to be like cole slaw. However, this cole slaw had more of a sweet bite, almost like mango salsa? One bite and I knew I should have ordered two! Their french fries are the best in the business as well. You can always tell a great restaurant from the fries. Since they are usually the first thing a customer puts in their mouth and the last thing they are picking at after their meal, some could argue they are the first and last impression of an establishment! Either way, the fries were hot and fresh just like my halibut taco. Tay had the shrimp taco and saif the same thing, "We will be back!" ($14 for two people ain't bad!) Thanks for a great experience Fresh Off The Hook!

text: The Grand Sierra made a good first impression on me, but my opinion kept dropping though my 4-day stay. This could keep some kids and non-gambling adults busy for a while. However, after a little while, I started to notice all the little fucked up things - broken front door, leaky coffee cup, elevators that go in the wrong direction, some rude employees (and some good ones, to be fair), NASTY, NASTY buffet, broken iron and internet in my room, and pervasive cigarette smoke. It also bothered me that essentially nothing is included in the price of your room - coffee, toll free calls, use of the exercise room, and internet access all cost extra. I already mentioned the buffet, but let me reiterate, I found it inedible - I literally picked up a sandwich at the cafe on the way back to my room, because I couldn't find enough food I was willing to eat at the buffet. text: It's not hard to find a good meal and a nice glass of wine in Center City. The place is small and well-appointed, with rustic wood and exposed brick, a long bar and a big cool-looking metal wine rack behind it. Prepare to be elbow-to-elbow with your servers and fellow diners, and pray hard that no one spills anything. The close quarters give this place a convivial vibe, and you'll have plenty of opportunity to ogle other people's food before you order. All of the small vegetable starter dishes are tempting, and I recommend the roasted beets: a few firm, flavorful bites each of red and yellow beets, with pistachios, olive oil and creme fraiche, I think - whatever it is, it's delicious. Pizza is thin and tasty, with a chewy, slightly charred crust and simple, well-chosen toppings. The size is perfect for one really hungry person, one not-so-hungry person who wants to take a couple slices home, or two people to share. The wine list, with about a dozen choices each of red and white, is relatively diverse and inexpensive. The beer list is a snooze - stick to the grape stuff here. One last thing about the humble, omnipresent glass of water: Zavino's is just the right temperature and tastes really good.

text: Yay!! Loved this. Disclaimer: I am a big, big wimp. I dig the odd zombie movie, but in terms of scares and spooks I usually pass. I enjoyed this, enjoyed it a lot. However, the walk through/show is a full 40 minutes long, and it's super fun. You wait a bit, as they only let in about 20 people at a time, but you have a few kind of creepy, mostly wacky actors to entertain you with their silly rule announcements and comments. When you go in there is a very silly puppet show (with blood) that depicts the short life of the poet. Then, each room is a short snapshot of a Poe story. Things suddenly appear in corners and leap out at you, so watch where you stand if you're a wimp like me. The acting was very good. The fellow who performed "The Raven" was just top notch, and that's such a well known poem that I imagine it's hard to tackle. The graveyard girls in "Annabel Lee" were well made up and sang beautifully. As a bit of a theater person, I appreciate the work that went into something like this, and it was really wonderful. The show is creepy, but not scary per-say. No one screamed (too) loudly, just some very crawly skin. It would be good for older kids, especially if they've read some Poe. I imagine that if you didn't know a thing about Poe you'd be a bit confused. I myself have some stories to look up, some scenes that I couldn't identify. We laughed, we clutched each other, we inched wide eyed down creepy corridors. It was a good time, and a great way to celebrate the poet's 160th death day! Suggestions for next year: The Cask of Amontillado A real bathroom

text: Johnny's Po-Boys is a great little place with a HUGE menu. Their menu has something for everyone and it's a great place to try something new! Johnny's is small and a little plain, but the quality of food and the price definitely make up for it. The menu has an extensive variety of po-boy's as well as other items like seafood gumbo or subs; they also have weekly or daily specials listed somewhere off to the side. For those of you unfamiliar with a po-boy, it's a large sandwich consisting of a meat or seafood served on half a french baguette typically with lettuce, tomato and mayo. If you've never had a po-boy or never had a certain type of po-boy, this is THE place to try it out. You can choose from the traditional seafood pb's like soft-shell crab and shrimp, or you can pick an exotic one such as alligator! They also have the tried and true chicken tender, hot dog or tuna salad pb's for those feeling a little less adventurous. You can get just a sandwich or a combo, and everything is available as take out too. Some of the meals came out a little quicker than others, and if you end up being one of the lucky ones waiting on your food, don't sweat it! I ordered the special of the week, the half order soft-shell crab po-boy with a bowl of seafood gumbo on the side, all for about 15 bucks! I ended up waiting about 15 to 20 minutes for my food, so that did not make me too happy.....especially since I saw the others in my group getting their food very quickly. Well let me tell you, it was definitely worth the wait! I got my po-boy plain (no lettuce, tomato or mayo); a whole order must contain 2 soft-shell crabs as mine was the half and I only got one, but that was more than enough! I was served a baguette split down the middle with a deliciously crispy fried whole soft-shell crab sitting on top. They prepared the crab by removing the inside of the crab (guts, etc...), dipping it in breading and frying the entire thing. The sandwich was hard to eat in one piece, so I ate it open faced. The seafood gumbo was fan-TASTIC! Made with entire pieces of soft-shell crabs, large shrimp and crawfish and plenty of veggies and hot sauce, it made the perfect side dish. It came with a piece of toasted baguette as well and when I used that up, I used the rest of my sandwich baguette to sop up what little gumbo was left. I dipped the crab in there too; the entire meal was one to remember.......in fact, I'm not gonna lie.....I may day dream about it time and again when I get a craving for some good creole food......and you would too if you tried it!! So, in conclusion: Johnny's Po-boy's =legendary experience!

text: Zahav is amazing! So amazing, in fact, that I ate there tonight and I'm online writing this review now. Some friends and I stopped in this evening for an early dinner. Our reservation was for four people, but between booking the reservation and actually getting there we invited another friend. We were a bit worried about them allowing the change, but the hostess assured us that it was not a problem. We were seated at a corner table, and Michael, our super friendly and attentive waiter came over to introduce himself. Zahav serves family style tapas, so we all ordered different dishes and shared. We started with the Salatim and Turkish hummus. The Salatim was a cold salad sampler...very good. But Honey, that hummus. That hummus, I said! It literally melts in your mouth. I need to find out where they sell that hummus, because I'd make it at home and try to pass it off as my own. YUM! Ok, Ok, I also ordered the Crispy Haloumi, which is this fried cheese - it's really good. I also ordered the Fried Kibbe with Tahini, which is kind of like a lamb turnover - also good. I'm not going to sit here and try to remember everything that everyone ordered - everything was DELICIOUS, but there were a few standouts. 1. The Turkish Hummus (which was previously stated, but I just had to say it again) 2. The Fried Cauliflower, which is lightly fried and served with a yummy yogurt sauce. 3. The Sweetbread Schnitzel - which is made of melt-in-your-mouth veal. 4. For dessert, I ordered the Cashew Baklava. Honey, that baklava was everything that baklava should be. It was sweet, with a flaky crust and served with a white chocolate mousse. Simply perfect! The service was also great. Michael was ON IT. He made entree suggestions, which were really useful. The staff is great, our glasses were always promptly refilled, and dirty plates were taken in a timely manner. I cannot wait to go back to Zahav. Seriously, I've only been once, and it's now one of my favorite restaurants in Philly. We all LOVED our food, and you know that's rare for a group. Zahav is definitely a breath of fresh air!

text: We enjoy going to a few Tampa Bay Rays games per year and really believe the team deserves the support of all Tampa Bay residents. The current ownership does everything possible to make it a fan friendly experience. Good team, good ownership! We also enjoy Tropicana Field. There is a certain comfortable feel to the place; it's got good parking (free for many games with four in a car) and a really excellent amount of food choices. The food is overpriced (what public venue isn't) but great selection, well prepared and friendly helpful staff. Why two stars? Rays ownership promotes a summer concert series on some Saturday nights after the games. Last night we stayed for the Hall and Oates concert...a mistake! The sound system or those operating it were horrendous. An irritating slight delay in the sound (like an old movie out of synch) vs. the stage performance, a shriek of feedback with some regularity and a generally muddled sound made for an annoying experience. With every break in his lyrics, Daryl Hall would look off stage and make hand signals in a useless attempt for a correction. Obviously, the sound on the stage was no better or worse than what we were hearing. A show biz hothead or lesser professional would have walked off. It was uncomfortable to listen to and I was embarrassed for Hall & Oates and their band members. Haven't been to many "stadium" concerts but I know they happen all the time and must have better results. Tropicana Field either needs to get better personnel, better equipment or a better idea for after game attractions. A side note to parents of young children; if you're going to keep them awake past 11PM, then be responsible for them. The kids running around on the field unsupervised was another added distraction. Tropicana Field with a Ray's game earns four stars, add a concert and lose two stars.
label: NEG

text: Lunch date: March 22, 2008 Company: The fam & BF When people ask me where I am from and I tell them Santa Barbara the response goes something like, 'Oh...rough life! I can't believe people actually live in that paradise.' I immediately let them know that I am aware of my good fortune not just because I grew up here but also because I had access to La Super Rica my entire life. I have always believed that if you truly love someone you will show them by taking them to this Santa Barbara landmark and letting them experience some of the best Mexican food in the country. I grew up going to Super Rica with my parents who never eat out because their cooking is so amazing that there is no need to seek sustenance elsewhere but they love SR. I remember always sneaking in through the back kitchen door to visit the 90 year old woman who made tortillas by hand. She reminded me of my grandma and so I would call her Abuelita for years until she sadly passed away. I have more memories from meals at Super Rica than I can count and the only constant throughout is the #12-Pechuga Suiza and a small horchata. This is basically SR's version of a chicken quesadilla. No matter how many times I have tried to replicate it, it never quite turns out. A succulent piece of perfectly cooked chicken covered in cheese lies happily in between two homemade corn tortillas. If your lucky during its time on the grill some of the cheese will burn ever so slightly and the taste will change enough to blow your mind. I have tried pretty much everything on the menu but my heart stays true to #12. Other great ones to try are: chorizo con queso, Super Rica especial and gordita de frijoles (super spicy!). The last time I went was last weekend with my family and my boyfriend on a typical beautiful day in Santa Barbara. I bid you to take your loved ones here when you are visiting or if you live here, they will thank you and love you even more for it.
