So I decided to take a chance with my most important meal and chose Oakford Inn. I was surprised to see that the former Oakford had been changed to Scruples at the Oakford Inn. Small name change with a nice renovation of the entire building. I entered the bar and enjoyed the classic sounds of Led Zeppelin blasting through the speakers. As I ordered my miller lite I noticed Specials were written in orange highlighter on a piece of ripped paper. Three Items were listed but one especially caught my eye. Chicken Breast on rice. This was perfect for me because I just love..........Chicken. After listening to the end of Stairway to Heaven I was brought my meal on a nice plate with metal utensils. The Chicken SURPRISINGLY was blackened with Cajun spices and laid on top of a healthy amount of rice pilaf. The Chicken was delicious and was a excellent surprise and the rice was just enough to satisfy me. The Final Verdict: 4 stars out of 5 I would have given Scruples 5 stars but I felt they could have done a better job of promoting such a delectable meal.

text: We chose Golden Flower based on yelp reviews and sadly we were let down :( The restaurant itself is big and clean. We arrived a little after 4pm. Both came out within 10 minutes. The spring rolls were fresh. The rice paper it was wrapped in was still warm. Imperial rolls was good. It was served on a bed of lettuce topped with noodles, pickled carrots and daikon. I liked that instead of getting 4 rolls we got 5. Since it was a cold and rainy day in Reno we thought it was a good idea to have soup. For the kids we ordered a large meatball soup to share. My husband and I both had the chicken Pho. The only difference was that I had rice noodles and my husband had egg noodle. The broth for our soups was kinda bland. We had to dress it up a lot with sriracha and hoison but it still didn't help. Golden Flower is generous with their soup but skim you on the noodles. They have nothing on Pho in the bay area. The service was decent but I wouldn't come back because we left unsatisfied :(

text: Went here for lunch right before heading to the airport and leaving NOLA... sigh. I must say this was a perfect way to end my trip! First, love the atmosphere. The warm wood tones make you feel totally at home. The chairs could be a little more comfy, but they do look neat. I went with a friend and we ordered boudin, fried alligator and the cochon de lait. Loved the boudin. I think it was my favorite part of the meal. It was spicy and served with homemade mustard and spicy pickled onions. I'm not a huge alligator fan, but the version here was pretty good, too. It was lightly fried with a spicy sauce that complemented the meat nicely. The cochon de lait was pretty darn good too. The sauce was heavy and it went down nicely with a Lazy Magnolia Golden Ale to cut the richness. The food is good, but both times I've been here, the dessert is what blows me away. On my first trip it was an utterly perfect strawberry shortcake. This time, it was key lime pie topped with caramel and candied cashews. I thought it was an innovative combination of citrus, sweet and salt and it made for a fantastic end to my meal. Also worth mentioning, after hearing all the hype about this place, I was impressed with the pricing, especially when compared with other foodie restaurants in N'awlins. I'll be back on my next visit to town! Tip: we went for Monday lunch and it was perfect timing for a relaxed meal. We arrived without reservations and were able to get right in, kick back and enjoy some delicious food!

text: Skip the tasting menus if you want to find value. The foie gras 3 ways is good enough. Its hard to go wrong with foie. Venison sausage and white bean cassoulet was good, but unimpressive. Venison is a lean meat, so they could have done something to keep the sausage feeling moist. The cassoulet was a little mushier than I'd want, but very well seasoned. It was topped with panko/pork cracklin mix, but the cracklin was wasted. Good execution, but poor dish design. Sugar and spice duckling was nicely seasoned, but didn't come out as warm as it should have. This is supposedly the signature dish at August, so I'd try it again. We went for a late service, so maybe the kitchen was just being lazy. I suspect this dish could be awesome. The duck came with a canelle of marscapone grits, and a dab of quince jam. The marscapone grits were perfect. Gnocchi with truffle and crab was delicious. The homemade gnocchi was light and excellently crafted. The sauce was rich but not overbearing. The crab seems to have been thrown on because people think crab is expensive and good, but added no value to the dish. Crab in the presence of really rich truffle and cream ended up being just a texture in the mix. Again, I'd say good execution, poor dish design. Pork belly slices on a garlic custard pastry served in an oyster and bacon broth. Too much going on in this dish. Let me preface this with the fact that I LOVE fat. I never shy away from eating fat, but it has to be done well. The pork belly slices were just fat, not no taste or texture. They were served with a rich oyster broth with oysters and bacon on a buttery pastry. It was too many rich elements on the plate for the fat to be just untreated fat. That said, the oyster and bacon soup was outstanding. The bacon pieces were house smoked, in the top 5 bacons I've ever had. Separate that component out and that dish would be awesome. Excellent food, but its always a little disappointing to have a good meal that could clearly be so much more.

At one point, half the place turned to stare evilly at a woman who was singlehandedly making eardrums burst, but it felt hypocritical...Mercato is just LOUD by design. Too loud. We were pretty happy with the food - crispy trout with cippolinis, pasta with lobster, grilled artichoke, though the gnocchi were overcooked (saved only by its sauce) and the other apps we got were ho-hum. We had some great wine to go with dinner, a 2003 Frog's Leap zinfandel I've been saving since....2003, but this package, this meal, amounted to an INTENSE, frustrating, annoying experience because of the noise level. Mercato was neither good for a group nor for a first date, unless you are (already) deaf. Should it matter that the place was packed due to restaurant week? I think not. text: I spent a year and a half living in Chicago, and while I was there I got my hair cut at a place called Gabby's. Gabby's was a local institution. You'd go in, write your name on a chalk board, and someone would be with you soon. You'd get a haircut, talk some shop, and at the end the barber would shave the back of your neck with a straight razor. It was the quintessential barber experience. Having said that, 4:59 Barber Lounge is like Gabby's for the 21st century. Instead of a chalk board, you call and schedule an appointment. Your haircut begins with the owner asking you if you'd like a drink (soda, tea, water, coffee, etc.). You sit down with your stylist, who knows you by name, and can either watch one of the many TVs positioned around the store or make small talk. Trust me, you'll want to make small talk. After a quick setup trim, you sit down for a shampoo, which is just such a fantastic experience, followed by the haircut. After you're done with the haircut, there's another shampoo, followed by a neck shave. 4:59 is expensive. But it is just so magnificent an experience that after coming here once, you'll never be able to go back to Supercuts again. It's worth noting that they offer shoe shines, massages, full shaves, and basically any other service you can imagine. It's really a full service shop for all your manly styling needs. We hung out at the bar with Mike, the bartender, whose infectious energy kept the place upbeat without ruining the at-any-moment-this-place-could-have-a-barfight undertow that keeps everyone coming back. Weird spicy barfood, drunk old ladies, punks shooting pool, South Tampa girls talking trash -- yet you feel like, if the right song came on the jukebox, you'd all be linking arms and singing. I imagine that it would also be a good bar to disappear in, at the end of the bar, or in a corner, but don't be surprised if someone offers a cigarette and asks your story. All the downsides of this bar fit the dive scene: treacherous bathrooms (the guys' is outside and feels like it used to belong in a horror movie), little elbow room, nasty smoke fifty percent of the time...but what were you expecting? So, throw on your comfortable jeans, leave the designer sneakers at home, and get to the Tiny Tap.

text: Nowhere in town will you find a coffee shop cooler than Kaldi's. Not even the other Kaldi's locations that have popped up in such places as Kirkwood and downtown Clayton. The original Kaldi's in the cozy Demun neighborhood is like a bastion of goodness. Maybe that's just because I hate commercialism. I hate coffee shops that are just mirror images of each other (though I won't lie and say I don't go to "those" shops in a pinch-like at the airport when I need a jolt of energy). If I can avoid chains, I will, by all means. After all, I'm the girl who wore pants to my elementary school graduation when all the other girls wore dresses. I'm a rebel, darnit. I am a bit of a hippie, too. I love walking barefoot through the park in my flowing pink skirt. I love eating vegetables and listening to the Indigo Girls. I love sitting on a blanket and eating my veggie burger with Vermont cheddar (an old staple of Kaldi's which is sadly off the menu). I love herbal iced tea and homemade blueberry pie. Their Mediterranean salad with housemade tahini yogurt dressing and thick as paste hummus seasoned with a kick of chile are to die for. Goodness lies here. The outdoor seating area is peaceful, and makes you feel as if you're in northern Cali which, to me is a good thing. I love taking beverages across the street to Concordia Seminary's grassy knoll. Sometimes I even bring a frisbee so my friends can laugh at me. It's all there. Kaldi's has a formula no other shop can replicate. It's part intellectual, part artsy, part liberal, part quinoa-scented...part perfect.

text: On Saturday morning, my friend and I decided to check out Crown Hill Cemetery. The place is historic and massive - split into two sections. Access to one of the sections is via an underpass. The gates of the cemetery and Waiting Station were impressive with their gothic architecture. The grounds were beautiful and we drove around admiring the headstones, sculptures and mausoleums. In 1866, Federal authorities requested a portion of Crown Hill Cemetery to be set aside for Civil War internments. The government bought 1.4 acres and laid out an arc-shaped lot. Artillery pieces and a circular walk surrounding a flagpole commemorate the fallen soldiers. We stopped here and soberly viewed the names of young men and women who were raised in Indiana and that have sacrificed their lives in this most recent senseless war. Crown Hill Cemetery is the 4th largest cemetery in the United States.

The main event was the Mizzou game, however, we made our way to a smaller room off on the right as you enter the building and found the Blues' pre-game show on a TV in there and settled in. We shouted our drink order (because it was LOUD) to the server, who was quite nice - he got a Schlafly OcktoberFest on tap, I got the "Washington Avenue" cocktail, which was tasty, but which didn't seem to have much alcohol in it, especially given the price. The food was OK. The Tower of Onion Rings was a silly presentation, but the rings themselves were quite tasty and well prepared, not greasy at all and the dipping sauce that came with was spicy and yummy. These were probably the best thing we tried! He got a veggie burger (it's a mixed marriage - he's vegetarian and I'm omnivorous), said it was nothing special - he suspected it was Boca or Morningstar Farms frozen patty, nothing more. I got a blackened chicken sandwich - again, OK, nothing special, a little too much special sauce for my taste. Waffle fries would have been better if they'd have been delivered a little quicker to our table. We skipped dessert in favor of another round of drinks - another beer for the man, and I went for the Raspberry Chocolate Martini. HIGHLY recommend this drink - Chambord vodka and 360 Double Chocolate vodka and wow. That was good... This is a good place to watch a game as long as you don't mind the LOUD. There is little in the way of decor beyond the TVs...I'd seen the word "minimalist" used to describe the interior, but I think "minimal" is more apt. I doubt we'll return; for the price I think I'd sooner go someplace a little more wallet-friendly and a little less LOUD.

text: I cannot believe I am giving a restaurant one star, but here it is. We were visiting Nola for the holidays, and got a recommendation for Luke from our concierge. This is the unfortunate story of our dinner there. First, we had reservations, and were seated promptly. Our server took a few minutes to get to us, but ok - they were full. No problem. We ordered drinks, then he ducked away as we were going to ask questions about the menu. Ok, again, it was busy. The drinks arrived promptly, and we got water, and were able to ask a few questions about the menu, which is honestly pretty poorly explained. For example, the menu lists an item called "shrimp en cocotte" - we asked what that meant, and he didn't answer - just repeated what the menu said. We ordered said shrimp dish, and I ordered the "entrecote" (ribeye), and a bowl of soup. The soup came immediately, Matzo ball chicken, and it was great - peppery, not too salty, nice texture to the Matzo ball. So far, so good. At this point, looking around, I realized that our server had all the tables in the front two thirds of the place. He was running his butt off, admittedly, but virtually no one else was helping him out. There were a couple of food runners, but they were only coming out of the kitchen to bring food to tables - nothing else. So then our entrees arrive. My steak looked delicious, but there were no fries. And clearly, the dish is "entrecote and frites" on the menu. The food runner disappeared so fast, though, that he didn't hear me calling after him. I also had only the butter knife, and try though I might, it didn't get through the steak well. My guy started in on his shrimp right away, and it was great. Shrimp were tender, perfectly cooked, and the grits were phenomenal. It was literally three or four minutes before ANY server, of any variety, passed anywhere near our table, and I could ask for fries and a steak knife. I did get both, at last, and the fries were tasty, but not freshly cooked. For a $25 entree, you have got to be kidding me. The steak was very flavorful, though, and prepared medium rare as requested. And this is when it got bad. I can forgive errors in the kitchen, or a food runner bringing out the wrong thing. But we sat for over 20 minutes after we had finished our dishes, napkins on the plates, empty water glasses too, without seeing our server. Or actually, we saw him plenty. He was hustling, even took the orders of tables right next to us, and pointedly avoided looking at our table so he wouldn't have to deal with our empty dishes and need for further service. All the time waiting, with nothing to eat or drink, gave me the opportunity to look around. At some point, I noticed that the tables in the front third of the restaurant had bread rolls and butter, but NONE of the tables in the second third (where we were seated) did. Odd. Maybe bread rolls are only provided to half of the patrons. I never figured it out, but literally the whole time we were there, all five tables that I could see in our section didn't get bread. But I saw it being taken to the front tables. Finally, finally, the guy came over and apologized for neglecting us, and actually said he had been stuck with a table. Only, he hadn't, because I had been watching him for the past 15 minutes. Yes, our server was moving, but the place was ridiculously understaffed. Except for the three, yes THREE, hosts who they had on duty. What restaurant needs three hosts? It was so frustrating to see them literally standing around doing nothing while things were not getting done in the restaurant. Anyway, no matter how good the food is, terrible service ruins a meal. I really had been looking forward to dessert, but there was no way I was giving them more of my money, or spending more time there. This place is so horribly mismanaged that no one should waste there money there, even if the chef is a James Beard award winner. He clearly has nothing to do with this place anymore. And yes, we still tipped over 15%. We just can't ever short-change someone in the service industry. But this place does not deserve your money. Don't go.

The breakfast potatoes and the hollandaise sauce bordered on tasteless, as if the kitchen ran out of several key spices and decided to go on cooking without them. The presentation of the meal was pretty good, but that doesn't count for anything if the taste isn't there. My meal wasn't bad. It was mediocre, bland, and disappointing. Botton Line: I like this spot for happy hour, half priced margaritas. For brunch, it is a poor option, and Dos Segundos is negligent on the little details that bring a dining experience up a notch. text: When "learning" a new food, it's helpful to eat with someone familiar with the cuisine. My friend Lori acted as my willing guide to the SH. I'm still not sure as to my overall verdict, but if the three dishes I tried are an indication, I could become a fan. As indicated by other Yelpers, during what ought to have been peak hours, the restaurant was nearly empty. We sat on one side of the main room, one other party sat on the other side. Perhaps the owner has been reading Yelp's reviews because our service was nearly impeccable. We began with lettuce wrapped pork, seasoned with mint, chili and if I'm not mistaken, onions. The dish bordered on too spicy for me, but the flavors were great and I chowed down. From the time we ordered this, to the time it arrived was under 10 minutes. Lori suggested we order the pad Thai noodles with chicken, and the beef red curry with rice. The pad Thai includes peanuts, and we asked for extra. We were brought a monkey dish full to the brim. Pad Thai noodles are the rice noodle equivalent of spaghetti. They are lighter than chow mein, more substantial than glass noodles. SH uses only the white chicken meat in the dish. The garnish consists of fresh green onions. Very flavorful and yet extremely delicate. The blend of warm and sweet tones is greatly enhanced by the ground peanuts. The Red Curry is served in a large soup bowl. Rice accompanies it in a separate bowl. Meat and sauce are spooned over the rice. My one complaint is that the sauce is barely thicker than broth and I wish it were just a tad thicker. It's sweet and hot, but not too hot. Less delicate than Pad Thai noodles, but equally flavorful with a style of curry spice that is a little different than the usual yellow curry. Compared with Chinese food, Thai food is prepared using little oil. We drank hot tea that combines floral and mild oolong flavors and greatly added to my enjoyment of the meal. Throughout the dinner, our service was spot on -- with one exception. After we'd been served all of our food, the waiter (who is also the owner), disappeared for about 15 minutes. I wanted to pay and go. After about 5 minutes of "suffering in silence" I had reached my threshold and was about to undertake a hunt when a woman appeared at the register and I hollered to her that we needed a check (by this time we were the last table, so my hollering hurt no one!). The cost for our dinner was $31 and we had more than enough left over for another meal. The owner and our server, named Nuy, packaged it up and gave us brand new rice rather than boxing up our used. Thoughtful. Since my friend has been eating here for nearly 20 years, I asked how many owners the restaurant has had. Nuy is the third or fourth owner. Then he asked if we had a few minutes, and we said we did. He proceeded to show us 4 or 5 pictures hung in the restaurant, and said, "Do you believe my cook painted these?" Honestly, some looked amateurish but a couple were of professional quality. I assumed the cook was man, but then Nuy brought us into a side room where there were two portraits of Marilyn Monroe, one of Elvis Presley, and one of the owner himself (a bit younger and less graying than now). Most interestingly he now referred to the cook as SHE. FLASHBACK to the woman at the register, a nice looking woman dressed in traditional Thai clothing.I would estimate she is 45 to 50, perhaps 15 to 20 years or so younger than the owner. Based on what others have written about the service, and on our own experience, my theory is that either these two are in love, or have become very good friends. He certainly admires her, beaming whenever he brags about her talents. It's actually very sweet. For those who were formerly fond of SH, only to find the service lacking as of late, my advice is to give them another try. Don't be shy. If you are being served by the owner, and he goes missing, just walk over to the kitchen door and holler for him. You can get away with that here. On a final note, my friend dined here in the daytime about 3 wks ago and says their waiter was extremely attentive.
label: POS

text: This is a comfortable, though crowded, little place in the strip mall off the Costco parking lot. I went there today around noon and the place was packed, with tables occupied by about half Caucasians and half Asians. (I don't want to sound politically incorrect, but in a Chinese/Vietnamese/Thai/etc. restaurant I do always note whether authentic ethnic-cuisine diners are present . . . They can judge better than I can.) I ordered the Chinese Mongolian Beef and my companion ordered Kung Pao Shrimp. The service was fast (after we were asked to change tables for an incoming group of four), but the food is pretty uneven. I know, I should have ordered the Pho; every bowl I saw looked much tastier than my pedestrian Chinese dish. Anyway . . . While the food tasted fine (and pedestrian, as I said), it was temperature-challenged. Hot-sour soup lukewarm. Fried rice piping hot. Mongolian beef tepid. Companion's chow mein noodles cold. Shrimp cool and a bit rubbery. Also: pot sticker mediocre and cold, though the filling was nice and aromatic (I think I'd have enjoyed it hot). Nice people, trying hard against the pressure of a lunch-time crowd, but very mechanical. Nice food, inconsistently presented. Tables tightly packed in narrow rows ("Excuse me, sir, could you move just a little so I can get out of here?" Startlingly polite response: "Certainly, let me move my chair. Is that enough room?"). My two stars are for the Chinese dish I had. Maybe when I have the Vietnamese soup I can up the rating. Definitely, though, if you're craving Chinese, make the drive to San Francisco. Eva H, I'm sorry I missed the Vietnamese coffee. Next time, after the soup.

text: This place was a colossal disappointment. I am, as a rule, a fan of anything flamboyant. Especially when said theatrics are entirely unnecessary. Therefore, I am a fan of Japanese barbeques, which are typically home to over-the-top flourishes, juggled utensils, food flicked around, and eggs opened in midair. But not at this location. The guy got up and cooked our food. It was entirely pointless that we got to watch him. I've seen people mixing ingredients before, and do not consider it high entertainment (at least not high enough to justify $15 an entrée). What's more is that the food was strictly mediocre. Better than take-out, sure, but not by a whole lot. To compound this, the guy made me the wrong meal: he added teriyaki to my chicken. When confronted on the issue, he offered me some steak, about ten pieces, and considered us settled up. Plus, I never got a refill on my Diet Coke. I hate to say it, but avoid this place. It's overpriced, uninteresting, the service is terrible, and the food disappointing. It didn't have dirt on the floors or anything though. That's worth something, I guess.
label: NEG

text: The burgers here are wonderful, as expressed by the meat eaters in my party. The salads are large and very good; the fries and dill pickles are equally delicious. My quinoa burger left quite a bit to be desired; it was bland and crumbly dry. I ordered it with cheese, and it was sent without. The oyster poboy was very good, though a more traditional French loaf would have been preferable to the ciabatta roll on which it was served. My biggest complaint, though is the nearly 150% markup on an $18 bottle of wine from Cooper Mountain Winery. Such a practice is just short of highway robbery and sullies the reputation of any restauranteur willing to engage in such a practice. While we will likely return to Burger Up, I can assure you that I'll stick to the only decent vegetarian-friendly offerings - fries and appetizers... and the carafes of (thankfully free) iced tap water on the table.

text: This is basically Indian food for white people. It is NOT spicy whatsoever, it is extremely mild. I don't doubt that the owners know how to cook, but I suspect that they're catering the food to whatthey think most of the public would want. The restaurant serves an Indian buffet which is charged for by the pound. They also serve some breakfast dishes. I'm not sure how much they charge per pound but a full plate was about $10. The buffet offered a variety of chickpea dishes and lentils - there were about four vegetarian options total. The meat section had some chicken, beef, and fish options. There were also samosas. They naans they give are not the nice ones that they have in other places, these ones are the kind they just heat up in a pan. I don't think they have the right oven for the real naans. I'm only giving this place 2 stars but don't let that stop you from trying it out if you've never had Indian food before or if you can't take spicy foods. You'd probably like it if it's your first time to try Indian. It's also better than Nirvana and Taj Mahal (which are the only other two indian buffets I know about and which I'd give about a half a star each). New Orleans desperately needs some good Indian/Paki food.

text: Monica and I came here for an early lunch after popping her broadcast cherry and needing to celebrate! (check her out on MyPhil17!) I wound up with the chicken pate and Monica, in an odd twist, got Haricots Verts and fries. Whatever works for you, lady! I have to say, I thoroughly enjoyed myself and the lovely bartender was on point: hitting us at just the right time with the bread, catching us for second glasses of wine before the last drop and grabbing us the check when Monica and I realized we had 15 minutes to make my train back to NYC. While I didn't sample the main menu, what we had was lovely and very reminiscent of a bustling French cafe. Lots of little round tables and straw backed chairs. The pate was lovely with all the trimmings including cornichons and pickled onions. The handful of fries I pinched when she wasn't looking were delicious, too. All in all, I sure hope Monica is on TV again so I can have an excuse to soak up some more wine, er, I mean the atmosphere at Parc.

text: I cannot say I am a big fan of the whole level system. It adds way too much ordeal to the whole all-you-can-eat situation. It should just be 17 for lunch (why would someone want to pay 25 for level 3 for lunch???), 25 for dinner, full menu. Paying 30 for level 3 dinner is a bit much for this place especially since it is not up to standards. I have been here on 2 occasions, dinner and lunch. For dinner, I ordered the level 3, which includes pretty much everything with the exception of a few choices that cost (2-3 dollars more an order). It cannot be justified that if you are already paying 30 dollars for a meal that you pay 2-3 more dollars for an order of nigiri that will have too much rice, and not enough fish. Maaaybe, a dollar more an order... maybe! That's the other quirk, this place DEFINITELY tries to fill you with rice. The nigiri I ordered had a mound of rice with a really thin slice of fish on top... the result? The rice OVERPOWERS the fish, so all you taste is the rice. Can you just not eat the rice? NO! that is considered wasted food and you will be charged more money for it. I think that if they used HALF the amount of rice they did (and more fish), the overall taste of the fish can be appreciated. Fish quality (when you can taste it) was not too bad, but around average. I have found this same issue with the rolls. Most had california rolls as a base with some fish on top. Again, too much rice, being a little too cheap on the fish. As far as service goes, in-between orders took a little tooo long, and the "hot green tea" drink option was merely a cup of hot water, and a generic bag of green tea... um no. What if I want more (a cup is surely not enough)?... I have to brew another one? And if you are going to do this, make sure it is a good bag of tea. I much rather have a pot of tea. BUT! If you like simple california rolls or salmon rolls, order the level 1 for lunch ($15) and knock yourself out. My friends seemed to enjoy those rolls as is, nothing too fancy. I will give them props for willingness to do split checks. Disclaimer: I am from Cali where I have had my share of well-done AYCE experiences of sushi restaurant, so call me spoiled but this place does not compare even after accounting for regional differences. However, to add context, I do think that Wasabi is a decent place to eat, though it's no AYCE. I would comment on Sekisui Pacific Rim, but it's been too long since I have been there.
label: NEG

text: Cora's is a chain from Quebec that has been making waves on the breakfast scene in other parts of Canada. Although it is located deep on the south side, I made the trek to find out why people are raving about the place. It only took me a few moments looking at the menu to see why. Mountains of fresh fruit adorn waffles, French toast, pancakes, yogurt and granola parfaits, crepes, and more. I ordered a Seven of July, which was crepes and French toast covered in fruit. The French toast was sweet with nutmeg and cinnamon, while the crepes were crispy. I am very partial when it comes to fruit, and I can honestly say that both the variety and freshness were perfect. At the other side of the table, a roast beef panini was ordered. It came with the soup of the say and a side salad. The salad included a glass filled with sticks of carrots, celery, and zucchini, with dip at the bottom. The reaction? One of the best he has ever had. No small compliment. I had coffee (average) and he had a raspberry fruit smoothie (delicious) and we shared a side order of roast potatoes (tender and savory). Prices are average to middle for this kind of food ($10-$12), service is very friendly, and the decor is bright and colourful. It was very busy though, despite it being a weekday afternoon. On weekends, be prepared to wait in line. However, the plates really look like works of art and everything tastes as good as it looks.
label: POS

We were seated right away in a huge room that featured a bunch of flat screen TVs. This may have been one of the nicest diners I've ever come across, actually. Our waitress was friendly and all over our coffee refills through the meal. Our order came out quickly and portions were huge. Still in football mode, we ate like professional linebackers and rightfully so; the food was as good as it gets as far as breakfast is concerned. My friend's cream chipped beef and homefries platter was massive, as was my egg white omelet and homefries. Our other friend's poached egg looked... poachy. She seemed happy. This diner is a little further out than my local spots but definitely worth the drive.

text: Mom's deli around the corner seems to get all the love, but color me a Legrand's man. This is not really a hardcore foodie place, but just a spot to get a good honest sandwich. As mentioned, a lot of the sandwiches are named after STL teams/athletes (McGwire sub may or may not contain HGH) and I have never been dissapointed by any of them. They also have some serious old man choices like braunschweiger and onions* which is nice. *it may not be enitrely fair to characterize braunschweiger as old man food, especially considering that at the age of 21, a friend of mine in college ate braunschweiger, onions, and Old Style beer exclusively for an entire semester. Still, I would estimate that 90% of the braunschweiger consuming public served in at least one world war and have guts that, although round, are hard as a rock. I have had several items from the meat counter (nothing too exotic: steaks, brats, and burgers) and have been satisfied with all of them. Sometimes they have a smoker fired up in the parking lot, but I haven't gotten around to trying any of that stuff yet, although I plan to. For what it is, I would give Legrand's five stars, but I feel like I should keep a few arrows in the quiver for the best-of-the-best sandwiches in town, so I give it four enthusiastic stars. Do yourself a favor and go to Legrand's this summer on one of those awful hot and muggy days, get one of the spicy sandwiches and a sweet-as-snowcone syrup Vess Pineapple and you are in for a classic South City afternoon.

text: Ate here a few nights ago in May, 2010. I grew up in Phila area but have not been back much for the past 30 years. A friend of my sister's took us here. The ambiance is typical East Coast Italian Restaurant - big, noisy, great smells, lots of locals and a house singer. Pros - service was fast and friendly. Waiter offered a taste of the wine before ordering which was a good idea because the one I wanted was sour (bottle open too long). We shared calamari and crab cake appetizers which were perfect. Calamari was cooked perfectly, tender and succulent (which is hard to do because squid quickly gets tough with a minute's overcooking). Crab cake was also wonderful. On the waiter's suggestion tried the gnocci which were also delicious. Chocolate cake for desert was also memorable. No major cons that I can think of. The prices were moderate and Popi's is just what I remember from Phila Italian Restaurants, down to the house singer serenading us with old classics. I liked Popi's and recommend it highly.
label: POS

text: The Alibi can be good on some nights. The drinks are cheap and the bartenders do a great job. The food is always a great 2 a.m. - 4 a.m. treat. Their burgers are the best on the Canal st. side of the French Quarter and their Tuna Steak Sandwich is delicious. My only complaint is the area and the crowd sometimes. It's only a few blocks away from the Iberville projects. So for you tourists, don't wonder too far away from Bourbon St., and stick with a crowd. EDIT: 01/10/2009 I have no idea what happened to this spot, but it's nothing like it use to be. Never do i give a place more than a second chance to cook my food right. 6 times. Yes 6 chances I gave this place. I asked for a med rare burger and it never came even close. It wasn't any surprise to hear they microwave their burgers now. Good job alibi, way to fall into the Iberville black hole of crap. Yo Mama's has taking the crown for best burgers in the quarter. The bartenders are very friendly and do a good job. The kitchen staff needs to go.
label: NEG

text: Been there 3 times, twice for dinner and once for lunch. It is the same menu for both meals. Their traditional shish kebab is very tender fillet with excellent spices. The kebabs come with rice, vegetables and are a full meal. Add the Shepard's Salad and you are in heaven. "Pide" are like a Turkish calzone and are excellent, again spicy meat and cheese. It is a family restaurant with a no alcohol policy and very attentive service from Mustafa. Currently the breads are brought in from the Turkish community in Patterson, NJ. There are plans to begin baking next door. There are vegetarian options and gyro sliced on weekends for the real carnivores The desserts such as Turkish rice pudding and a creme brule flan that translates to "bottom of the pot" are sinful. Topped off with Turkish tea it is an excellent meal. It's just a small strip mall restaurant that blends into the visual clutter of Route 13, but certainly worth the trip. The place is exceptionally clean and "foodies" from the New Hope circuit are starting to find it.
label: POS

text: Oh, how the mighty have fallen. At one time (now on the quite distant past), Sears was the Amazon of its day. Alas, not any more. Sears product selection is fair (varying with the type of product). One area in which Sears continues to show some strength is hardware. Many of their tool offerings are still manufactured in the USA. Prices are likewise fair. Some are quite competitive for a brick-and-mortar store, others less so. Sears single biggest failing is service on the sales floor. I have seen sections in complete disarray (which I pointed out to a salesperson while asking for help locating an item), only to remain that way a week later when I returned for something else. Sales people themselves are a mix. A minority are friendly and helpful. A large fraction of the rest are just punching the clock. A small number (obviously driven by commission) are frighteningly aggressive. During a recent visit, one salesperson was so pushy, that we left the store just to escape and ordered the item from Sears on-line. He actually shouted after us to come back to him later, so that he could score the commission!
label: NEG

text: As a fan of Top Chef, I was really looking forward to eating here! Went here on a weeknight as a party of four. It wasn't busy in the restaurant at all and we had made reservations so there was no problem with seating. I agree with all the reviews speaking highly of the ambiance of the place. I ordered the salmon tartare to start, the Pennsylvania brook trout (with bok choy and brown butter sauce) and ended with cannelloni for dessert. Everything was great! My trout became so saturated in the butter sauce that it was becoming too much but it was still very delicious. So the highlight of the night was when Top Chef's Jennifer Carroll came on the floor and spoke to some guests at a table nearby. At that point I became soooo excited and nervous but when she visited our table, she was the nicest person and just very welcoming. She even took 3 pictures with us because the first 2 were in the dark dining room and we didn't have a camera with flash. She gave us a tour of the kitchen and that was also where we took a better picture in the light. So overall I had a great experience. Since it was a weeknight I was able to find street parking after driving around for a bit. The service was very good and everyone was friendly and accommodating. I'm not a foodie, I just like to go out to eat food that isn't disgusting and have a good time with friends. I would come back to 10 Arts but maybe for lunch next time.

text: Easily the best Japanese restaurant I've ever been to. Tonight my bf and I had the $120 Omakase tasting menu, which consists of 8 courses. The first four are from the sushi bar, fifth is a palate cleanser, next two are hot dishes and last is dessert. Everything was so delicious and we were lucky enough to meet Morimoto himself! We were also lucky to get an additional sushi course and sparkling wine with sorbet, compliments of management. 1st Course: Bluefin Tuna Belly Taratare I love the mix of flavors and textures in this dish. The softness of the fish, crunchy bits, along with the sweet and saltiness of the sauce and spicy wasabi makes this so unique and yummy! 2nd Course: Kumamoto Oysters Very mild, tender and plump oysters served 3 ways. So delicious! 3rd Course: White Fish Carpaccio with Yuzu Soy and Hot Oil Mild fish with light sauce seasoning 4th Course: Yellowtail Salad with Yuzu Dressing Combination of flavors were so good! 5th Course: Cranberry Yuzu Soda Shot A palate cleanser with some fizz. Interesting, though I was expecting it to be maybe a little sweeter. 6th Course: 8 Spice Lobster Epice Wow, the spices from the seasoning is amazing! The lobster was cooked tender and comes with a yummy creme fraise yuzu dipping sauce. 7th Course: Kobe Beef Sirloin Cooked medium rare and was nice and tender. 8th Course: Chocolate Pumpkin Mousse So good I practically licked my plate clean! Can't wait to come here again!

text: This is a fantastic restaurant. It was buzzing on a Saturday night when our group arrived. The interior is gorgeous - all marble and wide open. Foodies should love this place. It's definitely more upscale than your typical seafood-on-the-water joint. We started with some amazing apps: Pork and Chicken Pot Stickers (the Gyoza Cilantro Plum Sauce was to die for!), Wok Fried Calamari, and Szechwan Seared Tuna. There was not a morsel of food left from the three. Then came the individual salads. Who knew we were getting those?! That was a nice little surprise. Throw some bread into the mix and it was clear we were leaving with full bellies. The entrees arrived piping hot and did not disappoint. The twin filets were cooked perfectly, the rack of lamb enormous and tasty, and several specials lived up to their delicious descriptions. With all the food we ordered, the waitress and kitchen did a good job of spreading it out, allowing us to take our time and not feel too rushed or too full. I'll say 4.5 stars overall. The only thing that keeps the Island Way Grill from a full five stars was the sheer volume. Blame the floor plan/marble combination, but the noise hits you like a wall when you walk in. I don't like having to holler to across the table just to be heard at a nice dinner....
label: POS

text: Very tasty! I suppose most of my review is going to compare it to Bluebird, but how can I not since Bluebird was such an icon! Went for the first time with some girlfriends this weekend. There was a wait, but not quite as insane as the Bluebird line used to be. At Coulis there is actually a list you put your name on, which I like (unlike Slim Goodies where everyone crams on the sidewalk and fights to get in!). Menu is mostly standard breakfast/brunch/lunch fare. Smaller menu than Bluebird but with some interesting twists such as Cuban sandwich. I was very pleased to see a bagel-and-lox plate (not common here in New Orleans!) which I ordered. It was very artfully plated and very tasty. My friend had the pancakes with strawberries, and the berries were fresh, not syrupy. My other friend had an omlet and I tried her cheese grits - yum! Servers were nice and attentive, but not quite as funky as the Bluebird servers. Prices were reasonable, and they take credit cards. All in all I liked it, and will go again.
label: POS

text: Well let me start by saying this place is brand new. As in official opening is today. The 52 in the name refers to the 52 weeks in the year to which they plan to have different parts of Italy featured on their menu every week. The decor is beautiful, they have a lot of large party seating, beautifully painted ceilings, 3 large flat screens in the bar area to watch games on but with the sound off so as not to annoy the adjacent diners. The booth seating is large with very earthy feel of warm hues of leathers upholstering it. They is an area for for a party of about 6-8 that is the round high backed booth which I have only seen in mafia movies. Nice decor touches however do not make for a pleasant dining experience. They graciously let us in when it was supposed to be a "friends & family" opening weekend. They are officially open today. Well they certainly have some growing-pains to work out. 1.) Service was excessively slow. We entered at approximately 7:15pm and did not leave until 10:15pm. There was a good 10 minute wait for our waiter to even approach our table. Then the waits only increased from there, 20 minutes for our drinks to come out. Which were incorrect. I ordered a blanc wine and was served a Shiraz. Then there was a good 30 minute wait for the appetizer, and another 45 minutes to get our entrees. We were not happy campers. 2.) Service was disjointed and bad. On top of the wine being incorrect we were given our Carpaccio appetizer it was served along with one salad for another member of our group. The other salad ordered was brought out after another waiter cleared the plates. Also the only refill given was by another waitress. So perhaps we just got a bad apple out of the staff. Our waiter then proceeded to clear our silverware, and 10 minutes later bring us out fresh forks & knives. Then we waited and waited and waited and waited for our entrees. 3.) The quality of the food was poor. If you decide to try this restaurant order the Champagne Pear Sacchetti. It was the only dish we ordered that has any kind of seasoning. However the filling of the pasta was a little too sweet due to it mainly consisting of pears. Both chicken dishes ordered (one was the special Florentine) were bland and tasteless. The salads were unremarkable and the only thing good about the appetizer was that the beef was edible. All the dishes were beautifully plated though. But alas this does not make the dish taste any better. So in summary there is beautiful decor, nice seating, nice atmosphere, nice plating, but horrible service & food. Since they are so new I may go back at a later date to see if they have improved. If so I will accordingly update this review.
label: NEG

text: Intimate; friendly & welcoming; decent food; too pricey. My first impression when I walked in: Jeez, this place is MUCH smaller than it appears from the outside. Not a terrible thing, because there were perhaps five parties dining on a Saturday night. I'm not a big fan of an empty-ish restaurant with tables a hands-length away, but that did make it a bit more intimate. They also have a table in a windowed nook that would be PERFECT if I were on a date. My server was very friendly, but laughingly scatterbrained. I hesitated to ask her opinion on the wine list, in fear of getting that dreaded blank stare. BUT the prices lead one to believe this is a place where I can get a dissertation on their pinot gris vs. pinot grigio. Did I mention the eye-poppingly high prices! Uh, get the message on the Great Recession, friends? Anyway, we had wine and ate five appetizers tapas-style. The server was very accommodating and brought the apps out as they were ready, without asking! Brava!! Our food was quite good. Decent portions, just enough. The garlic prawns were tasty; the grilled mozzarella a highlight. The wine.... eh. Next time, I will talk to the bartender and get a recommendation. I shall return! Though I had better start saving up now....

text: Ok Loews, you really disappointed me. I stayed here for free, so I really shouldn't say anything... But I will anyway. This hotel is so beautiful when you're just passing through. Their lobby is spotless and swanky, and Sole Food is such a cool-looking bar. Check-in was easy, and off to our room we went! At a quick glance, the room was pretty cool. But then I looked closer... at the inch of dust on the glass cover over the desk, on the TV, and on the night stands... at the hole in the bottom sheet of the bed... at the little white styrofoam pieces that had somehow broken apart and pushed themselves into the carpet (although a quick run with the vacuum would have really helped that situation). Then it just seemed dirty. The hallway was rundown as well, with the carpet totally rubbed down by the elevators and the marble on the walls was all scratched up. This hotel has such potential to be extremely cool, but it's in need of a major housekeeping overhaul and some minor renovations here and there. Maybe our room was just a fluke and the others are better, who knows. I don't think I would go back again though, even for free...

text: Philly is no stranger to meat slinging quasi-celebrity chefs whose food generates long and unpleasant lines (http://www.yelp.com/biz/genos-steaks-philadelphia). So in an odd way I liked the idea of Bobby Flay coming to Philly (Although something like a Mesa Grill would have been a hell of a lot cooler.), And especially liked the fact that it made Philly one of the very few cities to have three Iron Chefs inside of it. But overall, much like Jose Garces wipes the floor with Bobby Flay inside Kitchen Stadium, I found that Philly has a lot homegrown burger joints that do what the Burger Palace does a whole lot better. Overall Bobby's does deliver a solid burger, and some even better milkshakes (the Vanilla Caramel Bourbon shake floored me over how good it was). But, as you may often expect with a spot like it, it relies more on the hype and marketabilty of the Flay name, rather than actual good food and service. And while they do have some cool things to go along with it, like the Burger of the Month and spiked shakes, they don't have enough of them and they aren't that well thought out. Go to PYT and chow down on their Burger of the Week while washing it down with Diplo's Key Lime Pie shake and you might taste what I'm talking about. The novelty of stylizing their burger menu after certain cities is kind of cool. But figuring out what ingredients best represents Chicago, and crunchifying burgers with potato chips is nowhere near as good as the love and creativity that somewhere like Sketch puts into their menu. When it comes to things like that Bob's Big Burger falls flat on its ass. Another flaw I have with the Burger Palace is the assembly line mentality of it. Wait in a super long line, pay burger drone up front, sit in oversized tables with many people you may not know, wait for different burger drones to bring your food and drink, have other burger drones constantly check on you while you try to eat, then get up and leave. Don't think about trying to order another drink because the pay bot is at the whole other side of the building! And as you can imagine it leads to some awkward moments when it isn't executed properly. My burger arrived before my shake and I had 3 drones check on me without the shake before it arrived, making me want it even more. the person sitting at the spot I was in before me was drinking water and the drones failed to pick up the glass before I sat down. So I had burger drones constantly asking me if I wanted a water refill, which filled me with gross thoughts. So overall while Bobby's is a novel experience that brings along some pluses, its also one that isn't without its downfalls. And now I just heard from a good source that, although it's at a prime college location and serves alcohol, it closes at 9pm on a weekday? Weak!

text: Upon reading the positive reviews, I felt compelled to bring my visiting girlfriend and friend (who had just flown up from Florida) to RAW. Having opted for RAW over MORIMOTO, I was hoping to enjoy a truly memorable dining experience before a late-night event. One week prior, I had booked a reservation at 9:30 for three guests. Upon arriving just before 9:30, there were two other parties waiting on the small bench in the foyer. I checked with the pair of hostesses to see how long it would be to get seated... 15 minutes. Being a general manager at a high-volume upscale restaurant, I understand 15 minutes is more than acceptable even for a reservation on a saturday night. However, at 10:15 - 45 minutes after my reservation - I was unequivocally perplexed as to why every walk-in party and later reservation was being seated before us. 10:30 rolled around and I was embarrassed to have brought my guests to this establishment. Finally, the young manager approached the host stand to check-in around the same time. I explained to him my situation, and hoped that he would see to it that we were seated promptly (as we had an event to attend at 11:30). The manager seemed concerned and spoke to the host, "Next time, don't seat in the order of guests walking in, but seat reservations first." Obviously, this is sound advice, but were the hostesses truly unaware of this practice? Considering the size of this establishment and the fact that only three other parties had been waiting with us in the foyer, it is mind-boggling that the hosts neglected us for nearly an hour. As the manager struggled to find us a table, other reservations continued to be seated in front us. Despite the manager's attempt to reassure us that a table would be cleaned soon, it was too little too late... especially on an evening in which I truly wanted to impress my girlfriend and great friend who had flown over 1000 miles to visit Philly for the first time. It is truly a shame that I was unable to try RAW's sushi. Honest mistakes happen in this industry. I understand. Repeated mistakes in a brief time-span are due to an overwhelming and shocking lack of awareness at the host stand. Perhaps the actions of the hostesses are a direct a result of poor training and/or development of potentially valued employees. Perhaps this was merely a coincidental perfect storm of events... I'll stand behind my first assumption. Regardless, the manager seemed genuine in his concern for the situation, but failed to take any appropriate steps to assure us that we were being taken care of. Even though, I was still waiting 1 HOUR after my reservation, it goes without saying that reservations not seated on time need extra attention. In any restaurant I've managed, any reservation that cannot be seated within 15 minutes of the respective time will receive a management visit and complimentary starters or drinks. Small gestures like this go a long way... perhaps enviable service flow, effective communication and genuine hospitality will one day define the RAW experience... just not on this special evening.

text: Perched just outside the French Quarter, the Melrose Mansion is a gorgeous antebellum mansion that is meticulously maintained. You have to walk through the residential part of the quarter to get to most of the restaurants and tourist locations, which is okay in the cooler months but can be murder during the summer when the heat and humidity beat you down after a couple of blocks. text: Dim Sum Garden is a good place everyone should try once. The place is called Dim Sum Garden so one may think you should come here and eat dim dum, but the place doesn't serve dim sum. Don't worry though there is something much better on the menu. At Dim Sum Garden, they serve Shanghainese soup dumpings, called xiao long bao. Its the first and second item on the menu. If you don't know what Shanghainese dumplings are, let me explain to you. These aren't your regular dumplings. Each dumping is a little pouch filled with meat but also this rich gelatinous soup. When the dumplings are made, an icecube of stock is also wrapped in there with the meat forming a soup dumpling when it is later steamed. When you eat these dumplings don't just pop them in your mouth. They are piping hot! And don't bite into it spilling the juices all over your shirt and plate. If you do, you just wasted the best part. Instead grab one out, put it on the spoon, bite off a little piece of the skin and slurp the soup out of the dumpling. A little vinegar soy sauce may be added to the dumpling too. Then consume the whole dumpling. Repeat 7 more times, since each basket comes with 8 dumplings. Go to Dim Sum Garden and order the Shanghainese dumplings. There are other items on the menu but I don't think I will ever get around to eating them, except for the scallion pancakes. To my knowledge this is the only place in philly you can get Shanghainese dumplings. If you are familiar with Joe's Shanghai in NYC, this philly equivalent is just as good. I think they're damn good eats and at 5 bucks a basket you can get a great snack anytime of the day.

text: We went for an early table on New Years eve. Usually the best time to hit a restaurant before they get overly busy. The restaurant was almost empty when we arrived - there were 5 front of the house staff available for the 6 tables. The seafood was subpar at best. We started with the Chilled Seafood Pleateau. For $60 - Maine Lobster, King Crab, Oysters, Clams, Lump Crab Meat, Shrimp Cocktail, Tuna Tartare. The seafood plateau arrived at a bare table - dropped off by one of the runners - and that was it. We had to ask for plates and a cracker to get past the shells. The lobster and crab meat were fine. The shrimp over cooked, the tuna stringy, the oysters small and the clams to fishy smelling to eat for our taste. This was a fast food version of a seafood tower after the one we had for our anniversary at the William Douglas steakhoust in Cherry Hill, NJ. That was the BEST we have ever had - the seafood so fresh and amazing. Next we tried the Hot Plateau seafood tower for $50. Crab Cakes, Roast Oysters,Steamed King Crab, Crispy Calamari,Coconut Shrimp, Steamed Mussels, and Clams Casino. It arrived at a table full of dirty dishes and it was amusing to watch the runner attemping to put another tower onto a full table. We not only had to ask him to return to take items off of the table but also for additional clean plates. The Hot Plateau was inedible! No crabcakes. The oysters had a burnt color to the breadcrumbs and a scorched butter smell. The clams looked exactly like the small oysters. The steamed mussels were in a very spicy curry sauce. The calamari were heavily battered and at best were a cheap premade frozen varity. This was sent back - enough was enough. The service was weak and inattentive. The food was not fresh by any standard. The manager - never even one trip through the dining room! Not worth the $100 spent!

Now I mostly go for the burgers. The Widow Maker burger is one of the greatest burgers on Planet Earth, plus, they will cook your burgers however you want. Husband likes his burgers RARE, as in pass it under the heat lamp and bring it to the table RARE, and Claim Jumper is one of the only places left that will do that for him. I also love the cozy atmosphere. I love the booths with their high, closed-in divider walls. And in the winter you can't beat the bar with its grand fireplace. Sometimes I like to just sit in the bar in front of the fireplace and only order dessert and coffee. I have heard some stories of bad service at this Claim Jumper, but I have never experienced it myself. Another big bonus since I have had the Kid is their extremely generous child service. Come here with a toddler and they will not only supply a placemat and a bib, but your server will also offer a free drink and a free "Baby Plate," which includes a turkey roll, two cheese sticks, applesauce, and a bowl of mandarin oranges. In short, there are a lot of reasons to go to Claim Jumper, even if none of them include the pricey and not-so-tasty Dinner page of the menu.

text: I got this 569dine flyer (the kind of enterprise that delivers from many restaurants) in the mail that said they now deliver food from Delmar Restaurant and, after looking at the menu, I was VERY excited. The menu listings and descriptions were amazing. My mouth started watering at the Sweet Potato Fritters all the way through the last item, simple Red Beans and Rice. It read like a hole in the wall New Orleans Cajun restaurant and I was instantly ready to order, but I decided to go there instead. It was a Saturday night and we got there around 8:30p and sat in the back (they still have smoking). It really had that Bourbon Street bar and dive kind of feel to it, definitely not fine dining, but my interest continued to build. They had a very good band playing that night, kinda bluesy, jazzy, New Orleansy. Interest still building. We got a drink fast, but had to go get the menus (first bad sign). I looked at the menu and it was the same menu that was on the flyer I got. Excellent! And so I began ordering the items that had attracted me to this place -- half dozen fresh oysters, a chopped salad (w/ "egg, bacon, cheddar, and creole buttermilk dressing"), and an oyster po' boy. I first asked the server where the oysters were from and she had to go back to the kitchen to find out (second bad sign). She said they were from Bob's Seafood (good sign, best wholesale fresh seafood distributor in the Lou). But that still did not answer my real question, but I decided to let it go. But here's where it went south, very far distant south, like to the Pole. When our server brought the fresh oysters, they looked ok, but they smelled and tasted OLD (another really bad sign). Maybe only a day or so old, but nevertheless old. I said to my companions that night, I wonder who's working the pass in the restaurant because they should have caught this quality issue before it even left the kitchen. And then there was no horseradish with the cocktail sauce (and the c-sauce needed all the help it could get - bland-city) ... that even wasn't helped much by adding the oh so bland horseradish (how can you have bland horseradish?). We called our server over and she took it away and said there would be no charge (how about my physician's bill? I'm a funny guy). She was very nice always. Then the chopped salad came and ... they added things to it they did not have on their menu description (another bad sign). I did not think that I had to tell them about my food allergies (hey, it wasn't in the salad they described on their menu), until this salad arrived with both tomatoes and sweet red peppers (nightshade family, deadly to me). Our server took it back graciously. The creole buttermilk dressing was quite good btw. By this time, we were all a bit shell shocked, but hoped that our oyster po' boys would be good ("with remoulade, lettuce, tomato, and onion"). It's the way they would dress it at Mama's in New Orleans. I am a very positive guy and I held out great hope (maybe not "great", but at least "some"). Hopes were dashed on the boulders of the entree, as they produced the worst po' boy I have ever had in my life. The bun was just out of the pepperridge farm plastic wrapper, not the crusty french bread that you would expect. The remoulade was watery and bland. The lettuce was WILTED, cut up iceberg, but limp as a dish rag, like it might have been left over from the lunch service (but they have no lunch service). And finally the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back - no onions, none (it said on the menu, there would be onions). Had to ask for them and they finally came, but by that time the french fries, which were very good when they were fresh, were limp as the lettuce. And finally, the oysters were, again, not all that fresh (but fresher than the raw ones). The decent cornmeal crust on them must have also helped a bit. But it was (and I repeat) the worst po' boy I have ever had. So, I got suckered in by the New Orleans vibe to this place, and forgot that it's still in St. Louis and still several hundred miles away from N.O. What it felt like to me was an owner who developed and published an "aspirational" menu. You know, a menu that tells the diner the kind of food that a place aspires to produce, but, in the end, doesn't live up to. I wouldn't call this place a total fraud, but it never delivered on it's potential. GET A REAL CHEF WHO KNOWS HOW TO COOK NEW ORLEANS STYLE FOOD, or ... change your menu to reflect what you get here. BTW the server was good and the band was GREAT! Go for the music and drinks but stay away from the food.

text: When Alexander's opened recently near my home, I honestly wasn't planning to check it out. It looked, um, a little questionable to me. But my mom and her husband went, and she raved about the size of the chicken wings, so I began considering it since my oldest son loooves chicken wings. Add the fact that Alexander's also has blooming onions, and I was there that very evening. Almost immediately after being seated, we were brought a basket of warm, homemade, seasoned potato chips. They tasted pretty good and were a nice touch. We ordered dinner- a steak for myself, hot wings for my son, kids mostaccoli for my younger son, and a soup/sandwich combo for my sister. Shortly thereafter, out came the blooming onion. Now, not being an expert on these things, but having some knowledge considering that I've worked in a restaurant which served them, I can only describe the onion as disappointing. A blooming onion is traditionally crispy and the onion petals pull easily from the onion center. Well, this was on the soggy side, and the onion petals had to be cut off of it, which resulted in the onion coating coming off (even more so since it was soggy). Disappointment number one. Then my sister's soup was brought- french onion, without the cheese melted on top. I believe the cheese was in a cube in the center of the soup instead. I don't eat french onion soup, so I'm not sure if this was abnormal or not. But I've only seen it with the cheese melted on top.... so, your call there. My kids were getting pretty antsy by now for their own food, starving and all, as they were. The server brought out the main dishes, and I immediately noticed that the 'wings' were boneless pieces of fried chicken. Basically, chicken tenders. And didn't have any sauce on them. Hmmm. I inquired about it and the server assured me that those were, in fact, the wings. I asked if we could have some sauce, and the server took them back to the kitchen to have them tossed. When they came out and my son finally got to eat, they were waaaay too spicy. Now, you may be thinking- well, he's a kid. Shouldn't have gotten the hot wings. Let me say, however, that he is a wing nut, and has had wings from all the mainstream restaurants in town. Never a problem. Which indicates to me that Alexander's wings are a bit spicier than most. Something that would have been beneficial for the server to have mentioned, considering that my son ordered the wings himself and it was very clear to the server who at the table would be consuming them. However, I will take fault for this. I don't blame a restaurant for myself or my guests not 'liking' the food, if there is nothing else wrong. (On a side note, I did mention the wings later to my mom, and she was very certain that what my son received were NOT the wings that she and her husband had ordered. Maybe the server made a mistake there, I really don't know.) On to the mostaccoli- ordered from the kids menu. Had a decent taste, but was garnished heavily with green basil. And the sauce was chock full of tomato chunks. If you have kids, you know just how picky they can be. I was surprised that Alexanders served a child's meal covered in basil and with chunks of tomatoes, two items most kids would rather do without. I spent part of my meal separating noodles from tomatoes, in an effort not to waste that portion of the meal as well. My sister's sandwich (some type of spicy chicken) was good; she did say it was pretty spicy (multiple times) but she ate it and seemed to enjoy it. Of course, I was paying and things had already been somewhat downhill, so maybe she was just being pleasant. And finally, on to my steak. It was served medium rare; I had ordered medium well (yes, really, I LIKE shoe leather). I cannot, will not, eat a bright pink steak. Soooo, that dish officially sent back to the kitchen. The server didn't seem to mind, but when he brought it back I had to bring it to his attention that the kitchen had included my potato but not my veggies when they sent it back out. The server promptly returned, with my plate, to the kitchen to get the vegetables. Ugh. Once all of the above issues were resolved, things went fine, I suppose. I shared my steak with both sons, while my older boy (who doesn't mind tomatoes so much) ate his brother's mostaccoli. My sister took the wings home for later, but never ate them. The table was not bussed after our main meal was served, so we sat there with empty soda glasses and plates crowding us. A nice woman, presumably the owner/wife, comes around to your table while you are dining, but did not come back to ours after our main dishes were served, so didn't get to mention any of it to her. Seems their intention is good, and could be a decent restaurant IF the staff were improved- both kitchen AND front of house staff. Hostess was super nice, and I'd maybe consider going back, but probably not with my own money. $60 WASTED.
label: NEG

text: UPDATE: *WARNING*, do not use this place to mail any packages. I've used the store's 'postal sub station counter' several times. Not just a bad shop, but a dishonest one. - - - - Unfortunately, the odd yet unique spelling of this little shop's name is the end of anything special about ESpecial day. The shop is a mish-mosh of sparse and dated greeting cards, shelves of stuffed animals and bric-a-brac items ranging from the obligatory faux wooden signs saying things like "Believe" and "Live, Laugh Love" which one would find in any similar 'gift shop' in a dieing tourist town, to dusty Beanie Babies and perfumey off-brand candles. text: You know how it is, sushi is good until you have an absolutely fantastic piece and you realize how good it could be. Well, Sushi Brothers isn't going to show you that light. It's fine, until you realize there is better. We went in late on St. Patrick's day because it was the only sushi restaurant we called without a long wait and were immediately seated at the sushi bar. In our towering positions, we surveyed the crowd - what appeared to be locals and college students (many in green!) - and the sushi rollers - exactly who you'd expect. Starving, we overordered and were brought our dishes in rapid-fire succession (much faster than you would expect it to take, should it have been created with careful thought and attentiveness). There was nothing unusual, nor extraordinary, about the soups or the edamame. The rolls, however, were bland and literally doused in souces. Those that weren't, such as the vegetable and asparagus tempura, were flavorless. I must admit that I had a magical connection with the house special souce soaking through the pieces-too-large-for-your-mouth of the FEMA roll. text: I've reserved my first 1-star review for a truly deserving venue. The Gargoyle, hands down the worst music venue in St. Louis. First of all, The Gargoyle is not really a club...it's not even a building. It's a room located in the basement of the Mallinckrodt Center, home of the bookstore and Edison Theater on the campus of Washington University. About 10-14 times a year, this all-purpose room (it resembles a former cafeteria, with low ceilings and tile floors) becomes The Gargoyle, a student-run concert venue that brings nationally recognized acts to town. Since getting only 1 star is a remarkable feat within itself, let me break this down for you. 1. The layout - This is a big, rectangular room with several support poles and a very low stage in front. And when I say low, I mean low. As in, if you're further than 10 feet from the stage, you probably won't be able to see the performers. And if you're short, well let's hope you can sit on your boyfriend's shoulders, otherwise you might as well listen to the CD at home. There's a portion about halfway across the room that suddenly juts out which allows additional room, but no one stands, on account of the fact that the sightlines from there are abysmal. 2. The atmosphere - Have you ever been to a frat party at a morgue? Well, that's what's in store for you at The Gargoyle. Since it's on the Wash U campus, that means they have to play by campus rules, which means no alcohol, no rowdy behavior, and the campus psudo-cops flex their muscle any chance they get. This includes dispersing the crowd immediately following shows. What's that, you want to hang around and chat with your friends? Nope, get out. Oh, you want to talk outside instead? Nah, can't do that either. Doesn't matter if you're a student or not. The second the show is done, the lights come on and you're expected to go back from wherever you came. Of course the students don't help out their own case. Since it's a "dry" campus, students show up already drunk, sometimes not in the best mood. In addition, tickets for students are free, so there are always some people who go for the simple fact that it's free for them. This group of students are almost too annoying to bear, showing little to no respect for the band performing. 3. The management - This is a student-run organization, so in reality there really is no management. 20 year old communications majors who have never run a business don't hold much sway. Whether or not a show is "sold out" depends on the opinion of security, along with the sloppy head counts done while students are stumbling through the door. If a conflict comes up, security and the campus cops take over, and as a result the organizers really have no influence on the show itself, apart from booking the band and cleaning up afterwards. 4. Sound - This is probably the only category that wouldn't get 1 star, technically speaking. But like any small venue, bring your earplugs if you enjoy the gift of hearing. And of course the quality varies greatly based on where you're standing in the cavern...er, room. 5. Parking - Your best bet is the street (good luck) a visitor meter spot (again, good luck), or underneath the visitor center for $1.00/hour. During the school year, Wash U offers the most unfriendly-parking situation of any college or university in St. Louis. If you're brave enough to park in a spot that requires a tag before 10:00PM on a weekday, just assume you're going to get a ticket. I could probably go on, but I'll just let it rest here. I've seen many shows here, just because the band was so good I couldn't NOT go, so I grin and bear it. But I always know what to expect, and always groan when I hear a band I like is playing here. The Gargoyle's worked hard for the worst venue in St. Louis, and it's in no position to give it up anytime soon.

text: I came here over Thanksgiving break while visiting my family. Living in CA now, I can appreciate the whole sustainable organic local food principle vibe this restaurant wants to maintain. But overall, we had an incredibly spotty experience so I can't recommend it, although I'd like to give them some slack since they're fairly new. The place is dark and stark, which was cool for a bit of atmosphere. Very austere. It was about 8:15 pm when we arrived for our reservation, and the place was empty save for 2 large parties. Yet the 2 waitstaff were running around very busy, often disappearing into the kitchen for minutes at a time. When we sat down, we were immediately informed that about 1/4 of the menu was no longer available for the evening, including some of the best dishes. When my aunt and cousin ordered the sea bass that was supposedly still available, the waitress came back to inform us that the large party to our right had just taken the last portions of the sea bass...my relatives were hard-pressed to find other things they wanted on the menu. Overall, the menu was a bit ambitious...a bit like the cook just got out of culinary school and wanted to experiment with a bunch of "fancy" ingredients to show off his chops. Seemed a bit crass to me. But I was interested to see if the chef could pull the flavors off. It took a long time for our food to come. I will say the waitstaff was friendly and competent, but unfortunately, they were dealing with 2 large parties (and a slow kitchen). Anyway, the flatbread that my mom ordered was decent. The fois gras appetizer was cool in places and hot in others - very uneven, and the delicious sauce it was dressed with had congealed on the plate from sitting too long in the kitchen. My beet soup was bland and bitter. Not a good start. For entrees, my aunt liked her pumpkin ravioli with sage brown butter, but given you can find this dish in many Italian restaurants with better prep, I was not impressed. My cousin liked her chocolate mole monkfish. However, my mom's quail dish was boring and uninspired. My crispy pork belly arugula risotto came out cold. I was so hungry that I didn't wait for them to reheat it. It was also salty, and the crispy pork belly, while good, was no different from the crispy pork you get in Chinatown duck houses. Thankfully, they took the crispy pork risotto dish off the bill since it was cold. We didn't get dessert - the most tempting dessert (the creme brulee trio) was no longer available for the night. To top it off, the large party next to us was obnoxiously loud. Given the room acoustics, their bellowing and shrill laughter was amplified, making it really tough to talk over. Root had some promise, and hopefully it'll improve past its growing pains. But based on my experience, I wouldn't recommend it to my friends.

text: I went to Distrito on Monday, October 18 for the $25 all-you-can-eat taco and enchilada Monday football special. It was my first time at Distrito, and I hoped that this would be an inexpensive introduction to the restaurant so I could decide whether I'd want to come back for the normal menu. The tacos and enchiladas also came with a Chilango chop salad, which was fine--it tasted good, not great, and it wasn't the most original thing ever. We also got black beans with rice, and refried beans. Both were very salty and not very good. Overall, the tacos and enchiladas weren't very impressive. All of the enchiladas were overwhelmed by their sauces. The crab in the crab enchiladas tasted like mediocre crab cakes from the prepared foods section of a supermarket. The mushroom tacos tasted a bit like cream of mushroom soup in taco form, which wasn't bad, but I would've liked distinct layers of flavor instead. The tortillas the tacos were served with were often cold. The hamachi tacos tasted fine, but they were still too close to generic fried-fish tacos. The carnitas tacos had good flavor, but the meat was a little dry. The cantina, where the event was hosted, wasn't busy, but there was a bit of a wait involved ordering each item and receiving it and then being asked what we wanted next. I ate enough to be full, and between the two of us, we tried one of each thing. I was disappointed that I didn't like anything enough to want to order a repeat (although some of this had to do with the wait involved). We ordered two desserts separately from the special, El Fuerte and the churros. Both were the highlights of the meal. The cake had lots of textural contrasts and nice hits of salt to balance out the sweet. The churros were crunchy on the outside but pillowy inside. Overall, I don't know whether tacos aren't Distrito's strong points, or if they called it in because we were somehow lesser customers. I might try Distrito again sometime for their real menu, but I'm hesitant..
