text: Come on, people, show PHL some love! This place has improved exponentially over the years. I've seen it grow over my three and half decades of life. As a child, my dad was an airline pilot, so I got to explore the place, way back when security was quite different. I knew the place well, yet it always seemed, for what seemed like nearly 20 years, to be in a constant state of construction. But now, construction is complete, and thanks to the terrible state of our nation's airlines, it's a good thing. Delays and cancellations are inevitable, and not due to the airport itself. So PHL has entertainment! First, they have a great rule that all vendors and stores must sell items and food at the current 'street rate' in the Delaware Valley. So no overpriced food unless it is overpriced everywhere. You won't get gouged just because you are in the airport. A beer won't cost $10--hooray! There are rocking chairs in which to sit. The food court is clean and has local chains like Bassetts, not just McDonalds. There are souvenir shops to keep you occupied while the rain delays your trip. The concourse has an entire shopping mall to satisfy our need to shop and consume. Best of all, there is art! Pick up a map and tour the terminals. (You don't have to stay in your airline's terminal, you know.) Get some exercise in, and check out the exhibitions. I am always impressed by their curator's choices. Exciting local art mixed with some folks from far away. In March 2008, there was art made from the old trees from Logan Square that had reached the end of their life cycle. An earlier exhibit of felted sculpture was so gorgeous I called a friend to tell her to learn more about the artist. (Did I mention the wifi so that you could even Google the artist right there if you had a laptop?) You can catch a train right to Center City from Bag Claim. text: I really am excited, this was my first Cold Stone Creamery experience! I had to turn around and look outside to remind myself that I was not in Italy again with trays of gelati sitting in pans in front of my eyes. This is not your run of the mill hard hand dipped or soft serve ice cream parlor and you get to design your own creation. First you choose your flavor and if you are torn on which flavor of ice cream to have they offer free samples. Yay brain freeze! Then you choose your mix ins from a board, another dilemma but it always works out. They use two spatulas to work the ice cream back and forth until they have gathered what is needed for your treat. Then they place your ice cream on a frozen cold stone, add your mix ins, place it in a paper cup, a waffle cone or bowl, they are so cute and can be dipped into dark chocolate and wallah your master piece is ready to be devoured. I think they have a pep rally everyday before they open their doors, the servers are flying on a happy high which is contagious and it makes waiting to create your own treat comfortable and enjoyable, plus it gives you the chance to change your mind eleven million times. They have a large variety of ice creams and sorbets that are made with premium ingredients in each store daily, so the sign says, lots to read while you are standing in line. The toppings range from candies galore, nuts, fruits and ice cream sauce such as hot fudge, peanut butter, marshmallow and caramel. I bought some cute double chocolate ice cream cup cakes to refreeze for later, they also have whole cakes, smoothies, shakes and ice cream blended coffee drinks. I love pumpkin ice cream, heck I love pumpkin anything and they are featuring Fall flavors now and once I finally decide on how to create and design this treat I shall return. What I did ultimately decide on was the coconut ice cream with pineapple, bananas and pecans with a drizzle of hot fudge. Oh stop, it was delicious and I had it in a chocolate dipped waffle bowl. My second choice was a coffee ice cream with roasted almonds, health bar crunch pieces and either caramel or hot fudge, but tomorrow is another day. Hubby had chocolate ice cream with peanut butter cups, brownie pieces and hot fudge, it was so good! One of the first things you notice after the "go get them" approach from the order takers is each time someone leaves a tip in the jar they sing! My gosh you have to leave a tip to keep it going! Okay, I have to share a story with you. For pecan, do you say pe-can or pe-con? Both are acceptable but I used to say pe-can until an elderly southern lady corrected me and said "honey, it is pe-con a pe-can is what a truck driver uses!"

text: We were interested to try a restaurant in Reno that wasn't a casino restaurant or a buffet, although there are some very good ones here. We love fine dining and wanted to do something special for my husband's birthday. We are so glad we did. First thing to be aware of is, the restaurant is not very visible from the street! It is set back from the street, up a short unmarked driveway. The only marked driveway you see is the one before it, for a place called Reflections - don't take that one, take the next driveway, go up an incline, and it leads to a small parking lot that is behind the restaurant. It is unassuming from the outside, and resembles a country house, but inside, the decor is clean, and cozy with dining areas in separate rooms. There is also patio seating. The service was professional and thorough. Our server, Tim, knew the menu well and explained the dishes in detail. For our appetizer, we ordered the Pimenton Spiced Duck Rillettes with a mango salsa, cilantro and soft blue corn tortilla triangles. The duck meat was deliciously spiced and served in a small dish, ready to be spread on a tortilla and topped with the mango salsa. What flavor! Our soup was a carrot-ginger puree with a yogurt swirl - it was so flavorful and perfectly balanced. You could taste the sweetness of the carrot, followed by the ginger spice. So good! My husband ordered the Pork Tenderloin, which was served with Tuscan Kale, Serrano Ham, and little Romesco pasta balls. The pork was moist and tender, with a wonderful pork flavor. It was the best pork tenderloin he's ever had, and that's saying alot! I had the Grilled Wild King Salmon, served on a mix of Elm Oyster mushrooms, white corn, summer squash and red and yellow cherry tomatoes. Those mushrooms had such a unique flavor and really sent the vegetables to a different level. The salmon was fresh and flavorful, and was so moist! The meat was soft and smooth on the tongue, not flaky or dry as can happen when salmon is overcooked. That was definitely the best salmon I've ever had! For dessert, he had the Poppyseed Angel Food Cake with Blackberry Curd & Creme Chantilly. Tim served it with a tall skinny candle in honor of my husband's birthday. My husband said that was the best creme he'd tasted besides his mom's. It was a delightful, light cake with a rich blackberry sauce with the creme for contrast. I had the Scharffen Berger Bittersweet Chocolate Ganache Torte with a Pecan Crust & Caramel Sauce. It was very chocolaty and rich, but not sugary sweet. It went well with the pecan crust, a nutty blend of pecans and butter. The cocktails were poured well and they have a nice variety of wine and after dinner drinks as well. GM Carol Wilson, stopped at our table to greet us and was very personable. We told her how much we enjoyed the meal and she seemed genuinely appreciative. We could taste the difference with the fresh and organic ingredients, along with the talent of Chef Natalie Sellers. Both of them have extensive fine dining experience from San Francisco and it shows here. We noticed that there were a number of regular customers. Even though we're not local, we're close enough to make the trip again soon and are definitely going to be coming back to try more of their items. We highly recommend you try this delightful restaurant!

text: I've been frequenting Nimbus since the bar was roughly 8' long, chairs were bench seats pulled from old cars, and there was one toilet. Yes, a single unisex toilet. Times have changed but the quality beer has not. There's now a beautiful art deco bar with nice interior tables and even a balcony-style seating area, all nestled into a nice warehouse brewery--storage tanks in back (I believe you can arrange for a tour). Nice garage-style door out front leads to a large patio with great views of the Catalina Mountains. Trains going by and aircraft landing at the air base only add to the scenery. Is it tricky to find? Yeah, I guess. Is it sketchy? Not at all. Never seen or heard of any issues. Great shirts and other merchandise for sale, as well as 64 oz growlers. Good food. When there's live music, it does tend to get quite loud in there. One last drawback: for a brewery that specializes in ales, I can't for the life of me figure out why they don't have an IPA on tap as a staple. Pale Ale is good enough though. They also now sell wine, but do not expect to order a Bud Light here--they don't serve it (thankfully!). Go "find" Nimbus for youself!!

text: My lifetime affection for dive bars was born here, at the humble Old State in Media, PA. Jukebox wails out old country, eighties metal, and the occasional Dead song. Drunks shuffle between the pool table and the bar, paying in change, sometimes running a tab and ignoring it for weeks. A fryer behind the bar spits out wings, fries, and other nearly-indigestible snacks to soak up some booze. Andy, long-time bartender and owner, rules with an iron fist in a velvet glove, remembering everyone's name and usual poison. If I lived closer I'd still be there on Saturday nights, getting insanely drunk and betting on the bowling game. Good thing I moved. But I miss it.

text: Heading up to Royal I was surprised to see Mr. B's was still full of people chatting over their brunch in the dining room shortly after 3pm - asking the host if they were still seating I was told "no, but we serve most of our best stuff at the Bar all day." Content with this I made my way over to the bar where I was seated next to a friendly fellow from Mississippi who insisted I "must" try the BBQ shrimp - his pick for the best dish in all of New Orleans. Explaining to him that I had every intention of doing so the waiter/bartender must've overheard our conversation and chimed in that the shrimp wasn't his favorite dish, but that it was very good. When I asked him what his favorite was he stated "The Gumbo Ya-Ya." With water filled and my choices already made by my neighbor and the bartender (the two item's I'd had every intention of getting anyhow) I sat back and chatted with my neighbor while watching the basketball game at the bar. Arriving without much delay was a hot loaf of crusty French bread with a great crisp exterior and pillowy soft interior - perfect for eating but moreso for soaking. Shortly following the bread was my cup of Gumbo Ya-Ya - the best gumbo I'd have on my visit to NOLA. Served piping hot and featuring a thick dark roux, light on rice and heavy on spicy andouille and shrimp - plenty of bite without blunting the nuances of the individual ingredients - wonderful. A short time passed and I reflected on the delicious gumbo before my second dish arrived - a half order of the famous Mr. B's Barbequed Shrimp. Three enormous shrimp - head and tail on, served with two pieces of grilled country bread and resting in a sauce that may as well have been 1/3 butter, 1/3 pepper, and 1/3 garlic with a bit of Worcestershire and lemon - the first time in a while that I've had to work so hard for food (shelling) but thankfully entirely worth the effort. First devouring the tender yet snappy shrimp that were accented but not overwhelmed by the sauce - and then soaking up the sauce with the remaining bread - I'm glad they publish the recipe online because it is definitely something I plan to do at home. To be fair, I can't think of a better way to spend an hour and $20 than the meal I had at Mr. B's.

From the time you walk in you are not greeted properly, frequently I barely get a hello, heck they somtimes don't even look at me the entire time i'm ordering. The black girl and the big girl actually scowl at customers, I don't understand it. The one exception in the tall girl who I think is the assistant mgr, she's friendly and great. But the rest make you feel like you would rather be at Panera, which by the way has equivalent food but much friendlier service. Oh, and for take-out orders, they put your utensils in the same little pouch with your bread, so that the handles are all greasy when you take them out to eat. Why? Management needs to do some work on the service and this place would be 4 stars.
label: NEG

text: I should've listened to these Yelp reviews, but i always have to find out for myself. Granted I went at a strange time (around 4:30 on a sunday), so they were just opening, which always makes for an awkward time. So I won't kill them for the lack of ambiance. My partner and I each got a beer (not very cold), and ordered some apps. The hummus and the catfish (not good). The hummus came in a huge bowl, and was probably enough to feed an entire party, and it also had at least a full cup of oil poured into it. I've had hummus with oil on it, but nothing like this. It was comically bad. The accompanying veggies were strangely presented, but the Pita was decent. The catfish and chips were bad. Thick cornmeal crusted catfish fingers, ridiculously greasy, with undercooked french fries. The accompanying sauce was okay. We asked for some ketchup for the fries and we were given a ramekin of tomato sauce. Seriously. It wasn't ketchup. All in all, everything needed more flavor and less grease. I can't say I'll ever go back. I gave them an extra star because the waitress was very nice.
label: NEG

text: Dear Rebecca S, The fact that you don't take SEPTA regularly means that you have very limited experience. If you need it to commute every day then you will discover how crappy it really can be. Have I had good experiences? Yes, a few. But they are far outweighed by the daily negative experiences which include: 1. Extremely dirty train cars-Spilled potato chips and potato chip bags, leftover wrappers, soda cans/bottles and spilled soda are de rigeur for SEPTA. Sprinkle in the odd leftover newspapers and fast food leftovers for garnish. 2. Extremely dirty train stations: City Hall routinely smells like piss. And to an extent many other stations smell bad as well. Not to mention the usual detritus ranging from digested sunflower seed husks/seeds spit out, cigarette butts, abandoned food wrappers, vomit, and other garbage. 3. Patron conduct-There's the people who sit in different aisles and yell at each other across the train. Then there's the cell phone breakup/relationship in termoil conversations, usually puncuated with loud swear words. Then there's the people that feel the need to share their love of X crappy artist on their crappy cell phone/portable radio speaker. Then there are the people that smoke in the train stations, despite numerous signs saying "Do Not Smoke". And the capper, those fellas who just can't wait and decide to whip it out and piss on the train platform. 4. Random train outages-This ranges from simple delays, which are to be expected to the full on "No trains are running past 19th St" announcement. 5. SEPTA customer service is uncaring and/or surly-They don't take change, even for low denomination bills even though at many stops there aren't token machines. They'll have conversations with fellow employees and travelers, letting you wait until they are good and ready to take your transfer. When I got stuck in the tunnel between 15- and 19th St. and had to walk out of the tunnel to the 19th St station, no apology or free transfer was offered.
label: NEG

text: This place is my corner pizza joint. I wish i had a different corner pizza joint. The ingredients are great, but the compositions are always disappointing. Not enough of this... way too much of that. I am consistently disappointed with nearly everything i've tried at Slice. I specifically suggest you don't bother with the calzones. They're super boring. Also, for some reason, they dont come with any pizza sauce for dipping. also, i hate that they are cash only. not only that, but they didnt bother to put an ATM inside the restaurant. so if you go and forgot that you needed cash, you have to hike at least a block to get money. stupid. on the other hand, it is super convenient and the pizza by the slice seems to be a good value. the crust is thin and the toppings are sparse, but you get an entire quarter of a pie monster slice. It fills me up in a pinch. And i guess thats what a corner pizza joint is really for.
label: NEG

text: This store is the size of a large-ish supermarket, yet somehow I never find anything to buy. The clothes are arranged by color! This is the most useless method I've seen in any thrift store, by far. Who shops that way? What good is something which is the "right" color but 5 sizes too small or too big?! I am a dedicated thrifter, and am normally willing to spend hours combing the racks for a good find, but this is so illogical I just get irritated and leave. The book selection is no great shakes, scarcely any paperbacks for some reason. The shoes tend to be both poor quality and out of style. Not a bad variety of kitchen goods. They have a vastly inflated view of what obsolete computer stuff is worth ($10 for a 1996 Photoshop 4.0 manual? hee!) but that's pretty much a universal thrift store employee issue. The few bright spots are purses and bags (this is where the huge selection is great), blankets (ditto), and, strangely, exercise gear? I've never bought a used stationary bike or rowing machine, but this is where I'd go if I needed one, I guess. Worth a stop if you're driving right by it, but it's been years since I made a special trip to come here from Philly.
label: NEG

text: This place is ok, and I will say that they do have pretty good strawberry daiquiris, but I do have two gripes...1) the shrimp aren't deveined (remove the poop shoot), and 2) I do not like sharing my table with pigeons. They were flying around inside the restaurant!!!! There is mayonnaise sitting on the tables all day, too. Doesn't that stuff need to be refrigerated??? The salad is shredded cabbage with a mound of Swiss cheese and a tomato, and is actually pretty good without all of the usual accoutrement. When I come here, I get a shrimp plate or a muffaletta. They are good in a pinch, but not somewhere that I go out of my way to frequent. Especially, since they don't take credit cards, and you have to pay to park in a lot if you are unlucky finding street parking. It is more for tourists. I give them a 1.5 stars.

text: I have been to Buddakan several times and I'm a bit obsessed, so I was pretty excited when a friend (with a $125 gift card! SCORE!) suggested Pod. Stephen Starr did a fantastic job with the layout. Sadly, we weren't seated in a pod, but we all agreed that we need to come back so we can get the chance to have dinner in one. Since we were going out drinking later, we all decided that sushi would be a bad idea, so we opted to share a few dishes. We ordered martini's and I chose the Blue Martini first, which tasted like tropical fruit. It was ok, not great. Since Pod serves the food as it is done, our Edamame came out first, which was nice, because we could sit and chat and have drinks while still munching on something. The Crab Spring Rolls, Butter Poached Lobster and Grilled Teryaki Salmon were all decent, but I don't think I'd order them again. Especially the lobster. The bok choy and tofu just didn't seem to work well with the lobster. However, the Asian Braised Short Ribs and Wasabi Crusted Filet were TO. DIE. FOR. Absolutely delicious. Loved the Udon noodles with the short ribs and the wasabi mashed potatoes that came with the Filet were delicious. So moral of the food story: stick to the red meat. While we were eating, the manager convinced my friend and I to try the Orange Martini after finishing our first round. It was ok. It was mixed with carrot juice and ginger...but it was a little heavy on the ginger and whatever spices they used. I think it would be a great drink to pair with some sushi, but it was a little tough to drink. To make it up to us, the manager brought over a free round of the Yellow Martini, which ended up being my favorite. I LOVE passionfruit, and the tartness of the drink was great. A friend ordered the green tea gin and tonic, which was seriously refreshing and delicious. We tried the Fluffernutter Spring Rolls and the sorbet, which was a perfect end to the night. We racked up a pretty serious bill by the end of the night, but luckily we had a nice friend to share her gift card with us. Next time, I don't plan on ordering as much, but dammit, I want to sit in a pod! And make sure you check out the bathrooms... they're definitely interesting...I felt like I was in an airplane. Kinda strange, but fun.
label: POS

text: I was a bit concerned since some of the reviews were seriously negative. We really enjoyed our evening here. On our visit the dining room was only about 1/4 full, but we were told (and could hear from the parking lot) the banquet facilities were full to capacity. Inside we found a quiet dining room that takes you back in time. It does look a bit like a grandmother's living room, but we kind of enjoyed that. Everything is clean, the carpet looks new, but if you could go back in time 30 or 40 years, I expect nothing has changed. The food is not modern. Go here if you want German food. If you know what sauerbraten is you will like this restaurant. Add to that the lowest markup on wine I've ever seen, and fair prices for entrees this is a great value. For my pallet great food, good prices. Service wasn't fast, but it wasn't slow like some reviewers mentioned. Take a little time and enjoy a good meal. I'll be back.
label: POS

text: (NOTE: I posted this review in January 2008 for the wrong Samurai Blue location so I deleted it and posted it here, which was where it all went down) Came here for sushi on a Thursday night for and ended up waiting 45 minutes for my to-go order. I sat at the sushi bar and enjoyed a large hot sake with my friend who highly recommended this place. He said he's seen Ronde Barber here once, which is cool. I ordered a custom spicy tuna roll, and they didn't have brown rice, which is no big deal - but would have been nice. I also got the Blue Moon roll, and one other basic roll. I got home, my wife and I went to town on the sushi, and she found a large fish scale (or maybe it was a large piece of aluminum-covered cardboard, it was hard to tell) in one of her rolls, which got caught in her teeth and freaked her out. I'm no sushi expert, but I don't think that was supposed to be there! :) I swear to God I'm not lying. The only reason I didn't give this a 1-star review is because the actual sushi (without foreign matter) was VERY tasty. I'm sure I'll give them another shot, but with waiting 45 minutes for 3 sushi rolls, and some cardboard and/or fish scales, I won't be rushing back.

text: It was one of those great meals. Classy joint, with classy decor and classy menus with classy wine lists. A once in a while place where the food is so good you continue eating even after you are full because it is just that good. Our waiter was very professional. Besides the fact that he was sweating a bit, he was charming and dealt with a table of 9 women well. That is not an easy task. We had 8:45 reservations, so by the time we ordered, they were out of almost everything. I was sad they didn't have my scallops, but it made my happy that when they say everything is flown in fresh that day, they aren't lying. I would rather have something else that fresh than the meal I wanted that had been thawed out "just in case". Smoked oysters. We were all blown away. So delicate and flavorful. As were the lobster dumplings, which were more like lobster ravioli from heaven. It was one of those things where we took a bite and all looked at each other in amazement. I miss them already. They didn't have the scallops I wanted (I can get those here, no biggie) so I had the lemon fish with crab and lobster butter. Wow. Others had the seared tuna, the veal, and the steak. No one was disappointed. It was rich, but I ate it all anyway. How often do I get lobster butter? Another dish worth mentioning is the mashed sweet potatoes with vanilla bean and banana. Good, but too dessert-y for me. Actual dessert lived up to the meal. Molten chocolate cake and apple pie. Both two of the best versions of each dish I have had, especially the cake. On the rich side, so we all just had a bite. If I could learn to recreate that, I would be one happy (and fat) lady. Five stars all around - if you are in New Orleans and feel like splurging, put this place on your list.
label: POS

text: I'm rarely a morning person over the weekend. So the sick sad fact is that that after 3-4 years of living Philadelphia I can still count the number of times I've done brunch on one hand. Pathetic I no but I'm getting there. after awhile one of my West Philly buds finally coaxed me to get up and do a West Philly brunch style. Since there's only really two brunch options in West Philly, and I already exhausted White Dog, RX had to be the place to go. From the moment that I was gazing at all of the old medicine bottles, scales, and other pharmacy products I instantly fell in love with the theme of the decor. The only things that really docked off that one star was the fairly long wait to get a table, and the fact that the seating arrangements had us a little too up close and personal with other dining parties. The beast thing about RX by far was the food. they clearly have a huge dedication to the buy fresh buy local movement and it shows. If the eggs I had were any fresher I would have been staring at baby chickens. the potatoes were sheer perfection, and the fresh squeezed orange juice was incredible. throw in the botomless cup of La Colombe that they provide and RX really knows how to treat your morning right. Finger 3 down now I'm ready for #4.

text: I stayed at Chateau Sonesta Hotel during my trip to New Orleans, and had a pretty good experience. This is a fairly nice hotel (and somewhat pricey too... I was lucky to get a special rate because I was there for a conference), and the location is as good as it gets: right in the French quarter, one block from Bourbon Street. The rooms are clean and big: our room overlooked the back courtyard where the pool is located, and I would recommend trying to get a room facing the courtyard as the street can get quite noisy at night. There's a pool, a (tiny) gym, and a couple of bars/restaurants. Do NOT get breakfast at the hotel: the breakfast place, called Tempo, charges $18 for a very mediocre brunch buffet... not worth it at all. 3-1/2 stars.

text: Wow, its been too long since we have hung out Juicys. The last time i went down to Juicys, on Wells St. the cheese burger combo was soooo juicy i even considered MAYBE superior to Scoopers, whom is arguably the best in Northern Nevada. Today i went to the Juicys on Glendale and Mc Carran and wow, disappointed. The service was great, everyone in the cook staff was very polite, too bad the food quality was terrible. I ordered a 2 cheese burger, turkey burger and 2 double cheese burger combos. The turkey burger was the only burger that was not dry. It was in fact tasty, my daughter tells me. The other burgers were so dry, we joked they should change the name to Dusty's. Overcooked to say the least. The bun was soggy and the fries were uninspired, they reminded me of the fries we choked down back in Elementary school. The only reason i did not mark this as 1 Star, is because they are Local. Also, the amount and types of condiments they offer in the shop is pretty good, and the salsa was great. Just kidding, they had a salsa space open, but the salsa was gone. I wont be going back to Dustys.

text: So I was looking for a place to get good street tacos in Philly and this is what I found to be recommended on Yelp. I'm not sure why it's rated so highly, and maybe I ordered the wrong stuff. At any rate, this place wasn't that great. Firstly, the tacos are served with iceberg lettuce, sour cream, and cheese. I was expecting an "authentic Mexican" place to air more on the side of cilantro and onions, and not Taco Bell style. I asked that I have these specifications to my tacos and they said no problem. Then when I got home, they hadn't done this, so my tacos were drenched in sour cream and lettuce. Dang. Next point of order: the guac. Sub-par at best. It was essentially just smashed up avocados. There was no black pepper, no salt, no lime, no jalapenos, and no onions. Boring guacamole with very little flavor. It was served with what I can only describe as a pic de gallo / tomatillo hybrid sauce. This was almost better than the guac (I ended up mixing them). I'd also like to comment on the hot sauce, arguably the most important aspect of a Mexican restaurant. I order the "hot" option to go with my tacos. It was not spicy and the flavor was not good. It was almost a smoky flavor, more similar to Tabasco Chipotle Sauce. So anyway, I'm wise enough to not completely write a place off based on one bad experience, so I'll edit the review and my rating if I go back and enjoy the food more.
label: NEG

text: I love ice cream, and on my last vacation to California I was looking for that perfect scoop since this year I started making my own concoctions at home. The great reviews of McConnell's took me there and I was ::drum roll please:: horribly disappointed. Why? I just didn't think it was anything special. The service wasn't great and the flavors weren't really original - not to mention they just weren't spoon lickable ice creams. I tried the Chocolate Burnt Almond because it is so highly rated and just hated it. It didn't have the deep dark chocolate flavors I was expecting, I found it to be a little icy and the burnt almonds just dried out your mouth. Sure there were a ton of almonds in it - but this was not a good thing - for me anyway. Got to give it to them - portions are huge and prices are low but definitely not worth it. Don't listen to the hype - the ice cream here is mediocre at best. Best part of the place - the ambiance. It is a nice, old-fashioned ice cream parlor. Cutesy.

text: Pretty darn good! I've been frequenting this place for the last 3 years or so and I think that the pho is up to par. I do have access to excellent pho in Philly's Chinatown section on a daily basis, and Bamboo does a pretty good job. I usually do takeout, but have dined there once for lunch and once for dinner. It has never been crowded when I'm there, but I think they do a brisk take out business. My hubby gets the Beef Stew Noodle Soup, which has a tomato base and is spicy. He loves it! Bamboo also makes and sells their own spicy chili sauce (akin to Siracha, but much spicier and with red chili slices). I am usually boring and order the same dish--the Chicken Pho--but I always like it. I have also had the vegetable noodle soup, but I think the chicken pho is more flavorful. The Summer Rolls are quite generous. One summer roll and a bowl of soup, and I'm done for the night. It is also an excellent remedy for a head cold/flu. A solid place to grab a warming bowl of soup and a no-frills, inexpensive dinner. Closed on Sunday!

text: I've been spending vacation time in Reno for years but I just recently dropped in on the Gold-N-Silver Inn. Like so many, I learned of it from the appearance on Triple D. Now I'm left wondering why it took so long to hear about such an iconic place. First thing's first -- this place is HUGE. I really wasn't ready for just how big it is. Went in for dinner and wondered if we'd have a wait, especially with the recent national publicity. They were doing business, but there was plenty of room and we were seated right away. This isn't the Ritz. It is, however, a great example of what a 24-hour diner should be: friendly, flavorful and filling. The menu has plenty to offer, throws some surprise curves and isn't over-the-top in terms of price. I went for the chicken fried steak, as did another in our party. A third opted for the turkey dinner. For me, the chicken fried steak earned my highest praise -- just as good as mom used to make. The steak was cooked perfectly, the mashed potatoes were just the right consistency, and the gravy ... that's the stuff that dreams are made of! To be fair, my fellow diners weren't as taken with the food as I was. My CFS compadre said he'd had better and wasn't nearly as happy with the potatoes and gravy. Then again, he's not much for potatoes so I discount that angle a bit. The turkey dinner diner didn't care for the dressing and said the turkey "wasn't what I'd expected." I couldn't get anything more detailed than that, so I'm not sure exactly what was amiss. And neither liked the coffee; I don't drink coffee, so I can't offer any insight on that front. But this is my review, so I'm saying great things about the Gold-N-Silver. The service was good; our server had a bit of attitude and a good sense of humor, just the right mix for this type establishment. I loved the food, the atmosphere and the entire experience. Next time I'm in town, I will head back to the Gold-N-Silver, a true gem in the Biggest Little City's wealth of dining options.
label: POS

If you don't like Pappy's, well, great. I love them and their ribs. So if that fair to Smoking Joe's? I don't care. Is it fair to compare Dom to Korbel?) Anyway...the chicken was actually better than Pappy's, but it was covered with a thick coating of rub. Which depending on what you like, may or may not be a good thing. The brisket was dry and tasteless. Thank goodness for their spicy sauce -- it helped to add both moisture and flavor to the brisket. For the sides, the cole slaw was a creamy type, but not horrible. The potato salad was about a supermarket deli level. But the mac & cheese? This was awesome. Awesomely bad. Apparently, they make the mac, then toss on some cheese (cheddar) then nuke it. Freaking nasty. The cheese had already started to congeal. And as Paul M. mentioned, it look about 15 minutes for the food to come out. I don't get it. Everything we ordered had to have been pre-made, minus the funky mac & cheese. In my last bitch, while the decor is a step up from the picnic tables of Pappy's, half of the restaurant looks like somebody reconstructed their Pottery Barn living room in there. As I told the wife, I'd give them two stars -- one for the ribs and one for having booze. But I also swore that I'd only come back if it was nighttime and I was craving ribs. text: This is great restaurant! The place itself is fairly large. Lots of exposed and painted brick give the space a traditional downtown vibe - not really classic French Quarter but with a very "New Orleans" feel, But that's really important - the star here is the food. Start with Emerils classic barbecued shrimp. Big, perfectly cooked shrimp in a rich and spicy creole sauce served with small rosemary biscuit. The smoked salmon cheesecake was dense and rich - not as flavorful as the shrimp but still very good. An entree of drum crusted with andouille and served of crispy shoestring potatoes and grill veggies (squash and eggplant - yum!) and touch of a rich and ever so slightly sweet sauce was mind blowing. DP's fillet served on top of marcapone pollenta with sauteed greens was superb as well. The steak was perfectly cooked and the pollenta was the perfect contrast in both texture and flavor. Dessert - Emerils banana creme pie- I had this one previously at Emerils Fish House in Las Vegas - and it's every bit as good here! I'm not going to try to describe it - all I will say is that it remains the best dessert I have ever eaten! This is not your mom's banana cream pie... The wine list is very hood as well, including some interesting by the glass choices. So you ask, why the four star rating and not a five? Well, he place is bit touristy and loud. Docking a star for that may be harsh but as good as this place is it doesn't quite qualify for five stars. All in all, Emerils is an excellent New Orleans restaurant. I'll be back!

text: To be fair, I probably caught them doing two things they just don't do well. I'm pretty sure their coffee is great. They turned out to be microwaved, and even though we were the only people in the shop, it took longer to produce them than if they had been made from scratch. And they were, in a word, gruesome. McDonald's breakfast sandwiches are better. They're about on a par with Lukoil microwave breakfast sammies. Were I in their shoes, I would just focus on good pastries and scrap the sandwiches. I also ordered tea, which is the one thing coffee shops (with the exception of Starbucks, oddly) consistently do poorly. This was the worst tea I've ever had in any coffee shop. It was cheap, generic food service-branded tea. (The kind that tastes like the water came from a used coffee urn.) Admittedly, I didn't pay a premium tea price, but I'm willing to pay premium price for a decent cuppa. I see this place in the evening (when I'm coming out of Shanachie Pub), and they seem to do well. I'm sure it's a great place for coffee and goodies. text: I went to Amada on 1/31/2010 with five others for the roast suckling pig. We sat near the front of the restaurant at a table with two benches. The atmosphere was nice. Although the benches weren't uncomfortable, per se, I did feel a bit fidgety throughout the evening because they were backless. We ordered a pitcher of red sangria and four tapas to share before the pig came out. I enjoyed the Sangria--it wasn't too sweet and the spicing was good. We got the patatas bravas, the shortrib flatbread, the melon with ham, and the fresh goat cheese with balsamic strawberries. I have to say, while all of them were enjoyable, none of them impressed me--they weren't new taste experiences, and the presentation was the main thing that made the dishes stand out. The patatas bravas were crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, and the sauce was tasty. But, I think I could've made something similar myself for less money. It just wouldn't have been as pretty. The ham with melon was nice, but I wish there had been a bit more crunch from the caramelization, and a bit more ham. The goat cheese was yummy, but it was still just a cheese platter. The flatbread was the least visually appealing item, and while it had a nice cheesy meaty thing going on, the flavor kind of reminded me of something from Taco Bell. Taco Bell is one of my guilty pleasures, so I'm not knocking it, but I expected something more sophisticated at Amada. My last minor complaint was that the number of pieces that came with each plate varied, so sharing was a tiny bit difficult. Service was alright. Our server seemed a bit impatient and not very warm--I hoped she would give advice about how much to order unbidden, or ask if we wanted advice, but mostly she just sort of stood there. Servers took plates away a bit prematurely once or twice--there was a small amount of goat cheese that vanished, and later in the meal, after the pig, they took some not completely empty plates when my dining companions left them to feed the meter. Between the tapas and the pig and the pig and dessert, they brushed the table of crumbs, but the table was pretty clean, so it felt more intrusive than anything. The pig was the best part of the meal. They brought half of it tableside, with the head, and carved it in front of us and heaped it on a platter. Afterwards, they brought two plates from the other half of the pig, one with meat, and one with skin and the ribs. The pig was tender, juicy, greasy in a good way, and had good porky flavor. The skin was crispy. The sides it comes with were also really good. We had charred green onions with a romesco (?) sauce, rosemary white beans, garbanzo beans with spinach, and roasted fingerling potatoes. Everyone loved the white beans, which were very flavorful and buttery. The potatoes must've been roasted in pork fat, and were crispy and had nice porky taste. The garbanzo beans were also good, although the texture (I don't know if they were cooked al dente or if they were crisped somehow) was disarming--they were crunchy, which kept surprising me. And the grilled onions had a nice balance of sweetness, smoky charred flavor, and oniony flavor. Lastly, we ordered desserts--two saffron rice puddings, a brown butter cake with plums, and mixed berries with cream. The rice pudding had an interesting flavor, although some of us thought it wasn't as thick as we would've liked. The brown butter cake was good but pretty small. The plums were nicely spiced. And the berries with cream was simple but good. I also tried some cafe con leche--I don't usually like coffee, but I did like this. We got out spending about 64 per person, give or take a few dollars, which wasn't bad. I would definitely go for the roast pig again, which was a fantastic value. We wound up taking home a serious amount of the pork and sides. If I had gone just for tapas, I probably would have been pretty disappointed. Again, they were all decent to good, but not exceptional, and to actually make a meal of them would be quite expensive. It may have also been an off night, as one of my friends said that she remembered having had some of the same things previously, and they were much better.

text: Two parts to this review, the station and Amtrak itself. Station: 1.5 stars. Amtrak Train travel in general: 3.5 stars. I really enjoy taking the train now. It is a new thing for me. Flying for years visiting relatives, although fun when I get there, is almost always torture. Squished together, the lines, check in, re-check in, security check, and now pat down/shoes off/power up laptop, take off jewelery etc.. ad nauseam... Amtrak has none of that nonsense. Advice: I always recommend the business class as it is only 20 bucks more, with the same lousy food naturally (hehe) but the seating is more spacious and comfortable with a lower noise volume which makes the comfort level goes up the scale to 100% in comparing to just regular fare. I have tried coach (LOUD and sometimes Greyhound-sque) & I have tried the lowest level of 2 person suite for travel (less leg room,) and I still prefer the business class. Perks: Business class you have 2 foot rests... one in front of you that you can rest your feet on and a leg/foot rest that props up like a lazyboy chair. You can lean back in your chair without disturbing who is behind you. There are 120V electrical plugs (for coach also) for every seat pairing. Pros/Cons: It is a longer way to travel, by train, but not that much longer if you are going to Chicago or Michigan. Sleeping our way to Michigan, rather then driving through the ice and snow is a blessing. Your luggage does not get searched, you can pack liquids and breakables as you choose, you don't have to take off your shoes, in business class you sit in a different (A LOT less crowded) waiting room. For $20 it is beyond worth the cost. Pros: Your luggage is always with you. You don't have to pack like someone might go through your stuff and you don't have to worry about your lip gloss causing an international incident etc.. If you pack something your big suitcase that is your favorite item, you don't have to worry about a luggage handler/sorter/etc.. lifting it off your hands. Carry that hair gel and in your carry on with no worries. This part is a big deal for me. Through many years of flying and the last few years of having to pack everything trying to keep in mind where to pack valuables (on me,) liquids of any sort (sealed in something and pray it doesn't burst in the suitcase.. oh the horrible memory of ruining a beautiful dress from Hair conditioner. :( etc....) .. THANK GOODNESS all I have to do is pack it up and go to take the train! Cons: Your luggage is always with you. Make sure ALL your luggage rolls or your shoulder bag is VERY light. Trust me. Your shoulders/back will NOT like you if you lug your heavy (or soon to feel that way) luggage around everywhere (thinking of Union Station and trading off to go to another hub.) The station itself: I like the location, as it seems a bit removed from the immediate area's traffic. The people who are working the ticket counter have 10 shades of attitude but they get 10 flavors of crazy going through there and not just mine. ;) (Good crazy is ok :p :D ) The fastfood joint is dirty and I couldn't bring myself to eat there. The chairs are horrible and there are no good places to put your luggage nor yourself for that matter. All sorts of characters walking in and out of there. I feel safe enough but I wouldn't have anyone I care about stay there too long waiting for me to pick them up. Always room for improvement. What's up: Take luggage that has wheels. Your shoulders/back/neck will scream at you if you try to carry bags everywhere. Pay the extra 20 bucks for business class for a much better experience. I love trains now. So stress free compared to driving/flying. Don't tarry at the station. Time your rides to be close to pick up time. I have heard many stories of VERY long waits for taxicabs, be warned. As you can call while you are on the train there is no reason to make people wait at the station for you or vise versa. Have fun! :)

text: When you live in the food snob capital of the USA, you have serious expectations when you dine out. My visit to Cochon in rebounding New Orleans, left me full, fat and happy! I hope it lasts forever so I can go back one day to be dined and delighted with pig parts and authentic southern cooking. The post-modern lodge style dining room amuses with porcine decor, sleek, utlilitarian picnic-style tables, benches and stools. A warehouse location and trendy bar crowd sets the scene. Complimentary bread has become so passez over the years, even those pencil thin breadsticks and wafer thin parmesan flatbread are so yawn that it's mighty refreshing when someone plops down a basket of WARM HOMEMADE POTATO ROLLS in front of you. Cochon makes a batch every 20 minutes and they contain real potato puree. The rolls and consideration for jaded-foodie palates gets 5 stars. Cochon does small plates and entrees so you can get your fill of local favorites and house specialties. Standouts from the Boucherie are fried boudin balls with pieces of pulled pork and deep flavor. My small plate of BBQ pork ribs came out cold though the sauce was tangy and sweet enough while I was looking for more smokiness. Fried pigs ears and rabbit livers I see more of a novelty for people like my dinner companion for whom having something fried and/or weird is a must for every fine dining experience. There's plenty of love for the local cuisine: My hen and adouille gumbo had a flavourful (and memorable) dark roux. Roasted Gulf redfish (a specialty of the chef) was picture perfect and it's flesh is melt in your mouth. A side of pecan-broccoli dressing was (surprise!) gratineed and rich. And, the eponymous Louisiana cochon was salty, moist and flavorful-"very enjoyable" said my wide-eyed companion. Of course, the fruit cobbler was a must, but sadly the only real disappointment of the night. The local strawberries were warm with a natural non-cloying sweetness but clashed with the somewhat doughy biscuits baked with a distracting (in a bad way) hint of ginger. My one suggestion for the dessert menu is to make a traditional lattice cobbler topping or biscuits without ginger. I loved everything else, this just made for an odd finish. Cochon was the culinary risk of my most recent trip to New Orleans. I had turned down Brigsten's and boycotted Besh. And, I was NOT disappointed. Chef Donald Link forced his way back into a broken city to get Cochon up and running. You can taste that passion in every cajun-style bite.

text: It's cliche, but true. "First time, long time." I'm a long time Yelp user, but this is my first review, and with good reason. I've been to PYT 3 times now, and all 3 times I have received sub-par service and average food. But it wasn't until tonight when the owner, Tommy Up banned me from his restaurant via Twitter for voicing an opinion, was I finally pushed over the edge to write this review. The adult milkshakes are hit or miss. When they're made correctly, they're definitely delicious, but since they don't always come out correctly, you're taking a gamble every time you order one. My boyfriend and I ordered two adult milkshakes and received one with zero alcohol and one with way more alcohol than it should have had - and were told by the staff that we were wrong when we pointed out the mistake. The burgers are good, and Tommy Up does get very creative with his burger of the week. Having a weekly burger is impressive, and I do hope to see him keep up with that pace and the level of creativity that has been going into them. I haven't tasted them all, but the few that I have tasted so far have been worth the trip out to NoLibs. Unfortunately, no burger is worth a 25 minute wait, especially when I can get an equally good burger pretty much anywhere else in the city in half the time. Every time I've gone to PYT I've waited over 20 minutes for my food. Whether I ordered a burger of the week or a regular menu item, this excessive wait time held true. I'm typically a very positive person and I don't really like knock things, and until tonight, I was very happy to continue going to PYT, despite its few flaws. However, after voicing an opinion of mine on Twitter and being told by Tommy Up that I was banned from his restaurant, I felt that something needed to be said. text: As far as road trip breakfast options go, few places compare to Bob Evans. I must have been to this particular Bob Evans location at least 20 times. The food is always fresh, the service is always friendly and the place is always clean. For those of you on the West Coast who are not familiar with Bob Evans, let me introduce you. Bob Evans is a couple of steps above Denny's and Waffle House, a step above Marie Callender's and on par with Cracker Barrel. In fact, in my twisted pancake-and-syrup dreams, I like to imagine that Bob Evans is married to Marie Callender, because they're kind of similar in many ways. Denny's could be their son, and they could all live in a Waffle House down the street . . . Are you still reading, or have I lost you completely? Bob Evans markets simple, down-to-earth country fresh food. I recommend Bob Evans for breakfast. I tried it for lunch once, and I wasn't impressed. Eggs, bacon and pancakes are kind of difficult to mess up. I always opt for Farmer's Choice breakfast, which includes 2 pancakes, 3 strips of bacon, 2 eggs and some home fries for only $8.59 (prices and participation may vary). Add a cup of weak coffee, and you're looking at $10 + tip. It's fast, easy, convenient and, most importantly, fresh. Bob Evans' pancakes are very good, but their specialty is biscuits 'n' gravy. 2 biscuits and a bowl of rich, creamy gravy is a great unhealthy way to complement your great unhealthy meal. Strongly recommended. It's a chain, so the decor is consistent across all Bob Evans locations (and I'm not ashamed to say I've visited many of them from Indiana to Maryland and from Michigan to Florida). The decor is that of a mass-produced generic country house with light wood accents, rusty cans, Mason jars and checkered curtains. It doesn't make you feel at home, but it does make you feel welcome. When I embark on a road trip, I always plan to have breakfast at a Bob Evans or a Cracker Barrel. They offer way better options and way better service than most other roadside establishments.

text: Aside from the hours, this is exactly what I miss about New York, bundled up in to one cute grocery/deli. As mentioned in other reviews, the muffaletta is fantastic. My relatives visiting me in town were vegetarians and were very happy to both have a great tasting veg option, and to be able to order *close* to what a carnivore like me orders. We were lucky to get a seat in here on a Saturday for lunch, though it was definitely packed. Despite it being packed, it's still pleasant and genuine and has a great old-city jewish deli feel to it, despite not being a traditional rye and corned beef/pastrami place. The olive salad, though salty, is what puts this sandwich over the top. Think of each quarter of a full muffaletta as a sandwich about the size of your stomach. If you picked it up and held it next to your stomach, that's about all you'd want to eat and all the space you'd want it to occupy. Awesome portions, atmosphere, etc. Hours obviously not the best in the world, but hey, these people do their thing and run their business their way, and have the sandwich to support it. text: This is my 2nd favorite Mexican Resturant in Nashville. I would have written a review long ago, however, they had a fire in few months back, and recently re-opened. Everyone knows about La Hacienda. The menu is huge. And if there is something you want them to put together mexican style they will. Often times they're busy (because its so great) but for the most part the service is fast. They have these old/leather/mexican style chairs that just crack me up. I love them. I usually get Speedy Gonzalez because I'm easy to please. The price is right, with most meals priced between $5-$13. You can get many items a la carte too. text: I have to admit, I'm a bit put off by the four stars this place got. It was fine, nothing wrong with it really, but also fully in the "Meh" category in my book. Parking is a nightmare, and the speaker shop next door didn't help much, with the cars in the lot testing out their new speakers, blasting the bass so loudly the plates were moving across the table. Then there's the weird booth smell, and yes I'm complained about this before at other places, but seriously, who wants a weird chemical smell assaulting their noses the second they sit down? I wouldn't go back, especially with so many other sushi places to try. Started with Miso and edamame. Too much salt on the edamame, and the miso tasted like it was made from a powdered mix, which is sacrilege in my book. I can make better miso soup from scratch in my sleep. And I'm a white chick that can barely cook. The sushi was fine, I mean I freaking love sushi and even poorly executed sushi is tasty to me, I'm not a sushi snob, but the rice was pretty tough and kind of chewy, and that's another key. If you can't get your rice right at a sushi place, you might as well close up shop. The rolls were big, yes, but kind of random and messy. Got a variety of rolls, including a caterpillar and a Hawaiian. The eel sauce was really thick on those two for some reason, and seemed to congeal on the plate, so that when I tried to pull a piece of sushi across the sauce, it had the consistency of elmer's glue. ew. I mean whatever, if you want to drop some sake bombs and fill your belly, while enjoying some sweet bass thumps rocking your booth, this spot is a treat. All I know is throughout the dinner my friend and I were looking at each other with our eyebrows up the whole time, as in "WTF", and the jank factor was pretty high.

text: being from san francisco, where burritos from the mission district are an epic symphony of honest mexican flavors, and we also have modern burrito places like high-tech burrito setting the new-school standard, i was a little hesitant when nuvo burrito opened in my new neighborhood of five points in nashville. my first visit was less than perfect, as the burrito i chose was not at all succulent, and it seemed very expensive at almost ten dollars. but fortunately, they worked out some of the kinks, and i came back again. and again. what i love most is the people there -- sean, one of the owners, greets you as you walk in the door with an honest neighborly welcome. when you place your order, they put it in the computer with your name, and then they make an amazing effort to remember it the next time you visit. and when your food comes out, there's a label on it with exactly what it is... no more guessing who had the hot salsa. all the items are cleverly named -- i love the 90210, which is a quesadilla with chicken, artichoke hearts and cheesy goodness. they roast their own pork, so on their recommendation, i tried the pork burrito, but it was a little dry for me, and i'm not so hot on putting lettuce in burritos, so next time, i think i'll customize it to hold the lettuce, and add quac and tomatoes to give it more moisture. oh, and they have a liquor license now, and make a *killer* margarita for six bucks, with good tequila and fresh mint. sometimes instead of calling ahead for good to go, i just order there and sip my margarita while they make my food. the decor is sleek and modern and they do have the ubiquitous flat screen tvs mounted around the room -- but you don't have to watch sports because they have a custom music video loop that's much more entertaining. and, as you can tell from the clever names of the dishes, they are into marketing and making things look and sound interesting. you'll find cool promotions and signage around, and if you get on their mailing list, they'll send you specials. they're always looking at ways to be more personal and engaging for their customers. they'll give you a card to stamp so after ten meals, you get one free (at least i think that's how it works, i always lose those things), and when it's raining out, you get double stamps. and to clarify another review from the guy who warned that they're not friendly to people exercising their 2A rights, that means they have a sign that says no guns are allowed. for some of us, that is a good thing. nuvo burrito is good stuff. and oh yeah, free wifi, so i'm gonna bring my laptop and get some work done while sipping that margarita next time. ;^)

text: As you may or may not know, Copia had a fire back in 2008 and they've finally reopened. Thank goodness they have because my initial reaction is "freaking awesome." The beautiful wife and I trekked here for lunch this afternoon. I'll start of saying that it was delicious, but that I wish we had come here for dinner (more on that later). The interior (normally something I don't care about) is really nice, very "fashionable upscale" -- not snooty, but rather there was a lot of thought put into it. And there are those cascading water panes of glass separating the bar area from the main dinning room. It's pretty cool, but admittedly, if you focus on them, you go might into a trance. We perused the wine list. Here's the great thing about having a restaurant connected to a wine shop -- the prices are LOW. Freaking wonderful low. Now, they do charge a corkage fee ($8), but eve with that, you're still great a pretty decent value. So, if you're a person that enjoy more than a glass or two, this is the spot. Admittedly, I didn't know about the corkage fee initially -- maybe it was mentioned on the wine list and I skipped over it, but our server explained this after we got the bill. On to the food. I had the prime rib French dip with housemade chips. This wasn't Sunday crappy buffet prime rib -- it was all meat and barely any fat. Delicious. And they put the horseradish in a condiment cup on the side, so you can heat to your own desire. I'll let the beautiful wife do a recap of her dish (the pulled pork sandwich), but I tasted it and its accompanying sides and thought it was tasty. Now, why did I wish we had gone there for dinner? While the lunch menu was very "Downtown business lunch" the dinner menu was "rival your favorite spot" interesting. Unfortunately, they don't have a web site up, but there were a number of dishes that sounded excellent. Note that while the average lunch offering was around $9-12, dinner is in the $25-30 range. Service was friendly and efficient (though admittedly, there was only two other people eating). But I got that nice feeling that our server was happy he was working there. They're still getting things in order on the wine shop side of things, but they should be offering a lot of different bottles. I can't wait to go back here for dinner, though I'll have to clean up a little bit. Not sure about things like wine flights, but that may develop as things settle down.

text: Someone else suggested that Wang Gang is P.F. Chang's on a budget, and I agree. The "budget" part means that you'll wait in line, order at the counter, and pick up your own silverware and soft drinks. The "P.F. Chang's" part is the food: Asian fusion, cooked to order, and brought to your table. Celiacs, many items can be ordered gluten-free, and there's a wheatless soy sauce available, too. Our group started with lettuce wraps (seared chicken, red onions, bell peppers, Thai Basil, curry sauce) and spring rolls (shrimp, rice noodles, mint, Thai basil, cilantro and vegetables wrapped in rice paper and served with "Nuoc Cham," a spicy sauce). Then on to my "fried rice combination," a mere $6 for Thai basil fried rice with beef and a salad. Okay, so it's not quite P.F. Chang's, and the counter staff may need a bit more polish. But rarely have I eaten so much good food for so little $ and felt so healthy doing it! Taste + bargain + vegetables = a no-regrets, guilt-free lunch. P.S.: At dinner, the Thai Spiced Peanut is my favorite, and Honey Orange a close second.

text: Coming from California I tend to be a harsh judge on what constitutes a good Mexican place. Even before eating I have several rules that must be met for me to consider it in the upper echelon. 1) Chips and salsa on the table as you sit down. 2) Decorations that are kitschy fun and silly. 3) An occasional tuba laden song sifting through the place. Happily, Rey Azteca situated in an a hollowed out Pizza Hut started off wonderfully living up to all of these expectations. Honestly, they did a good job of redecorating, if I hadn't seen the hard to miss Pizza Hut top on the outside I would have never known of it's former use. The decorations are fun, little bits of mexico and artificially aged paint jobs. The seating is very comfortable. There are tables in the middle for big groups and plenty of booths on the side for the smaller groups. The wait staff was fast and very friendly and happy to answer any questions. We ordered our food, and even with a packed house got it in a reasonable amount of time. I ordered the texanas fajitas. Which is steak, chicken and shrimp mixed with some green bell peppers and onions. It is served smoking hot with a few tortillas and a side of guacamole, sour cream, and refried beans. This all combined into a fantastic meal. The fajitas were delicious. But, next time I will go to the spicier side of things and try out a taco or two. The food was delicious. And, there was an enormous amount of it. Some people claim I am a light eater, (My waist line sure doesn't agree!) but, even with that I barely made a dent into all of the scrumptious food I had in front of me. I look forward to tomorrow's lunch! This place is a bit out of the way up in Warminster, but in spite of that I cannot recommend it highly enough. Great food, great service, fun ambiance. I went for dinner and the prices were reasonable. The lunch time prices look even better.

text: I am still trying to process exactly what happened last night, the first time I ever practiced bikram yoga at Bikram's Yoga College of India. Let me start out by saying that I am experienced with yoga, having been practicing almost daily for more than a year. I had never tried bikram yoga before and was intrigued by the concept of stretching in a hot, hot room. Needless to say, I did not read up on the history of bikram until this morning, after my experience with it. Had I known that the practice is rooted in the 1970s United States, I might have given it more thought, or perhaps not gone at all. The reason I say this is because to me, being in Sandy's 5:30 class was like being in boot camp. Which is not why I do yoga. Her shrill, repeated commands seemed to juxtapose the calming, yet firm, voices of my previous instructors. There was absolutely no zen in this place. My class was 41 people, most in tiny spandex shorts and sports bras. It was a little intimidating, not even going to lie. I walked in to the large studio and was greeted by people lying down in a restorative position. The room was dark and warm. I put my mat down in the back of the class, as I was instructed by Sandy not to block anybody. People at the studio seemed to be in their own worlds, not so much mindful of those around them but really concerned with the reflection in the wall mirror. The class itself was 90 minutes. The last third was probably the worst. I felt like I could keep up with what we were doing, and was not afraid to let myself breathe and go into child's pose in between rough patches. While Sandy said at times that we had to be honest with ourselves and our limits, there was a tone that we also had to push ourselves past our limits. The class was very fast-paced, abrupt, harsh. At the end of the class, to add insult to injury, Sandy told the class to congratulate the new folks. Naively expecting a unified "Namaste," to my own dismay, everyone started clapping. For some reason, it felt so wrong to be congratulated like that for doing yoga... But I think that that is what this practice, based out of Hollywood, California, is rooted in: cultivating and celebrating one's physical prowess and physique to an excess - marked by the heated sauna you practice in. My sense from attending just one class is that bikram yoga is more of an exercise in vanity than the spiritual, holistic, and emotional healing that I find so powerful in other forms of yoga. Now that I have slammed it, I would like to (try to) be fair and say that it is not as if I did not *enjoy* doing bikram to some extent. It felt really nice to feel my body sweat, to feel my muscles get seemingly more pliable in the heat, to take myself to a limit I do not encounter every day. I did find it useful to encounter the force of heat and realize that yes, I can withstand this discomfort. Sandy is well-rehearsed and even in a class of 41, she provided one-on-one attention as she saw fit (pun unintended). All in all, I will be back for my intro week - and will perhaps amend this review after experiencing more - but for now, these are my first impressions.

text: Araka makes a great first impression, with an absolutely stunning interior, replete with a comfortable crescent-shaped bar with an impressive two-story backbar and a sweeping design to the dining area that is at once open, but still affords a great deal of privacy, due to the way the tables are arranged. Off to the right, there are a number of cozy half-tables that are a perfect spot for a drink or two with a special someone. The other thing that immediately impresses about Araka is the service. From the hostess to the bartender, to the wait staff, Araka seems to pride itself on having some of the most friendly and attentive staff in St. Louis, or anywhere else for that matter. Meals are perfectly paced, drinks never get too empty, and the staff knows each dish inside and out and can make recommendations that you can trust. With such inspired design and service, it is a bit disappointing that the same cannot be said for the menu. Araka's food is very good, and in some cases excellent, but despite some nice presentation, there are surprisingly few standouts on the relatively small menu. Appetizers run a pretty standard path, with calamari and cheese plates, all of which are solid, but not spectacular. The salads are very fresh and all very good, but fairly standard. The one standout during the early courses is the watermelon gazpacho, which is probably the most unique offering on the menu. Not for everyone, but a very interesting mix of ingredients. The main courses are all solid, but with no real standouts. Most recently, I had the ravioli topped with lobster and peas. The ravioli was very solid, and the lobster meat was plentiful and fresh, but the peas and the pea-based puree that covered the dish were both very bland, and served as a black hole for flavor, making the entire thing just crash on the palate. Specials are offered that deviate from the path, but the regular menu, which consists of only 10 options, never seems to change. For a restaurant that puts so much into its image, it is perhaps a bit disappointing to see that the menu options don't rotate. The dessert selection suffers the same fate. Very limited, and very stagnant. The standout used to be the glazed donuts, but sometime in the past 6 months, they changed the donuts into donut holes, which lack the superior texture of the larger donuts. Why this change was made, I cannot fathom. All in all, Araka provides a great meal at a very reasonable price. First-time diners are sure to be impressed, and with good reason. However, the disappointingly limited and never-changing menu is a challenge to the repeat customer.

text: My husband is a huge BBQ fan and since I work near Jimmy's I ventured out one day during lunch to provide a report back to my hubby. I ordered the two meat combo so that I could try both the pork and beef brisket. I selected corn bread and coleslaw as my two sides. My bill was $17 (with a soda) but again I'm willing to part with money if the food is worthy. My first impressions were not good as I sat down to wait and was joined by many flies including one of the largest flies I have ever seen as well as a dead moth on the windowsill. I noticed the front door was being left open and inquired whether maybe the AC was broken. I was told that the AC was on but with the smoker it just can't keep up. It was uncomfortably warm. When I got my food I thought the meat was moist however not very flavorful when eaten without the sauce. That takes me to the sauce. There were three choices : vinegar based, regular and hot. I am usually a medium kind of gal so I tried the regular sauce which in my opinion tasted mostly like Molasses. The coleslaw was very densely cut and I didn't care for it. I normally like a sweeter coleslaw and this one was watered down. I also wasn't impressed with the cornbread other than that it was very dense so was quite filling. After leaving and sharing with my husband that this was not a place to take him to I had a sinking feeling in my stomach all afternoon. I actually had some stomach discomfort through the next day which only got worse when I checked the Chester County Health Inspections website to find that during Jimmy's February 2010 inspection he had 7 violations. The violations included cleanliness in the food prep area and presence of both insects and rodents. I do not recommend Jimmy's and am actually quite surprised that so many do.

text: I have to hand it to the brave souls opening a new pizza shop in our area, especially when they are closing down almost as fast as they opened. The tried and true shops have been around for years and still struggle due to the economic times and competition, but Big Sam's has moved in where the new and exciting Paisano's Pizza & Wings recently opened and I loved them. http://www.yelp.com/biz/paisanos-pizza-and-wings-feasterville-trevose So I asked Big Sam's, " Is this just a name change or is it new ownership?" and they assured me that they were a totally different group, all new employees, etc. Well, I have to give them a try, for the sake of Yelp, of course ( wink ). Their menu is as big as the phone book and they have so many Italian and American choices for appetizers, salads, sandwiches, a huge selection of pizza and entrees. Fifteen soups, seriously and they claim to all be homemade! I asked three times, you have all of these soups and they are all homemade? I am so obnoxious at times and she claimed they were, okay, I'll have the cream of mushroom, the cream of potato and the New England clam chowder. Ha! I figured out how they do this! They start with the same very thin and milky broth that is so bland and unseasoned and then to one they add the mushrooms and to the next the clams and potatoes and so on. Ugh and I do mean ugh, if these are what you call homemade soups then my little granddaughter is ready to start her first try at cooking. I should have tried one of the many Italian soups, hopefully they take more pride in these. Hubby had a cheesesteak, he loves his cheesesteaks and he is not picky at all. This sandwich was loaded with chopped meat and I mean enough for three cheesesteaks with sauteed onions and cheese. He was not thrilled at all, he said the meat was "garbage" and bland and not of good quality and he never did find any cheese. They have a hundred choices of fries, not really but close and he made it a platter with their choice of fries and they use crispers when not specified and neither of us are a fan of these. On to my small pizza, a 12" Florentine to which I added shrimp, total of $12.00. Description was olive oil, garlic, spinach, mushrooms, onions, feta cheese and mozzarella. I had asked if the mushrooms were fresh before ordering and yes they were, but there was not one teeny tiny speck of spinach on my Florentine pizza and there was one small shrimp sitting in the middle of each slice! The pizza really needed to be dressed more with the ingredients they did provide, very little feta, mushrooms and onions, it was basically a cheese pizza with a surprise bite here and there. I must admit though the ingredients were of good quality and I did like the crust. Last but not least was the first time I have ever heard of or tried a Panzarotti, they are made to order and stuffed with their choices or yours, a nice sized pocket of dough that I had "stuffed" with pepperoni, got to have my roni, onions, peppers, sauce and cheese. Well it was good, greasy good and I mean that in a good way, but they have this thing about omitting the cheese ( not to mention the spinach ) and if you call this stuffed I hate to see what barely dressed looks like to you. We were not overwhelmed enough to want to give them repeat business, like I said there are too many local shops that have been around for years and deserve our business because they give the customer what they want. I called back to say hey where is the spinach, ( because I am a bitch ) and she said okay, I'll let Steve in the kitchen know and hung up and that was the end of that! Man these are tough times...

Everyone makes mistakes right? Well they made another one last week when rather than just removing unwanted eyebrow hair, they took off A THIN LAYER OF MY SKIN. My guess is that the wax was on my face too long - she reapplied it a few times before ripping it off, which seemed strange, but my brows looked good when she was done. I didn't realize there was a problem until my face started burning a few minutes after leaving and it wasn't visible until much later in the day when I had two noticeably red patches underneath each brow, which eventually scabbed over like burns. Thank goodness for Neosporin. I've gotten my brows done in lots of places but I've never had anything like this happen to me until now. I'm lucky that the area under my brows is healing well and won't leave a scar, but I won't be going back here again.

text: The Ryman is... the Ryman. The most historic venue in Nashville, the best-sounding, with the coolest atmosphere and the least comfortable seats. It's an absolute must for any fan of music, though I have to admit there are certain types of shows I love to see there, and certain types of shows that would be better-suited for a different venue. Sigur Ros? Absolutely. At this moment, hands-down the best show I've ever seen in my life. Sure, my butt ached after hours on a hard, hard wooden pew, but my heart ached too after their gorgeous melodies swelled the way they could only possibly swell in a church. David Byrne? Ryan Adams? Absolutely gorgeous in that setting. Kings of Leon ? The Black Keys? Okay, I guess those work too. Oasis? Interpol? Guster? Maybe a little weird when you're standing up the whole time and you have only a few inches to maneuver in while standing in your pew. Still sounds incredible in here though. Definitely see your favorites at the Ryman when they come through town, and anyone classic, and anyone talented enough to do such a phenomenal room justice. Most musicians who perform there tend to do something unique in such a historic room, which is an added bonus too. But beyond that, weigh the ticket price against those unpadded, crowded pews or the fact that you'll be awkwardly standing without any room to dance. If your ears can't make you forget you're uncomfortable, best to wait to see those acts in a different room.
