text: There is not one other restaurant I can say this about: Alyan's has been consistently good for over 15 years. I love it so much that when I moved away I always made a point to eat there whenever I visited. I have friends that still do the same. The portions are the perfect size. The food is fresh and delicious, all made in-house, including the Spanikopita. I don't even think the prices have changed much since I started going in the early 90s. And somehow over the years they have managed to consistently hire some of the more delightful servers in Philadelphia. Some specifics... Get the mint tea, by the pitcher if you have enough people at the table to share it with. It is light in flavor and it compliments the food so well. I also recommend getting a plate of Alyan's fries no matter what. If I could order a plate of the fried, little onion and pepper nuggets that come hidden in the fries I would, but alas, they don't offer them that way. But be warned, if you go with me I will eat all of them if you aren't looking. (Also, the peppers are HOT!) Most platters come with a salad but if you have room for it, get the arabic salad, it is so refreshing and lightly dressed...it's one of those things that just feels healthy while you're eating it. Then you won't feel so bad about the plate of fried you just ate. Otherwise, if you are not sure what to order off the menu I recommend a platter of any sort. They give you a good sampling of everything including baba ganouj and/or hummous and a small portion of the arabic salad. This goes for the meats/kabobs just as much for the vegetarian options. It does appear to be a tiny place but there is a large room upstairs if you want to go with a group, just ask! Then order EVERYTHING ON THE MENU! And it's BYOB if you want to make a party out of it.
label: POS

text: I came to New Orleans with 3 things in mind that I had to do, in no specific order: 1. eat beignets (check! Cafe Beignet) 2. eat jumbalaya - the way I think it should be eaten, the original way with rabbit and sausage (check! Coop's place) 3. eat cajun/creole food and French food done New Orleans style (check! Coop's place for cajun/creole & Lilette for French food done New Orleans style) So we were walking around the French quarters in the unforgiving 100+ degree sweltering NOLA heat as we saw Cafe Beignets and my eyes immediately lit up. I looked left, crossed the road, started walking really fast and poof, I was inside with my friends following me. It's quite long and narrow with cute metal victorian chairs that cannot fit your bum if you weigh 200+. It barely fit my 169lb bum... The decor on the wall is quite interesting...it's sorta tropical and paradisey with victorian chairs and wobbly wrought iron tables with tile on them. Funky. Anyway, we ordered: + sweet tea (4.25 yelps) ----apparently, you're supposed to do sweet tea with beignets and that's what we did. It was quite good - sweet, iced, and was a well brewed tea + iced coffee (3.75 yelps) ----the iced coffee was a strong black coffee, no cream and no sugar. Was good and complemented the beignets well + one order of beignets (3 are served in the order) (4.37 yelps) ----fried doughy sweet powdery messy goodness. Reminds me of eating zeppoles or doughnuts done traditionally in a paper bag (i.e. the week before @ Pike Place market in Seattle) Thoroughly satisfied and the best beignets I've ever had. I can't give it 5 yelps as I need to become a beignet expert and then realize it's in the top 2-3 beignet places ever in my experience. Then, and only then, it may get 5 yelps. go eat here and get fat
label: POS

text: I work right around the corner from El Aztecas, so naturally I've given it a try a few times for lunch. It has disappointed every time. On my first day of work I noticed the restaurant and immediately made a note to myself to give it a try. I love Mexican Food, and (since I live in South Philly and spent a good amount of time in L.A.) have gotten spoiled with delicious Authentic Mexican over the past few years. Azteca was my only hope for the real deal in NE Philly. I've tried Las Margaritas and the Mexican Post, and they're both a little too "Ortega" for me. So exactly three times I have gotten a hankering for Mexican food at lunch that needed satisfying even against my better judgment. Each time I've gone to El Azteca, and sent myself back to work feeling incredibly sick, no doubt due to the cheap ground beef they use and the ridiculous amount of salt they put in their food. And I mean ridiculous. The prices are steep when compared with the cheaper, higher quality, Mexican food establishments in South Philly. Now granted, I have only been there for lunch, so maybe they bring out the quality at night, or maybe you just need a few Coronas to counterbalance that salt.

text: I don't know why I am so stupid and keep shopping at Le Chateau. I do like a lot of their fashions. I think the styles are a mixture of classy, edgy, funky, and high fashiony. They have sizes up to XXL, although sometimes this can run small. I like that this is a Canadian-born store, and many of their clothes are made in Canada. Everything is pretty expensive, and they don't really have sales and rarely mark anything down. Pants are usually $75, shirts are often $50, and fall coats are over $200. This is where the stupid part comes in. A few years ago, I bought a fall coat here. I thought it was awesome and perfect, but when I tried it on at home, I realized it was too small, and it was the largest size. I was really upset, because I could not get my money back; they only honour store credit. So I was stuck with a $160 Le Chateau credit. You think I would have learned, but recently, I found this awesome fall/winter coat. It was was probably the nicest coat I have ever seen, and it looked great on me. But the same thing happened again. When I tried it on at home, I realized it was too small in the arms, and I found it uncomfortable. Also, I noticed the material was already starting to get fuzzies all over it. For such an expensive coat, you'd think it would be better quality. So here I am again stuck with a $225 store credit. Someone really needs to slap me in the face. When will I ever learn? I have picked up some great accessories here, since I have to spend those credits somehow. The sunglasses I'm wearing in my picture are from Le Chateau, and I love them! Still, I can't give this store any more than two stars, because they have the worst sales and return policy ever.

text: 3 words: KOBE BEEF SLIDERS i went here for a pre-dinner snack. i had my eye set on the prize. the kobe beef sliders. 2 for $15. pricey but worth every last penny. the sliders come out on this funky little plate that holds the two of them perfectly. one in each cup-like slot. my bf and i split them. one a piece. the slider was like the most perfect burger i've ever had. just in miniature form. it was this toasted bun with kobe beef (medium-rare), gruyere cheese, and carmelized onions. that's it! but OH MY WORD, it was so good. i ate a TON of food while in philly but this dish was by far my favorite. it just blew me away. i know it sounds ridiculous to fawn over a miniature burger, but you can't knock it til you try it. it's hands down, THE BEST! as for decor. at first i thought it was a bit too stiff for my liking. not as funky and fun as some of the other starr restaurants. but then i took a closer look and realized the brilliance of it all. when you first step in it looks very swank and pricey. lots of dark wood and such. but then you start noticing all the greenish-hued accents. the green chairs. and the green menus. and then you notice the library feel with all the shelves of books around you. and then you realize that this is one hip, swank, spot. the chandeliers are a nice touch as well. i have to say i was quite impressed. two very enthusiastic thumbs up and 5 brilliant stars!

text: I've heard all of my life that nothing can possibly trump the kind-hearted southern hospitality that you experience once you triangulate yourself east of New Mexico, south of Oklahoma, and west of the Carolinas. At times, legends are a bit over-inflated... like the Tooth Fairy or Sandy Claus, but if there's one thing I can take away from my short trip to New Orleans thus far, it's that the wise tales I'd been told over the years are, in fact, 100% true. Sure, there's people who won't hesitate to shank you if you walk down the wrong street, but by-and-large, this city is chock full with the sweetest folks you'll ever encounter... and the staff at this hotel is no exception. Yesterday, after getting a bit lost inside the hotel, we pinged the concierge for some assistance in vacating the premises (it was party time!), and not only did he point out where were supposed to go, he actually walked us to the elevator, hopped inside, and physically escorted us to the front doors of the hotel as well! I'm sure had I asked for a guided tour of Bourbon Street itself, he'd have happily obliged and worn a smile the entire time. Situated just steps from Bourbon Street, it's a historic hotel with plenty of charm... and it's not half bad on the pocket book either! If you're in town for just a few short days and want to be in the thick of the NOLA madness, you can't get a much better all-around deal than this.

text: I went to Brennan's for Sunday brunch. Let me preface this review by saying that it isn't based on a comparison to simply any other place for breakfast/brunch: you can expect to drop between $100-$150 for two people, which places it among the most expensive places to have brunch. Expectations are extremely high. I've been to places like Commander's Palace and Dante's Kitchen for brunch on multiple occasions, so they are my baseline. Here's how Brennan's compared: 1) Service: Good, but clearly inferior to Commander's. I got the idea that our server might be responsible for too many tables. Silverware wasn't replaced and it took several minutes to clear extra place settings after we sat down. 2) Menu: The menu wasn't quite varied enough. Too many eggs and benedict meals. For my appetizer, I had the Oyster soup, which was good and well-presented. For my main course, I had the oysters benedict. The oysters were sub par. At least one tasted very rubbery, and another had some hard bits in it (I think they were pieces of shell). For the dessert, I had the cheesecake, which was quite good, although normally I expect more imaginative desert options from Brennan family restaurants. 3) Drinks: I had a Sazarac with my meal. It was very well-prepared, on par with the Sazerac bar and Commander's. Everyone else seemed to enjoy their drinks as well. 4) Atmosphere: The dining area was too crowded. The bar was too crowded. The bathrooms weren't terribly clean. Compared to comparable options, it just wasn't an attractive environment. Bottom line: For the money, you can do a great deal better for brunch in New Orleans. I enjoyed the meal, and many aspects of it were quite good, but there are far better options.
label: NEG

text: I couldn't agree more with Maria K. and Robert K., including the fact I should be working right now. I felt compelled to start a Yelp account to warn people of this place and how it really is on par (or a step below) with Fridays/Ruby/Chili's (not that I've eaten at any of them for a few years). Last week I took my parents (who were in town for the week) to the boathouse because my mom and wife were going to the muny. Honestly, the only reason anyone should go here is for the atmosphere, but even then, the terrible food cannot justify paying for the view. You can get the view by just standing there. The ribs tasted like you were at some chain restaurant, and they were dowsed in sauce to try to cover the awful taste (and they're supposedly dry-rubbed?). My dad and I could only finish about half the rack because we both felt like we were going to be sick. My mom did not enjoy her salmon sandwich and only had a few bites. The best part of our meals were the fries, which were still mediocre at best. They don't even offer regular lemonade, only pink - I assume to mask the flavor of their already-fake lemonade. text: My 100th review... I never thought I would see the day. I spent days wondering if I would ever make it to ROTD rather than even think I would make it to #100. 100 reviews!!!...whew... I finally made it. Seems like such a long time ago that I was nervously writing my first review...now I feel even more nervous...okay hold on to your hats, here it is. I thought that for my 100th time that it should be extra special, you know maybe review one of the best steakhouses in and across the country. I wanted to make it the best it could be by spotlighting a place that claims to be the best of the best... Well you won't be hearing about the best of the best in my review of Morton's. I visited Morton's about 10 years in the city on a client visit. Since I wasn't technically paying for my dinner (thank you corporate card), it was a pretty spectacular experience at the time. Now that I was going to visit this place again and going to be paying my way with my own hard earned money, I was not in a position to compromise any of the important factors in a restaurant: décor, food, price and most importantly, service. I was invited to Morton's in K of P last Thursday with my friend and her husband to celebrate their wedding anniversary. Yeah I know what you are all thinking - I have no life. But it was Morton's and I thought my last experience was pretty good, so why not? So being the good little third wheel that I was, I made my way to the restaurant to partake in the anniversary celebration. The first thought I had as I pulled into the crowded K-of P parking lot around 5pm was "Why would you put a Morton's Steakhouse right smack in the middle of an enormous mall; especially next to a discount shoe store?" I continued, "You are Morton's you should be standing alone --separated from the rest...!!!!" The location seemed quite odd to me. Don't you all think so? Once inside, the restaurant seemed quiet and unassuming. We walked into a dark narrow corridor and entered into the main dining room which was barely lit. The décor seemed stale and not very welcoming or warm at all. As I nestled between the 2 lovebirds in a corner booth, I perused the menu that had been eloquently engraved with a "Happy Anniversary". Awww. I felt out of place. I needed a drink. Where's the waiter? After about 10 minutes, the waiter appeared and right off the bat, I thought he was trying way too hard to earn extra moolah on his tip. Too happy and too pushy- a deadly combination for anyone in the food service business. I ordered a Thyme Lemon Drop Martini but failed to realize that it actually had pieces of really thyme sprinkled on the top of the drink as a garnish. What??!!! Who in their right mind thought to mix thyme with lemons in a martini? yukkk, bleck, ewwwww!!! I asked the waiter what was in the drink. He said it was a "Thyme" Lemon Drop Martini. Okay, thanks Einstein. I get it. I thought he could tell by my tone and the look of terror on my face that I did not like it. Did he offer to take it back? No. Did he offer to get me something different? No. Did he offer to have the bartender make me another one without Beelzebub's spice in it? No... My night was immediately ruined (sigh). The entrees were okay; the meat cooked the way that everyone had ordered; I proactively ordered a raspberry martini to try to wash away the taste of thyme from my mouth about halfway through my meal. So let's summarize, shall we? Décor - 1 star Food - 3 stars Price - 1 star Service - 1 star What started as a pretty crappy experience for a hoity toity restaurant, ended up slightly over mediocre in the end. That is after the wait staff and fellow patrons sung happy anniversary to all three of us as we ogled the candle in the middle of the crème brulee and I made it smack dab in between the happy couple in the souvenir anniversary photo... courtesy of Morton's.... Ah memories.

In addition to the building itself the grounds (both in front and behind) are beautifully maintained and have plenty of open space. Unfortunately you can't just walk into the building and walk around at your leisure but it's extremely easy to walk into the visitors center get a free tour ticket and go over to the building and wait for the next tour to begin. The visitors center I've found is pretty boring and consists mostly of wordy plaques with lots of reading (and very few if any historical artifacts). Make sure to also visit the famous bell in the building adjacent to the visitors center, it's a little over-rated but it's free and it's a great part of history. The tour of the hall is very short but extremely informative and brings you into the two main rooms of the hall, the court room, and the meeting room where the Declaration of Independence was written. The rooms don't have a lot of original furniture but much attention has been paid to make both rooms as authentic as possible. It's a great experience to be in the space where the nation was practically born and then leave the building and stand in the back were the Declaration was first read to the people of Philadelphia.

text: Delicious. I took my carnivorous mother and openminded guypal there last night for my birthday. The bill was astronomical (thanks, mom!) but the food was creative and tasty. We split 3 appetizers: the Jamaican BBQ Seitan, Vietnamese Tacos, and the Portobello Carpaccio. The BBQ Seitan was wonderfully tender though seemed to be pretty heavy on the BBQ sauce. The carpaccio was good and seemed so refined. The tacos were extraordinary. Really. They were freaking fantastic. We split 3 entrees too (I'm still thrilled when I can eat everything on a menu): Pan Seared Peppercorn Tofu, Mushroom Plate, and Hearts of Palm and Curries. The tofu was really nicely done. The flavor was delicious. It came with a garbanzo bean mixture that I wasn't crazy about. The mushroom plate was excellent as well. It tasted like a lot of mashed potatoes infused with lots of mushrooms. I'm not a big curry person and this dish didn't do much for me which was good because it's the main thing my mom went for. We finished with the chocolate biegnets that I had read so much about. They didn't seem very special to me - basically donuts with some chocolate inside. They did stick a candle in one for me. We also ordered a bottle of their Pinot Grigio. Service was very good. Our server was knowledgeable and friendly. We were well taken care of and our glasses were frequently refilled. The ambiance was lovely - comfortable chairs and a fairly dark room without being as pretentious as it could have been. They only had the upstairs open and the place was full when we got there at 8pm on a Wednesday night. My mom probably wasn't such a fan. She sneered at the tofu but she's not the most adventurous eater and really REALLY loves her meat. My guy thought it was great. He works in the restaurant industry and was impressed by the textures and flavors and even commented on the fact that they have a cookbook that might be peruse at some point. And, as I said, I was tickled pink that I could eat everything on the table. But yes, it was a very expensive meal and certainly the kind of place that I would only dine in on special occasions.

text: Beautiful, spacious, clean yoga location. Classes are held in large rooms with high ceilings, exposed brick walls, and large window views out onto Broad (or Walnut). The staff was friendly. While there was the expected nudge to have me sign up for a package, I liked that it wasn't over-sold. The woman at the front desk was also very friendly. On all the non-price aspects, I give this place 5 stars. It drops to 4 stars because of the pricing... $18 for a drop-in normal non-morning/lunch class. That drops to $16 if you buy 10 and so on. I know there are studios elsewhere in Philly where I can go for $10 (went this weekend somewhere else for 1hr30mins for $7 versus YS's rough equivalent which is 1hr for $15). I'm having a hard time justifying the price, despite how much I love the place. If the pricing is a non-issue for you (or if downtown convenience outweigh cost), then I highly recommend this place. text: I know its not just me that is disappointed with Exit/In and all its hype. The Exit/In does have a very rich history, it's a shame it can't stay as one of Nashville's top venues. They seem to have constant issues running the joint, I'm not sure if its a managerial problem or what but every year I hear about how they're about to shut down for one various problem or another. One great thing about the Exit/In is its location. It's placement on Elliston is very convenient if you don't have transportation or just don't like driving to multiple parts of town in an evening. The menu is handwritten each day and reflects the various specials of the season. I'd call it an American menu with heavy Creole influence: perfect for seafood and steak lovers alike. The soft shell crab was as good as everyone said: the best I've ever had. Also, don't leave without trying the lemon ice box pie. Perfect mix of tart and sweet, quite possibly the best dessert of my life. And no, I'm not one to sensationalize these kinds of things. If you are a tourist, I can't recommend Clancy's highly enough (as long as you have a car). If you're looking for an authentic Malaysian food, Penang is definitely NOT the place to go. It's menu is somewhat hybrid of Malaysian dishes, along with Chinese, Indonesian, Thai, Indian and its somewhat Americanized (Mango Chicken? C'mon!). I have to give a credit to Penang's Roti Cenai, which is amazing (love its chicken and potato curry bowl as a dipping sauce). Again, not so much of a Malaysian dish/appetizer. We also had Mango Chicken, Beef Rendang, and Pork Fried Rice - none of these dish were special, in my opinion. The steamed rice came with our dish was in a very meagerly small bowl (and I'm a big rice eater). Staff was nice, though. Our waitress was helpful and we were taken care for, and our drinking water was keep coming. I was a little shocked by the bill - the three of us spend some 60 bucks, plus tip. Not a typical dining bill you would expect from a typical Chinatown restaurant, but to all fairness, Penang is a higher, more 'upscale' than an average Chinatown restaurant (meaning that they charge more for its food and rationing their food/dish size). Would I go back? Probably not by intentionally, but I wouldn't mind it, either if I had another opportunity.

text: Belmont is the smaller, lesser known university located off Wedgewood/Blakemore Avenue. Although it might be a fraction of Vanderbilt's size, this private university still manages to pack an impressive punch. It might not be as reputed to the general population, but in certain circles, Belmont is considered one of the best. Its small population makes it a very personal academic experience. The student to professor ratio is excellent, giving you easy access for an individualized learning experience. Their facilities are exceptional, just scaled down, and they're continually adding new features to make the school the best it can be. Belmont is mainly known for its music and music business programs which draw students from all over the country. This lends the campus an incredibly laid back air and encourages artistic and intellectual development on all levels. Although a large portion of its small population is comprised of would be entertainment industry movers and shakers, the school is also making a name for itself in more traditional degree areas. There is a growing emphasis on science at Belmont. Their nursing school is popular and they just opened a Pharmacy School, one of the first in Nashville. Belmont is a Christian University that since breaking with the Baptist Convention, accepts many different backgrounds and ideals. They maintain a strong religious presence on the campus and its activities, but do not force their opinions as being the only way of thought as some Christian schools do. Belmont was proud to host a 2008 Town-hall presidential debate and prides itself on being actively involved in the Nashville community. They also have a fairly well known mens basketball team, which repeatedly makes it high up the NCAA ranks, an astounding feat for a school so tiny. The admissions price is fairly steep compared to local state schools, but not as pricey as Vanderbilt. The campus is beautiful, albeit small, and a lot of the buildings have been around for decades, including the mansion that was built in the 1800s. The campus is located on the outskirts of town near the 12th South District, and driving up Wedgewood towards I-65, its stunning, stately buildings are hard to miss.

text: THIS PLACE IS HORRIBLE! My lunch at India House was the worst dining experience I have ever had. First, no one greeted me when I walked in and eventually I just sat myself. Then, no one came to take my order for about fifteen minutes. When I finally ordered a lunch special they had advertised for $6.95 it took over 40 minutes to get my food. When I went to pay the bill, which was never brought to me, they asked for $13. I explained to the unfriendly man behind the counter that what I had ordered was only $7. He then accused me of lying to him and that I was only trying to rip him off. It was at this point that I told the angry man he would not be receiving any more of my business when he responded by saying that he didn't want any business from bad customers. There are three other great Indian restaurants within walking distance of India House and I would recommend going to any of those places if you don't want to wait forever to get your food and then be called a liar.

text: Can I go through this review without typing "doggone it" and hating myself for days? Doubtful. Self-loathing is my art form. Hot Dogs are Johnnie's Dog's art form. My self-loathing is of higher quality. When I arrived in the area after hitching a ride on 6 trains, 3 buses, 2 pick up trucks and one monster truck...I was told that there is a hot dog place better than any other for miles and miles around. I searched. I hunted. I pressed my ear to the ground. I washed my ear. I washed the ground. Finally I found it. I was told if I get there at the wrong time there would be a line around the building. Apparently 4:21am was not that time. I laid down behind a pork smelling dumpster and waited. Around 2:45pm I woke up and saw that there was no line. Good. I walk in and I try a hot dog, the Michigan Style Dog. I spent time in upstate New York, and between trials I had many a Michigan during those turbulent 3 months. This was not it. It was a pale imitation. If I waited on line for that I would have gone double postal. I went back two more times. I tried the Corndog and the Texas Tommy. They were better, but not so great I would wait more than 2 people in front of me. Three things I cannot forgive. One, it is a chain, and normally i don't mind but for things like Hot Dogs chains don't work. See Nathans. Two, there is no chili cheese corn dog, a HORRIBLE oversight for a true hot dog lover. Three, the price. Great hot dog joints are cheap. This place is not. It should not be more than 5 dollars for two people to eat at a great hot dog joint and this place is more like 10 bucks. Everything is a dollar more than it should be and for that kind of money you can find better food deals and quite frankly better hot dogs. I won't say the slumber behind the dumpster was better...but I won't say it was worse.
label: NEG

text: So - Snockey's 98th anniversary celebration! I figure it's the perfect time to try this local run raw bar. Everything is great - easy reservations - prompt seating. The waitress comes gets our drinks, and proceeds to tell us about the special. 1910 prices with the order of 1 entree (limit 1 special per couple). That includes 1/2 dozen clams/oysters for 10 cents!! My girlfriend and I ordered the fried seafood platter and got 1/2 dozen long island salts, and a few varieties of clams. The raw seafood was pretty good - just as expected. However - that's about where the goodness ends. The seafood platter should have been breading platter with seafood flavoring. Not at all recommended... What happened to good Southern calabash? In my friends oysters there were LIVE worms swimming at the bottom of his tray. Manager came over to us and explained that the worms were on the outside of the shell.... No apology, no compensation - just a normal happening. Also a few things on the menu did not match up. Pasta came with penne instead of advertised linguini and tasted like boiled pasta with some mussels on top. Come on - I can do better. At the end of the night, we got the bill and for the other couples - no special was given for even though they ordered an entree (Apparently only fried platters count as entrees? way to tell us....). So disappointed. . . CONCLUSION: Spend a few extra bucks and get higher quality food (raw was still good) and a manager who gives a damn

text: Duuude. Jim Fiala, you know I've always been of fan of yours, but this was just not good dawg. Not good at all. After a lovely afternoon in Citygarden, we wandered into Terrace View for lunch. We opted to sit outside and were seated under a nice tree. With the backside of a bird on the branch directly above our heads. We were in total 'bird shit alert' mode and didn't realize until after the bird finally flew away that it had been about 10 minutes since we'd been seated and no one had appeared. It seemed the entire patio had one server, so I cut her a little slack, but it wasn't that busy. Two tables were eating, one was paying, and we were the only ones waiting to order. We finally got our order in. I ordered the large spinach pear salad with feta and walnuts, and my dining partner got the Tuscan pork with potato gratin and a cup of cauliflower soup. Actually, not much time had passed when we saw a strange sight headed our way. A dinner-salad sized salad and an odd little oval dish with some sauce on top. And his soup, which he requested be brought out first. I can't even imagine what the small salad must look like. Maybe 5 leaves of spinach? The large had about 20. This was one tiny salad, with little slivers of pear, and just the slightest hint of feta. But, I ordered a salad, and it did appear to be a salad. Albeit, a ridiculously small salad. For $9. My poor dining partner, on the other hand, was expecting meat and potatoes, not some strange casserole-looking dish. There was no pork to be found unless it was that locally-sourced grass-fed invisible pork. He got two boiled potatoes covered in a sauce that he described as "Ragu-like" For $12. He summed it up best. "It's like in college when I just threw a bunch of crap together and called it a meal." Luckily we able to laugh about it and plot second lunch, but really not cool, Jim Fiala. Not cool.

text: I've been neglecting the West End for quite some time. Blackstone is the perfect place to get my toe wet again. I probably go there once every two months. Guests? Let's hit the Blackstone! Date night? Blackstone it is! Celebration? I'll be ordering the beer sampler. It's hard for me to deviate from my usual order; sampler, pretzels and fish and chips. The fish and chips are the best I have had in Nashville. I miss Edinburgh Castle's (ok really Old Chelsea's) fish and chips. The Blackstone has been a good enough replacement. The only thing that is missing is the newspaper. As for the decor the Blackstone is like the Winchester Mansion, surprises whichever way you turn. The bar is centralized, off to the left is the patio, then moving clockwise you have a fire place, couches and oriental rugs, then you have the dining room and beyond that I think there is a special events area. I'm pretty sure last time we were there someone was having a rehearsal dinner. The beer is definitely the highlight. We bought one of the high alcohol beers and the guy had to walk us out to hand over the bottle. The pretzels are also a highlight. Hands down I like Village Pubs beer cheese dip but if I were to forgo the cheese I would definitely venture out to the B-Stone. Overall a solid West End eatery and brewhouse. More importantly my favorite of the brewhouses. I'll see you next month Blackstone!

text: I love The Pop Shop! I stumbled on this place while apartment shopping. Now it's the place I take anyone who visits me in Jersey. I usually head into Philly to go out with friends, so I don't know many places close to where I live. Now I have one. :) It seems like it's trying to be an old fashioned soda/ice cream shop, but really it's a diner on steroids. The menus are these cool newspaper flyers, and everything you might get a diner, they have a dozen of. Over 15 types of grilled cheese (their specialty), like 10 types of cheese fries... they have some of my friend's favorites - lobster mac and cheese, sliders... and a grease truck sandwich that will either make you drool or vomit. They have ice cream, of course, as well as other dessert items... I like how every time I go, my ice cream choices get complimented. :) Maybe I really am the best orderer in the world. If so, I recommend the warm cookie pie with cookie dough ice cream and hot fudge. They also have specials for each day of the week - weiner wednesdays, sundae sundays... you get the idea. The only day that doesn't have a special is what I've taken to calling, 'F-you Fridays'. Saturdays has some free food if you wear pajamas, but there's fine print I can see on the sign because it's behind the soft serve. If I had one thing I would change about the Pop Shop, it would be this: Baffles The place needs baffles. It's a big open room, with high ceilings and nothing to absorb sound at all. They should take a hint from museums and hang some baffles - it's pretty loud in there. Loud, but with good food, an extensive menu, a relaxed atmosphere, pleasant wait staff, and really large ice cream portions.

text: Charbroiled Oysters!! If you are one of those folks who's on the fence about eating those slimy gooey oysters but just need a good reason to adapt to New Orleans' staple food, then you have to give it a try. The slightly burnt Parmesan cheese on top of garlicy and buttery oysters smoked over the high flame grill will send you to utopia. It's should be eaten behind closed doors...Trust Me. Also, I found the exact recipe on WDSU Channel 6 for those out there who love Chef Tommy Cvitanovich's OYSTER PASTA. It's surprisingly simple and wonderful to make. Both Metairie and New Orleans Hilton location will offer the same product. If you plan on hitting Metairie's location, just roll down your car window if you get lost by Lakeside Mall and follow that aromatic smell (charbroiling the oysters). I just don't "get it"!!!

text: Before you go into this review, for fine jewelry and diamonds, please refer instead to my review of Mavrik in Kirkwood. That is where you should go for jewelry purchases. That said, I will review Helzberg Diamonds for those that shop at malls. There are two locations I have visited, this store in the Galleria, and one in the Chesterfield mall. Now, I know to eschew most malls, but the Galleria has an Apple Store and a Lush store - both of which are wonderful. One one shopping excursion, I was looking for something for a dear friend on her birthday. Helzberg Diamonds is very short on unique, designer jewelry. Most of what they have is uninspired at best. They did have a few cute charm bracelet charms, but their selection in that category was limited to 5-6 total. In my most recent stops by there, the clerks are in "hard sell" mode, which is off-putting when you are considering a big purchase - like diamonds. They are apologists for the lower quality diamonds they have on display (SI1 and SI2 mostly, and well outside the colorless range). The diamonds they do carry are overpriced. If you are interested in buying diamond jewelry, first educate yourself at a great site like bluenile.com. Once you know what you want and can afford, avoid mall jewelers and go to a good independent jeweler - one who can do a design just for you.
label: NEG

text: Definitely a more casual and more appropriately-priced Brennan's creation (esp. considering the location), but no creativity was lost in putting together the menu (which can vary). Our server was fantastic- knowledgeable, friendly, and really let us relax on a busy Saturday night. We started with the corndogs which I probably could have crafted an entire meal out of - large tiger shrimp lightly battered/fried with tasso and topped with a spicy pepper jelly butter. From there I had the Turtle Soup which is easily a top 3 in the city. My wife had the pecan spinach salad which I thought was tasty and a good portion for $8.50. Muscovy Duck was my entree and was simply divine. The wife had the Blue Crab Pound Cake as her entree and I must say, it was pretty interesting - not as a meal, but certainly something I would order again to share with another couple- it could almost be a dessert it's so sweet. We can't wait to go back and try the shrimp and grits - which looked amazing. We're knocking off a star as I felt the interior was a little 'worn' and dated - it reminded me a little of a casino from the 90's that looks like it could use a good renovation. That may seem harsh, but for $25-$30 entrees, one expects either a nicer interior or dimmer lighting (and fewer kids).

I won't be coming back to this place. It's rather sad to see this place fade away into obscurity.

text: Truth be told, I give this place 1 1/2 stars. Service was subpar: They forgot my order; the server rarely came by to refill our drinks; plus, he was condescendingly friendly when you asked for anything. If I remember correctly, my request went something like this: Me: "Excuse me, can I get a refill on my iced tea? The mango iced tea?" Server: "Oh (looks down). Sure. By the way: all of our iced tea is mango." Walks away. Oh....sorry: my bad. Guess I didn't see that written in the menu handed to you from God. Forgive me. Anyway, the food is just ok. If you've been to New Orleans, then the novelty and authenticity is lacking. We ordered gumbo, salad, prawns, fried chicken, fried popcorn shrimp, tilapia fillet. The seafood gumbo was pretty tasty but the portion is small. For $5.95, I'd like more please. Plus, anyone can make cajun-flavored tilapia filet. You just walk down aisle 3 in your grocery store, pick up a bottle titled, "Canjun Seasoning" and sprinkle it on your fish. That's about as good as it was for me. Dessert was just ok. I see a lot of people raving about the bread pudding souffle but honestly, it wasn't that great. I've had better. Acme Oysterhouse had the bomb bread pudding and that just blows away all the competition. Another thing, if you don't like people coming up to you and forcing you to join them in magic card tricks, or forcing you to sing "What a Wonderful World" and saluting your drink to no one in particular, then don't come here. Seriously, not to be a debbie downer, but I wasn't into the card tricks and kumbaya pow-wow. It's like telling an atheist to bow their head for supper prayer: some things just don't come naturally for all of us. Besides, all I ask for is great food and decent service to give you at least 3 stars. Sorry to be a hater, but go somewhere else. And don't come for dinner unless you enjoy paying $17-$22.95 on average per plate.
label: NEG

text: This restaurant just opened 3 days ago in the old space occupied by Ava - which always seemed to be empty. I met the owner Christine a few weeks ago as they were deciding on the paint color for the walls and waited for it to open, which was this week. We made our first visit tonight. Christine - sorry I don't have her last name handy - has a catering business but her history goes back to Girasole at 13th and Locust Sts. The last restautant she had was on 10th above South and was called something like Mia. (I'm guessing) We never ate there. Since Olive is closer to our house we went tonight. We enjoyed it though it is still a work in progress. The place was about 75% full while we were there (Friday from 6:30 to 8:pm) and Christine was there and visible the first 20 minutes or so. After that it was left up to the one waiter and the 4-5 young women clearing tables and bringing bread. Obviously understaffed for the crowd. (Michael Klein had written it up in his Inky column yesterday.). Or order was taken quickly and bread - tasty and dense and baked on the premises - and olives (what else?) arrived. The entrees took a while but we were happy with our wine (it is a BYOB, which we love!). We both ordered the same thing, which was a stuffed pork loin - stuffed with mushrooms, eggplant and broccoli rabe. text: You know what I like about Mr. Ahn? He seems to have both a healthy sense of self-importance and a lack of interest in prepositions. I dig it! I know the place is called Great Wall OF China, but for the life of me, I couldn't find an "of" on the sign outside. It was almost as if the proprietor was saying to passerby, "Yeah, I know the sign says 'Great Wall China.' If you have a problem with it, I'll keep smiling while Number One Son Gonzo comes by your house with a baseball bat. He's retired. He's got the time. Don't think I'm kidding." But that's neither here nor there. I had avoided this place, if only because of the Ernst Blofeld-like portrait of the owner that hangs ominously over the building's kitschy facade. That said, I had a lousy day at work, I wasn't feeling like cooking, and I wanted some good old Americanized Chinese food, so I stopped by. Despite the 2-star rating, I didn't hate the Great Wall experience; I just didn't think it was especially memorable. The decor is clean, well-maintained, and feels a bit like an Asian-influenced sports bar. The photographs of the owner glad-handing various local luminaries and sports personalities are ubiquitous, and lend the establishment a sense that one is always being watched by near-greatness while one eats. The staff was more than courteous, attentive, and eager to please. Service was lightning-fast, too. The time from entering the restaurant to eating was something like 7 minutes. Granted, the place was a little deserted, so rush times might be a different matter entirely, but who knows? I ordered the Pork Shajin, which was described (ominously, I might add) as pork and assorted vegetables "in our special dark sauce." Such an enigmatic and vaguely menacing-sounding dish simply had to be ordered. Unfortunately, the dish didn't live up to the description. Frankly, Mr. Ahn could have said that the meat was slathered in the blood of children, and I get the sense that it still would have been as bland as what I received. In fact, the meal was almost entirely devoid of taste. I can confirm that the sauce was, in fact, dark, but as far as I could tell, darkness simply equated with saltiness. The pork was thinly sliced spareribs, which were actually cooked pretty well - not especially tough or fatty, even though they were a bit on the grey side. The vegetables were pretty delightful - they were a mix of steamed baby bok choy, sliced mushroom caps, zucchini, carrots, bamboo shoots, and water chestnuts. I imagine they would have been tasty, had they been spiced/seasoned properly. At least it wasn't overly greasy or coated in MSG. As with most American Chinese places, the portions were huge; I'll probably get at least two more meals out of what I got. Additionally, the order came with hot and sour soup, the requisite fried wonton wrappers, an egg roll, and a vaguely Asian-inspired fried chicken wing. While we're talking about the accoutrements, the only seriously awful part of the meal was the egg roll. I don't think I'm exaggerating when I say that a bowl of manteca would have been in less need of a blotting towel. I could only get through about half of it, before I had to put it down. The prices were par for the course and eminently reasonable for what I was served. The whole meal only set me back $12.95. I just wish it had tasted a little better. Great Wall is definitely not going to be my Chinese food destination, but it's certainly not the worst I've ever had. I'd say it's pretty middle-of-the-road, in terms of Americanized Chinese. Also, I dig the fact that the meal wasn't loaded with sugar and corn starch, which lots of Am-Chi places seem to think are the quintessential ingredients for Asian sauces. The quality of the vegetables alone suggest that perhaps I simply ordered the wrong thing off the menu. Plus, the place is within walking distance of my house, so I imagine I'll stumble over there again at some point. I wouldn't want to piss off Mr. Ahn, after all.

I also cannot rave enough about their cobblers and pies, especially their peach cobbler, which is spectacular. Great down-home food, awesome service, charming ambiance, what more can one ask for? There can be a bit of a long wait on Saturdays and Sundays for brunch but it's always been worth it for me. As for disgruntled vegetarians who can't stand to acknowledge the existence of meat...the menu is on the door. This is obviously not the place for you, it's a typical Southern meat-and-three place, though with a broader menu that most. You will smell meat if you go inside. Judging an entire restaurant's menu based on its veggie burger alone is a bit harsh, methinks.

I'll usually save their salsa cups for use with other Mexican food that I get later. If you like fake cheese nachos, then this is your place. But do yourself a favor and tell them to hold the onions because, otherwise, you'll find one has exploded in your container and it will take you two days to get the taste out of your mouth. The best part about this place though is the price: cheap, cheap, cheap! Most of the combos run about $5 and include an entree, rice, beans, one tortilla and a couple of salsa cups. text: I despise Macy's and since the location I'm reviewing is in Mid Rivers Mall (which I think is where stores go to die and rot in hell), it doesn't help it any. For my wedding I received this GORGEOUS Kate Spade crystal vase from Macy's but it wasn't the right pattern. I decided to take it back (the person was awesome and gave me a gift receipt) and exchange it for another place setting of my china and use a gift card (also a wedding gift) for another place setting of my flatware. I checked online before I went and it appeared that while my china was the exact same price as at Bed Bath and Beyond (where we registered), the flatware was actually less expensive. AND, they had both in stock so I got to take them home with me that day (rare). I thought I'd hit the jackpot. Wrong. China: same price. Flatware: TEN DOLLARS MORE! I could have overlooked the price (since I had the gift card anyway), but then homegirl at the cash register decides to lay on the Macy's-guilt that I didn't register there and have subsequently "missed out" on their 15% off "sales event!!" for newlyweds. Um? What good does this information do me now? You already know I'm married, so why are you making me feel bad for the inability to go back in time and register for my china at Macy's in hopes of attending the elusive "sales event." (Bed Bath and Beyond gave us 20% off, by the way, you dumb cow). She literally stopped scanning my items (as if in shock) when she heard I didn't register at Macy's for them. Like it makes a bit of damn difference? I'm spending almost $200.00 here now! And just in case any brides are trying to gather some info about registering at Macy's in comparison to Bed Bath and Beyond, here's my two cents. BBB will carry all of the china patterns you like at Macy's but for less money - PLUS you can get ALL of your other household stuff there for way less money. But in case you need more convincing, here's why I didn't register there: In February (shortly before my future husband and I registered) I went to Macy's to get a gift for a friend's wedding. I waited in line for TWENTY FIVE minutes (behind ONE customer) to have the sales woman (we'll call her Sales Associate #1) pull a registry for me. I had another sales associate (we'll call her #2) approach me TWICE and ask if there is any way she can help me. I said BOTH times, "Well, I just need to pull a registry." And both times she gave me a blank stare which made me want to stab her with my Kate Spade flatware. Not to mention, the rest of the time, #2 was aimlessly wandering around the sales floor looking lost and bewildered as if she'd recently escaped from a nearby convalescence home. Once I got in front of the customer who felt the need to use #1 as her personal shopper for what could only have been 10 different weddings, the associate informs me that she CAN'T pull a registry (which I am still sure is absolute B.S.) and that I have to get it at the self-serve kiosks. I guess I could have looked around for it, but they have it stashed behind the wall and I really didn't see it, plus, you'd like to think #2 would have informed me when I told her not once, but TWO TIMES what I was standing in line for. Long story short, my friends registered for a bunch of really expensive crap (and I'm poor). So instead of giving them a gift card from Macy's, I got them one to Bed Bath and Beyond. They should have registered there to begin with. And thus, I decided not to put my wedding guests through the same circus. So don't register there, and unless you have a high threshold for pain and annoyance - don't shop there either.

text: This review is for the catering only - we have eaten at this restaurant many times and love the food. My (now) husband and I decided to hire Ono to cater our wedding, as we had our first date there. The first problem (which I'm sure others won't have) is that the catering manager changed three times between the time we booked the catering and our wedding. We met several times at the restaurant with the catering manager(s), and thought we had everything worked out perfectly. We chose our menu and worked out all the details and the only thing we had left to decide was what we wanted to drink. The wedding was for 125-150 people and we were quoted $500 for beer and wine. We questioned this figure, as it seemed quite low, but were assured that this was the average price for a wedding of this size. Nine weeks before the wedding, we decided on specific beer and wines we wanted and asked for the specific quote. Three weeks before the wedding, despite numerous requests we had yet to have a firm price (this was during the transition to the third catering manager, it seems). Finally, two weeks before the wedding we got the quote - $1200. Really? We were told this was due to the wines we had chosen ($200/case), as well as the fact that we wanted 2 kegs (one domestic and one microbrew). When we called to see if they could work with us to get the price down, we were bluntly told that 'those are our prices' and there was no offer to help. A second call revealed that we could switch to house wines ($100/case) and either get 2 domestic kegs, or 1 domestic and 1/2 keg of microbrew and that would put us closer to $800. So that was what we decided. We were in fact charged $130 and $160 for the cases of wine (white and red, respectively). This beverage pricing issue was our main complaint. One of the appetizers we had ordered for the wedding was not actually served (regular tomato bruschetta was substituted for shrimp and pineapple bruschetta). The staff at the wedding did do a very nice job. They were friendly, helpful, courteous and overall kept things flowing smoothly. One other thing that surprised us: the bar staff started packing up at 9:45 (the reception was planned to go until midnight). When we asked what was going on, they told us that their contract stated they were done at 10. A detail that, apparently, they were keeping to themselves.

Tricia ordered the prime rib sandwich. No problem, right? Well, The sandwich arrives, and literally one half of it is fat. Not nicely marbled prime rib. Just really nasty fat. I'm happily munching on my pizza when I notice Tricia's not eating. In fact, she looks sick to her stomach. When I see the huge slab of fat (a good four inches by three inches, no joke) I have to slow up on my slice. Ugh. We sit for a while until the waitress comes and Tricia meekly mentions that she wasn't prepared for that much fat. What follows is a lecture from the waitress about how prime rib is loaded with fat. Now, I'm no rube right off the bus. I luckily get to eat at Ruth's Chris every once in a while. When I lived in upstate NY, there was a little hole in the wall called the Red Osier, which served the best fucking prime rib I'll ever eat. I know what prime rib is. I've been served prime rib. Honey, this ain't no prime rib. What Tricia was served was one solid piece of fat with some meat attached. (And by the way the waitress got her back up all quick, they must get a few complaints about this sandwich.) I will say, she was nice enough to have the manager take it off the bill, but when we were presented with the check, Tricia got ANOTHER lecture: "And just so you know, prime rib is a fattier cut of meat." We thanked her for the education, paid, and left. Fuck that noise. I've got to find another pizza joint.

text: This is the review where I discovered that yelp entries can't be longer than 3000 characters, and I was only halfway through by then. I can sum up with an old joke. A woman walks up to a market stall with a fish in her hand. She approaches the owner and shouts, "Yesterday, you sold me a fish, and not only was it smelly but it was small too!" The vendor replies, "Well aren't you glad then that it was just a small one?" Anyway, I went here last night with my boyfriend for the $23.50 prixe fixe dinner. We had a 7:30 reservation but had to wait half an hour for a table. The servers took so long getting our meals to us we damn near starved to death. First course was a salad of spinach leaves, tomato, and red onion tossed in olive oil. Second course was some sort of beef dish which looked and smelled like cat food. It was even presented on a flat white plate, a pile of small chunks of meat in sauce in the middle, just like in the Fancy Feast commercials. For the entree, we could choose between shrimp risotto, roast duck, and filet mignon. I had the risotto, which was extremely runny and the rice so mushy it might as well have been porridge. There was a lot of shrimp in it, but they were on the very small side. I tried my boyfriend's duck, and it was all right, but not the best I've eaten. Having consumed most of it, he flipped it over and found a long hair, which was very evidently neither his nor mine. We alerted the waiter, who apologized and said he wouldn't charge us for my glass of Zinfandel (it was the only drink we ordered). There were two option for dessert. I had the chocolate marquise, which just tasted like bittersweet cake icing. My boyfriend had the teensiest creme brulee I've ever seen. You could literally use one tablespoon to scoop up the entire thing. I had a taste and found it to be entirely unexceptional. In all, it took us fully two hours to get in and out of there, waiting half an hour between each "course." It was just enough food for little old me, but my boyfriend was famished and grumpy when we left. We went to Denny's where he ordered a burger and a shake. I can't believe this place won over Bouchon for best French food in Santa Barbara. Tragic service, mediocre food in small portions, and hair in the duck. And to top it off, they don't take American Express. No thank you. Two stars because it was cheap and didn't give me food poisoning.

text: I would agree with Daniel's assessment of Cottage Hospital's inadequate facilities for labor/delivery. I am the proud father of 2 beautiful babies. We had 2 babies here in the past 15 months, both 15+ hours delivery. Out of the many different nurses/staff members during both deliveries, I would say 80% were great. However, both times I was sent home around 2 hours after delivery because they did not have enough rooms. For the first baby, when my wife delivered at 2:15am (hadn't eaten since 11am the day before) the nurses didn't get her any food until the 8am breakfast time - close to 6 hours after 15 hours of delivering a baby - unreal! Couldn't believe with our 2nd baby when they said I had to leave because visiting hours were over (my child was just born 2 hours prior). Also on the 2nd delivery we called ahead and tried to get in at 10pm when contractions had picked up. We waited in the emergency room for at least 20 minutes for someone to get to us. Luckily they had masks and signs instructing people to wear them due to the risk of swine flu and seasonal flu - great to see right before delivering a baby. Talking with a colleague in the Bay Area...they had a private room the whole time, bathtub in the room for the mom relax during labor, meals for both people and most importantly - they did not kick the father out after the birth of his children. This is how a birth should be treated at minimum. When I returned to "visit" the day after my second child was born I asked to pay for my meals so I could spend more time with my family - of course they missed the lunch I ordered and I waited over 2 hours as they kept telling me "it's on it's way." Ate lunch around 3pm and of course they were going to charge me for the meal. People come in from Santa Maria, Lompoc, Santa Ynez, Goleta, Santa Barbara, Ventura and even Oxnard to have their baby in this city and after Cottage shut down the Goleta labor center it is a mess. If you have the option, go somewhere that keeps up with the current standards of care.

text: Not only is Bevo Mill a consistently great place to dine, it's a St. Louis landmark as well! As the story goes, Bevo Mill was built by August Busch Sr. so that he had a place for lunch. He built himself a decadent private room to dine in so as to get away from work for a bit. The name came from Busch's non-alcoholic beer of the same name that was being sold during prohibition, and was a combination of the Slavic word for beer "pivo" and the English word "beverage." Ok, now on to the review - There aren't many cooler looking places to eat at in St. Louis, so it's worth a visit for that fact alone. Add to that scrumptious food and you've got yourself a winner. There's a reason this place has been here since the early 1900s! The food is phenomenal! Their specialties are favorites of mine, and this is one of the only places that I will eat a pasta with cream sauce. Typically cream sauces can be clotted or really oily, not so here. If you're willing to be adventurous, try the German rabbit [Hasenpfeffer] and you'll be delightfully surprised. What's great is that the service is just as spectacular as the surroundings. text: New Owner. Stay away! Stay away! Stay away! I would categorize Coconut Bay as slightly more upscale Chinese fare. But alas, things change and in this case, Coconut Bay has a new owner. Unknowingly, I visited recently with a group of 20 for a Birthday Party. The evening started rather auspiciously with watered-down, and insufficiently supplied duck sauce to go with our deep-fried crisps. When we asked our server, who also happened to be the manager, for more sauce to complement the crisps, we were met with rolling eyes. In fact, after several minutes of waiting, we asked our server again, this time pointing out that some tables were missing sauce entirely. He proceeded to roll his eyes again in disgust as he trudged to the kitchen to retrieve just a single plate of sauce. As for the entrees, well...the food is still good, however, all the portion sizes have been reduced. Each serving of soup is roughly half of what was provided by the previous ownership. But the worst part of the new change in ownership is the service. After notifying our server/manager of a few mistakes on entrees (forgetting to hold mushrooms and forgetting to hold imitation crab because of lent) our server/manager proceeded to show us his note-pad and claimed that we were mistaken, having never provided the additional instruction. But wait, it got worse when it came time to settle the bill. Now, I understand that with a party as large as ours, any restaurant would be inclined to include gratuity. Totally fair. But what these people did was utterly ridiculous. Not only did they charge us a 20% gratuity, they calculated the percentage based on the Total INCLUDING TAX! When I pointed out what I surely thought was a simple miscalculation, our server/manager proceeded to lecture me that this was their policy and that no one had ever complained about it before me. Huh? Who are you? Do you take me for a fool or are you just clueless? Needless to say, I will never return to this establishment and hope that you save yourself the headache and steer clear of this ridiculous place.

text: This place definitely has potential. For take-out, I'd probably rate it a star higher. The service was friendly and fast, but we were the first customers of the day. I went with family and most of us got a pizza, which turned out to be huge. At around $12 for a medium pie and $2 per topping, it's not the cheapest stuff and the quality certainly reflected that. My cheeseless (too much cheese makes me feel sick) pizza with mushrooms and olives was great-- since it's essentially dough, sauce and toppings, all of these needed to be quality ingredients, and they were. I highly recommend the brick oven-style, and my sister really enjoyed her "bar" personal-sized margharita pizza. My boyfriend got a huge Sicilian (they were out of the smaller size, and upgraded him at no charge). I had a bite, but didn't really care for it...something was off about the dough, but he liked it. Another member of our party had the plain white pizza, which was pretty tasty as well. Anyway, you get the point: the pizza is decent and accommodations were easily made. The atmosphere, however, is where this place loses stars. I didn't enjoy sitting next to a humming refrigeration unit, and the floors and bathrooms looked a little cheap and dirty. The tables and benches were also off-putting and I couldn't think of a good way to explain it, until my boyfriend said "this reminds me of a pizza place at the shore." The cheap long table and "wooden" plastic benches have their time and place, and that time and place is (and can only ever be) the Jersey shore. The plates fit right in with the dirty shore corner pizza parlor feel. The artwork was somewhat amusing, a combination of Pink Floyd-inspired canvas paintings mounted on the wall, some plastic plaques featuring names of Italian cities, and a creepy fat Italian guy statue looming in the corner amidst some fake plants. I feel bad bashing the setting, but the pizza is actually good. And I might actually go back if it was a nice sit-down place. But even for takeout, Buckingham Pizza still wins in my book. We went here because my dad had a restaurant.com coupon, so if you have one of those, it's no big loss. Overall: meh, but tasty leftovers!

text: There are a few advantages to living in the original "sin" state. Liquor prices, at either Ben's or Costco, are among them. Those living on Planets California or Washington can generally pick up the good, brand name stuff cheaper in Nevada -- specifically at Ben's Liquors -- than they can get the no-name equivalent on their home planet. My husband has Washington relatives who buy 7 or 8 cases (no they don't drink too much!!) -- ahem, for themselves "and our friends," before leaving the state. They figure, even if they lose gambling, they come out way ahead on the deal due to the savings on liquor! I have occasion to visit Ben's Liquors several times each year to restock our bar for several guests who drink, or to buy liquor as a present for out-of-state friends or family. The store is large, has great parking, is conveniently located to downtown, the old Southwest and Northwest Reno. But there are several Ben's locations dotted around town, so there's likely to be one near you. I just happen to live closest to this one, which was newly remodeled recently --- thank you very much. Employees are generally helpful, though somewhat transitory, and the store gets the occasional dingy one who may be helping themselves to the wares. One house-guest drinks Gin Martinis, and Ben's has the best selection of vermouth that I have ever found. Rarely busy, the store is a quick in and out stop, and I appreciate being able to do an errand quickly. On the downside, you'll pay a fortune for lemons or limes, provided Ben's even has them in stock.

text: It was bound to happen--my very first one star review. This is no joke of a rating either; I'd make it negative infinity stars if only Yelp were so kind (or unkind, as it were). How was I wronged, you may ask? Let us count the ways... 1. The girlfriend and I, coming off a day of shopping, were debating whether or not to eat here, and we took our decision right down to the wire. Consequently, we entered the restaurant sans reservations (probably a mistake on our part). After waiting a good two or three minutes in a deathly quiet "foyer" type room, we were finally greeted by a host than looked us firmly up and down to decide whether we were sponge-worthy (I mean, worthy of seating...sorry). We apparently did something right, as he consequently turned away three parties who came in looking for dining, despite the wide open spaces in their "foyer" room. Strike 1. 2. The host only took a liking to us so far as to give us a table in aforementioned "foyer" room. To describe, it's a fairly sized room at the entrance of the restaurant. Only after being seated did we realize there was a "back" room in which the true restaurant experience happens. Word of caution--if you're being seated in the front, chances are your dining experience is going to suck. It reeks of a hospital waiting room--eerily quiet with strange smells and unfriendly faces going back and forth. Strike 2. 3. As for those unfriendly faces...promptly after seating one of the waiters (more experienced, I'll assume) took the liberty of taking a younger waitress to task right in the middle of the "foyer" room, explicitly using words like "stupid" and "fired." Naturally, he promptly sent the waitress to serve our table. In retrospect, he was probably right, as she was terrible. No reason to yell like that, though. Strike 3. 4. By now, you're probably wondering, how many strikes does one get?! It gets worse. Quick one here: they may or may not have given us the wrong year for the wine bottle. Strike 4 (ish). It's been a while, and I remember being fuzzy about this one, but never bothered to fully investigate. You'll promptly see why. 5. We went for the Revillon menu (a prix fixe Christmas menu), which featured a healthy selection for a great price. Of course, my girlfriend decided to go with the Soft Shell Crab for the main course. The waiter mentioned that he "didn't know" if they had any left available (apparently, those are "reserved" for the customers of the happy room), and he would go check. Coming back out later with our first course, he still hadn't figured it out. Wait to be on the ball there, chief. Strike 5. On the plus side, I really enjoyed the Gumbo. Emphasis on past tense there. 6. Here's the biggie. The second course was the salads. I ordered the standard, which is apparently lettuce with vinaigrette. Fancy, I know. Terrible job. Not as bad as my date's, though. She got the salad with artichoke hearts (just like mine, but with artichoke hearts), and upon reaching the middle of the salad, discovered a decapitated beetle taking up residence. Strike six times infinity. To the infinity power (you see why one star is way too many?). 7. Upon seeing the bug, we promptly hailed down the first waiter we could find. He saw the bug (and may have gagged a little), and took the plate into the back. Then passed five minutes before we heard from them. We saw the original boisterous waiter that had yelled at the mediocre waitress. He passed by without so much as a glance. We never saw mediocre waitress again. Finally, we were greeted by the original host that had led us to our table, whereby we informed him we were taking off, since eating there sounded a fate worse than death. He, of course, went off to make a call. Uhh, what? Strike 7. 8. He returned after the call to inform us that, yes, it would be okay if we took off, and he was very sorry that we could not stay and eat more (on the house, of course). This would be, of course, because we were looking forward to the crickets in our main dish and some worms in the dessert, I'm sure. We declined as politely as humanly possible and dashed off to Bourbon Street to drink the pain away. Then we ate some Krystal Burgers, where at least we knew bugs in the kitchen would be perfectly acceptable. But seriously, don't eat here.
label: NEG

text: I am giving Harvest Moon five stars because it is as good as it gets -- in Tucson. If I was in another city, then it might not stand out very much, but I'll take what I can get here (meaning a decent Chinese restaurant). This is the best Chinese restaurant that I've tried here. Lunch specials are fairly straightforward -- pick a dish and it comes with a bowl of egg flower soup or hot and sour soup. They serve jasmine rice or brown rice. I especially liked the steamed fish that we had for dinner last week. It came in a flavorful sauce (mixture of oil and soy sauce) that tasted as authentic as Mom's. The restaurant has an Asian-inspired decor that is clean and modern. No tacky red and gold decorations here. It seems like a family operation with a few youngsters and teens hanging around, which increases the friendly vibe here. Harvest Moon is located in the Rancho Vistoso center off Oracle, so it is a bit of a drive for those who live in Tucson. That said, if you're going for a hike in Oro Valley or doing some sightseeing up north, then give it a try.

I stick with the seaweed salad, Florida roll, and Snake roll which are super yum. I also highly recommend the burger, duck spring rolls, and the calamari. This is not the best sushi I've ever had, but the whole experience and the extensive and creative drink menu make it worth the wait. Overall I would be happy with fewer Belmont wannabe-hipsters, a larger bar/patio, and some better servers. The guy with the curly hair is awesome and has been there for years, but some of the others are more into themselves than serving you. If you have a really large crowd, are over 40, don't like to wait, have kids, and want a quiet dinner then head somewhere else. text: Named for the stream that once flowed where 43rd St. is today and is now contained in a giant sewer pipe, the Millcreek Tavern has a swampy, fetid quality much like its namesake. There's no reason to go here unless: 1. You have a friend in a band that's playing here. 2. You live within two blocks. So for those of us who find ourselves still supporting our aspiring rock star friends, or for those who live in this lovely little corner of West Philly and are too lazy to hike a few extra blocks to get drunk (alas! how I miss my old apartment), here's a brief survival guide to the Millcreek. First, you should know that Millcreek has managed to duck the smoking ban, perhaps because it meets the criteria or perhaps because it's owned by an ex-cop. Be prepared to be hit with a wall of USA GOLD smoke. You should also know that it's really two connected bars. The east side (entrance on 42 and Chester) is newer and superficially less dingy. This is where your friend's band is playing, on a shitty little stage way in the back corner. The sound will be both ear-splitting and incomprehensible at the same time. The sightlines and acoustics are dreadful, so you might want to show up early to get a better seat. Don't order the food. You'll save money and get your food quicker if you pick up something a door down Chester at the Five-Star Deli. That said, if it's late (the Five-Star closes at 11), the chicken fingers will suffice. The western side (entrance on Chester) is an older bar once known as the Track and Turf. (That's why USP kids in the know call it "The Track.") This side has more character. Character is a euphemism for wood paneling, dart boards, and a colorful cast of neighborhood alcoholics. You'll also find Larry on this side. Larry is a Southwest-Philly-born-and-raised bartender with a thick Philly accent. Larry can smoke a whole Winston without once removing it from his lips. Larry will encourage you to get the pitcher. Larry may not notice that something is floating in your beer. Larry likes you more if you have breasts. I like Larry. A few other tips. The jukebox will eat your money. Larry may or may not offer a refund. The Millcreek no longer serves actual Yuengling Lager. Instead, they carry a generic lager with a phony, cheesy tap that says "Millcreek Lager." I think they pump it up directly from the 43rd St. sewer pipe.

We bodyboard and there's usually something that you can ride, whether it's stand-and-drop or paddle to catch a wave. In the summer, I've been able to wear a shortie and even just a vest. Most of the time, though, we're so cold-blooded that we need full suits since we're in the water for a while. Definitely more comfortable though than Santa Cruz area, closer to home. It seems to be warmest in the summer and early fall. So, Labor Day get aways are warmer than Memorial Day. One thing that can be a funky is that sometimes there are small oil slicks and you'll get tar stuck on stuff out in the water. It's minor, but some people kind of freak out over it. Local hotels have little tar removal packets. After spending the morning playing around in the water, call in a to-go order at The Spot. Pick it up and chow down on the beach. See the envy in the kids eyes who have their nutritious, but less fun whatevers. I have tried maybe half of those. The prices seem a bit steep at first but you can easily fill a box of cannolis and cakes and another box of mixed cookies for around $20. The cannolis are great, not the best I've ever had but I come from a town known for its cannoli so that's only fair. The cookies are awesome and for someone who could normally care less about a simple butter cookie, I would give my right arm for one of the butter cookies topped with sprinkles. The chocolate cakes are rich and wonderful. The cream puffs are standard good (although eat them right away because they don't fare well over time). And the raspberry thumbprint cookies are seriously out of this world. Writing this review is just making me want to head down to the Italian Market for another visit. text: This place was really crowded when I went. Every booth was filled, and from the waiting area it seemed as if I wouldn't be able to hear my own thoughts, let alone the words of the person I was dining with. I also expected a long long wait. Luckily, the wait was only 5 minutes. They do an admirable job of getting the food out and bussing the table after people leave so even with a full house the waiting was short. And, after we got to the table the din of the crowd combined into white noise, so we could even hear the 50s hits over it all. I ordered a bacon cheese burger (healthy!) and french fries. My dining partner had a cheese burger with tomato and lettuce and onion rings. The burgers are small and inexpensive. If you decide you need more cow you can easily order a double burger. The bacon was crispy and delicious. They say they have a butcher on site and the meat is fresh, and that might be true, but I can't understand why they cook it so much with such fresh meat. It wasn't burnt, of course, but well done. Still in spite of that flaw it was a tasty burger. The fries were a little bit too potatoey for my tastes. I prefer my fried foods to lose any sense of naturalness, so that might be a personal quirk. There was a bunch of them, though! The onion rings were huge. I didn't taste them, but I heard they were quite good. Now, on to my favorite part. The sodas they have a huge list of flavored sodas you are allowed to try. From toasted marshmallow to boring old cola. I liked these sodas so much that I think I drank too much, and that might have affected any complaints I had about the food. I had two colas, one orange soda and one lime soda. Not a big fan of the lime but the cola and orange were very good. I think I could spend a day there just trying their different soda flavors. Of course this would cause me to quickly float away. I will be back for sure. Perhaps just to have a milkshake which looked really good on the tables all around me. And, much like the sodas, your are provided with a cornucopia of choices. The only thing I know is that my shake will involve chocolate. The ambiance was fun. The waitstaff draws their names on their hats, and if you ask they will give you a hat and some crayons so you can feel like you are part of the family. They have the 1950s thing going on, but it's not so strong that they come up to you and ask you to sit on it, or say that your hat is neato. So, it's not too pervasive. The staff was friendly and quick. It's a fun place to go. Good prices and good food.
