text: I live near Jose's and love their tacos. However, I work in South Philly and decided to stop by El Jarocho today on my lunch break. BAD IDEA! First of all, I was not greeted upon arrival and I clearly had a puzzled look on my face as it was my first visit and the restaurant has an odd setup. I eventually spotted a pile of take out menus on a two-top table where patrons sat dining on their meals. I went for one and saw few vegetarian and pescetarian options. So, I decided to ask the one server working (who seemed to double as the take out person also) if they have fish and/or shrimp tacos. Turns out they do. They are off menu. So, I placed an order for fish tacos with the 3 tacos, rice and refried beans, and horchata. Pretty soon, the restaurant was buzzing with activity as people came in to dine for lunch and picked up/placed take out orders. The one server was clearly getting overwhelmed as she was going at it all alone. Meanwhile, I sat waiting... and waiting... and waiting (luckily, the culture at the office where I work is pretty laid back and I have the option to take extended lunch breaks). After about 30 minutes of waiting, the server approached me with a huge bag and announced my order of "3 orders of fish tacos. $35..." What!?!?!?! I was mad confused. "I wanted 1 order of fish tacos with the three tacos." The server sighed and disappeared to the kitchen. She finally returned 3 minutes later with my order and frankly said "$18". I made a credit card payment and she returned the check presenter by placing it on the table and did not even say thank you. I worked for many years in the restaurant industry so I still left a tip even though I was not pleased at all. Making matters worse, I returned to the office and found the fish tacos to be very bland. The onions, cilantro, and unseasoned fish did not impress me. In my 35 minutes of waiting, I did see some pretty amazing looking food come out of the kitchen, soup and enchiladas. So, I will return again and give them another try. However, I will probably never go again on my lunch break and I'll probably pass on tacos. I'll continue to rely on Jose's for tacos. They are MUCH friendlier, make better tacos IMO and are really close to my apartment.

text: Okay, let me preface this by saying that I know coffee and have had an LTR with her. I am not a coffee snob but I can identify, enjoy, and recommend a fantastic cup of coffee. My tastes range from a light fruity cone drip to a thick paste-like degreaser from a french press. I have my favorite 3.99/can Bustelo and my precious Bluebottle (San Francisco) and my Cafe Vita (Seattle.) Needless to say, I run the spectrum of the bean. I have had some great coffee in NOLA. Fairgrinds, Rue de la Course, even Cafe Du Monde has it's sweet spot in my heart. PJ's, on the other hand, is undrinkable. This is the nearest coffee spot to me yet I am loathe in the morning to drop by for my daily americano or drip. The machine is a horrible lifeless pushbutton affair that tastes like it hasn't been cleaned since manufacture. The baristas pull the shots until all essence of the cursed grounds are extracted, extruded, and damned into your cup. And then the shots are ruined further by sitting untouched for over ten seconds. I counted. All the iced coffee varieties have flavors. What if someone doesn't want flavor? What if someone wants a basic simple easy to order, easy to drink cup of black coffee? It boggles the mind. Rue De La Course is my ultimate NOLA choice so far, and I will avoid all 50,000 PJ's in the region. I am open to suggestions though. I will say that the staff is friendly, very fast (with the automatic machines) and professional. I give them two stars for the staff, efficiency, and cleanliness. And yes, I'll say it: Starbucks blows this place out of the water with their charry goodness. That's right!

text: I'm not sure how many people know this, but in case you didn't, here it is: Amtrak's Acela Express trains are built for speed and fantastic-ness, this much is known. What might not be as well known is that very few tracks used by Amtrak in the Northeast Corridor are set up to allow Acela Express trains to function at their full potential. The tracks are too close together to allow the trains to tilt safely, which is one way that the Acela Express trains achieve higher speeds (by tilting on the tracks when approaching bends, and whatnot). Also traveling any faster than 135 miles per hour requires a constant tension catenary (those cables above the train), which are limited to only certain lines, (for example, NY to Boston, if I remember correctly). Knowing this, don't waste your money on the Acela Express if you're traveling anywhere in Pennsylvania. You won't get there much faster than the regular Amtrak trains. Unless you just like to say that you took the Acela Express so you can feel special. As far as regular Amtrak trains go, I'm very pleased with the service, the timeliness, the prices, and also just the general upswing in clientele when compared to, say, SEPTA? I could get used to the nice seats, and the friendly conductors. And can we say comfortable? I've never had so much legroom on any plane I've been on in the last... a long time. I've never really had an issue with not arriving on time, because... well because I've always arrived on time. As a caveat, I feel it's important to note that my Amtrak experiences have been limited to Pennsylvania. I find that getting to NY via SEPTA/NJ Transit is significantly cheaper than the Amtrak route. The R7 to Trenton is $8.00, and then it's something like $15.00 to go from Trenton to NY. You're welcome. Overall, fantastic experience that is only limited by the fact that long distance trips seem to cause ticket prices to rise exponentially, which kind of defeats the benefit/purpose of taking a train over a plane. If you have the money though, it's not a bad way to go.

text: Abstract: Nice Modern Football Stadium, with great viewlines, modern amenities, and passionate fans. ------------------------------------------- Time to yelp - Eagles season ticket holder since the Vet. Long time Birds fan (first game at age 13, 1972). Easy parking if you are coming from the north on 95 the Naval Yard Lot is easy on/off, but its a bit of a hike to the Linc. Game day parking is pricey ($15-$20). Tailgating is allowed but only in specific lots around the Linc. If in doubt, ask the attedent and look for the porta-johns. Check the Eagles website for more details. Public consumption of alcohol is sometimes policed. Dump the beer in a big plastic cup just in case. If you have some cash, arrive early and check out the "Head House Plaza" in the front of the stadium. The 100,000 square foot plaza features a giant video screen, entertainment, food and beverages, a team store, the Miller Lite Tailgate Zone, Touchdown Club and the Sovereign Bank Interactive Zone featuring an array of games and entertainment options for kids and adults alike. I cannot remember the name of the food stand (in front of the team store) that has an excellent pork sandwhich and Prima Pils beers on tap. I also like Fat Jack's BBQ. Outside of tailgating/HeadHouse Plaza or McFaddens at the baseball park there are zero other places to eat/drink outside the stadium. Once inside - look for the Chickies and Pete's (a Philly institution) - they feature Crab Fries and some nice spicy Chicken Fingers. Big Modern stadium with nice views. I sit in the upper deck, so its also a hike (up the sometimes swaying ramps) to get there. Greg P. finds us a "bowl full of A-Holes" and as a long time Eagles fan I'd have to agree that 10% of my fellow fans might just be that. Many fans avoid the Head House Plaza and drink to excess in the lots before the game. Eagles fans are high energy as compared to the 70 year old Giants fans (from the Yale Bowl Days) that snooze during most Giants games. Note to fans of the visiting team: I wouldn't wear a Red Sox hat to Yankees stadium - please don't wear your Packers/Giants/etc Jersey to the Linc. The boorish 10% will make your life miserable. It may not be "right" - but its a Philly thing. Its become more civil then the Vet but barely. At least they don't need the in-house courtroom any more (like they used to have at Vet Stadium!) Kimberly H writes "For the men: apparently there are only stalls and no urinals. Just an FYI...". This is partially correct. The old Vet had SERIOUS problems with the quantity of the ladies rooms (hour waits were common.) so they overbuilt the ladies rooms at the Linc. They converted a couple Ladies rooms to Mens Rooms (which is disconcerting as you go in to see only stalls!) Also, if you look around you can get good beer. Prima Pils are often available, and sometimes upstairs near my seats they will have Red Hook ESB on tap.

The houses and rides all had less than a 10-minute wait. ALWAYS visit in the 2nd-4th weekends of operation. PYRA SAYS: Did I mention value???? For that price HOS is definitely a YES!!! The server dropped it and ran before I could say anything and it took a good five minutes before she returned. Taking my plate and promising to correct the problem, she disappeared into the back. text: I cast the unpopular vote once again. Steakhouses specialize in one thing and serve that one thing to every single customer. Meat. Steakhouses serve up dozens upon dozens of portions of meat. If I'm not being clear, let me rephrase. Steakhouses only serve meat and should know how to cook it. Fleming's in Tucson has a large square dining area and a long, narrow room just beyond the main dining area. I would assume that this long room was meant for private parties, but on the night that I visited Fleming's this room was set up with tables for 2-4. This back room is where I was pleasantly seated because the loud noise from the main dining room did not resonate into the back room. For appetizers we ordered a Caesar salad and the French onion soup. The salad was decent. A vinaigrette dressing, average tasting croutons. The onion soup had an instantaneous zing flavor. I had one spoonful of soup and proceeded to eat my salad. Half-way through eating my salad my boyfriend told me he couldn't stand the taste of his soup any longer. We switched plates and I could not eat more than a couple slurps of his soup. It was too flavorful, in a bad way. I asked for my salad back. The meat. I ordered lamb and my boyfriend ordered a tuna steak. I ordered my lamb rare. I guess I don't know what "rare" means because my lamb was dry and overcooked. It was served with a champagne mint sauce which was meant to be poured all over the lamb as the meat had no flavor on its own. The tuna had an abundance of peppercorns sprinkled on top, completely covering up the tuna taste (and making my boyfriend sneeze). I ordered the creme brulee and my boyfriend had the hazelnut chocolate mousse. The creme brulee was most definitely the highlight of either of our meals. Hearty, creamy, light, flavorful. The caramelized top consisted of raw sugar and cinnamon. The mousse was not good at all, not light, not fluffy. The service. It was slow. It was unfriendly. I appreciated that the gratis bread kept coming throughout our first course but saddened when it was taken away with our appetizers. I do not like having to constantly ask for my drink to be refilled.

text: Visited Frenchman on a Saturday and we came here because there was no cover and saw that there'd be live music in a few minutes at 7 and DJ spinning "japanese electronica" at 10. They also have tapas style food served on small plates, but like I said, we weren't hungry. The drinks are pricey. We finally decided on a $15 300ml bottle of sake. Unfortunately, they were out. We got a different bottle for the same price but which sounded less appetizing. And it was. Then we got another bottle of sake, this time the cheap carbonated one. It was a 250ml bottle for $12 and tasted great but I was rather disheartened when I read that the alcoholic content was 7%. After that quick bottle I felt really sober. And I was, we'd already dropped $30+ and weren't even buzzed. I started buying $5 sapporo drafts (tied for cheapest drafts they have), which were good, but after I had three and she had two and somewhere along the way I'd broken down and ordered the "seasoned octopus with wasabi" (ugh, slimy canned octopus) we'd spent over $60 with tips and were just barely scraping a buzz along. There were a couple reasons why we stayed there for as long as we did. One, there was a cool black and white japanese movie being played on the top corner of a brick wall. Two, Fi Yi Yi, the drum circle band played most of the time that we were there, which was cool, but we really wanted to hear the DJ spin jap-electronica and dance but we ran out of funds and left. Not sure if he ever showed up. In a way, I feel like Yukis takes advantage of their uniqueness. Sake isn't the cheapest way to drink, especially at a bar. It's just like buying wine at bars and restaurants, and beer for that matter; obviously it's going to cost more. Yuki's just didn't have any reasonably good sounding cheap options. Except maybe the one they were out of. And then their beer is expensive as well. I just can't warrant that kind of expense for half of a mediocre buzz. Maybe they think that because they have food they can charge restaurant prices for booze. Or maybe that's just Frenchman St. for you. I don't know yet, I'm new here. Left at midnight and went home feeling too sober and broke. And my bum hurt because those red stools are uncomfortable. Will I be back? Probably, because I don't learn well from my mistakes. That and I like sake and Japanese kietsch. Next time I'll just make sure I'm drunk first.

text: The Green Hills Library is housed in a large new building just off of Hillsboro Pike. If you live nearby, this library would be a great place to come and study, thanks to the many large wooden tables by the windows and comfy reading chairs distributed throughout. Actually, the setup of this library reminds me a lot of the one at the college I went to. They have a great selection of adult fiction and nonfiction books, DVDs, audio books, and a small music section. What really makes the Green Hills Branch unique is the children's section. It's HUGE! Since kids get their own separate room, parents don't have to worry as much if their children make a little noise. There's even a designated "Toddler Computer," which evokes funny images in my head. Speaking of computers, Green Hills has over 30 public computers, so hopefully that means the wait is never long. If you like to own books as well as borrow them from the library, Green Hills has a great biannual book sale for a few days every May and October. Adult books cost $0.50, children's are $0.25, and there's also a decent free section. Once you've picked out your books, you can grab some fruit to munch on at the nearby Green Hills Farmers Market, find a bench at the Sally Brewman Green Hills Park next to the library, and get lost in a good book.

text: I have visited the Star Cafe two times, the first time being for takeout and the second, dine in and I didn't find anything to brag about either time. I tried it two times before deciding that I didn't just catch them on an off day. The first time I thought perhaps it had to do with not being able to experience the inside atmosphere. I was wrong, the food doesn't get any better eaten inside. Actually, there's a newspaper clipping on the wall showing they won an award for an excellent burger. My husband tried to order a burger and they don't do a grill menu any longer. So umm...why do you keep this on the wall??? The negatives: The catfish was probably straight out of a bag of frozen pre-battered catfish and run of the mill. The tarter sauce was probably homemade and the best part of the meat option. Mashed potatoes and gravy: since we live around so many meat 3's, you have to meet the basics or exceed and these potatoes were just pitiful. Too soupy with chunks of hard bits and plain out bland. The gravy on top had an "off" taste, like the grease had went a bit sour, and it too was under-seasoned. Mac n cheese: oh man, this was BAD. It was of the casserole/baked variety. The pasta was just plain turned into mush, the cheese sauce had separated, so it was in a puddle of white fluid and curds. There was orange crusted cheese on the top, at least what would have been the top if it had any structure left to it, that was edible at least. I had to scoop it up with a spoon to even try it. Again, no seasoning or very little The meatloaf: was mushy, no crust and a small amount of runny ketchup on top. The flavor wouldn't have been awful if it had at least some seasoning in it other than onion. Sad. The cornbread: had decent flavor but wasn't browned AT ALL. There seemed to be a trend with textures, mushy. The Peach Cobbler: where's the PEACHES? It also had some uncooked doughy chunks. I guess that was the texture part of the meal. The positive: it's cute inside, the people are nice enough. And the white beans were really good with onion. But did have to add our own seasoning, since nothing is seasoned. This is a sad, sad excuse for "country cooking." If I were traveling and wanted a taste of the South's infamous meat3's, I'd never want it again.

text: Okay-- first thing to understand is that when you are only paying $68 a night, your expectations should not be very high. Second thing is that the first couple floors are "Residential" (week to month-long stays), and that's not exactly the best quality clientele for a hotel. Final thing is that a hotel is, at heart, merely a place for you sleep and bathe while you are in a place where you lack those things and need them so you can do whatever it is you are there for. That being said-- this hotel is conveniently located just off I-76 at City and Belmont Aves and has a mini-parking "garage" in the rear. Every room offers at least one bed, a working bathroom with a bathtub-shower, and TV with cable, including HBO. More importantly, you can stay for a week for the same price as two nights in just about any other hotel in Philly (besides the Blue moon, anyway). The staff is nice, if disinterested. I have used the North American for real reasons and party reasons in the past, and I wouldn't hesitate to stay there again (unless I get rich before the next time I or someone I know needs a spot to stay). However, some important caveats: 1. I don't recommend leaving anything very valuable (from watches to laptops) in the room. 2. I do recommend bringing your own sheets and towels (though purely for quality and not for cleanliness). 3. Be forewarned that your stay may include the pleasure of a vibrating bed from the thumping bass pounding upwards from the crazy foreign wedding taking place in the "ballroom" and restaurant on the ground floor. 4. Be forewarned that your next door neighbors might just be crackheads who decide to fight all night long (when they're not slamming their bed into the adjoining wall). 5. Remember that all through high school my friends and I partied here on occasional weekends, and that kids still do. 6. Remember that a functioning bathroom does NOT mean the shower faucets won't leak and that the toilet won't rock. 7. Remember that "smoking rooms" doesn't always just mean cigarettes. If any of the above sounds intolerable, than you, like the previous guest who stayed in the room I got the last time i was there, "should've stayed at the Hilton"... But, if pure utility and cheapness is your aim-- the North American is the spot for you...

text: Going here was the worst restaurant experience of my life, no question. Sam runs this joint as a one man operation in Printer's Alley downtown. When I first walked into the tiny room (couldn't have been more than 250 sq ft), I was pleased at the sight of such an informal, distinctive, divey kind of hole in the wall. Horrible, yellowed posters as decor, cracks in the floor tiles, no air conditioning. I usually love little places like that (e.g. Edgefield in East Nashville). I was, however, sorely disappointed. Sam, who many people on this site and on City Search sympathize with for reasons unknown to me, is a complete jerk. The first greeting I received was "NO WRITE ON MENU". I was studying the small laminated menu, trying to decide what I wanted to order. I guess he assumed I was going to mark on it, the way a lot of sushi places have you order. I placed my order and specified what type of nigiri I wanted with my roll, as it didn't say on the menu what type came with the sushi combo plate. Instead of explaining things, he snapped again, "You no get to pick all three same! You get what I put on plate!" I took it and assumed it was my misunderstanding. I was careful to handle him with kid gloves and not get upset, as it's a relatively common occurrence for good restauranteurs and chefs to be prickly, neurotic, irregular characters. I have interacted with people like that before and had some of the best food I've ever eaten served by them - one of those "good artists are drug addicted and suicidally depressed" sort of phenomenon, except "good chefs are insane and total jerks". I figured his personality might just be the price to be paid for outstanding cuisine. I was so, so wrong. When our order was up, I went and grabbed it from the bar and sat down. The first thing I noticed was how sloppily it was assembled. Sushi is one of those culinary niches that takes pretty exacting technique and attention to detail. It takes practice and focus to make tight, neat maki, which is why it isn't something delegated in kitchens, but reserved for a specific sushi chef - a guy who knows what he's doing. Sam, with way too much rice spilling out of his maki and his loose wrapping, clearly does not know what he's doing. I picked up a piece of yellowtail nigiri, dressed it up with some wasabi and dunked it in soy sauce. I popped the nigiri in my mouth and the first thing that hit me was the soy sauce. I have never had such cheap tasting, horribly salty soy sauce. I know soy is salty, but this was terrible. Pretty much any sushi place I've ever been to, upscale or divey, usually goes with the standard - plain old Kikkoman. I dont know what horribly cheap brand he was buying, but the salt was all I could taste, which as it turns out, was not such a bad thing. I tried another piece of nigiri, no soy sauce this time. I nearly gagged. The fish was not only at room temperature (which was warm, considering the place had no a/c or circulation), but also was very, very obviously not fresh. Before I totally gave up (and because I was hungry), I tried a piece of crunchy shrimp roll. The shrimp was bland, the tempura not at all crispy or light and once again it was definitely not fresh seafood. The biggest offense with his roll, however, was the rice. The grains seemed bigger than they should be, making me think he was using regular long grain white rice, instead of the slightly more expensive sushi rice. Additionally, I found out part of the reason why his rolls are so sloppy, other than the over stuffing. When my roll fell to bits when picked up and when I tasted the rice, it was clear there was no vinegar in it, meaning it was not prepared correctly for sushi and therefore, not sticky rice in the least. Let me reiterate, this guy has no idea what he's doing. I only had one or two whole pieces of his stuff before surrendering. The friend I was with, however, wasn't quite as critical as I was (and also didnt order nigiri, the most offensive part of the meal) and said I should box it up and he would eat it later. We took our stuff to Sam to be wrapped. He drilled us for a while: "Where are you going after this? How far away is your house from here? Are you going to refrigerate this right away? You know this is RAW FISH, right?". At first, I thought it was cute that he would care, but he made it clear pretty quickly what his motivation was - "People get sick, they blame sushi restaurant. I not want to get sued! You could just go and leave in car all day. I have good restaurant! I not get in trouble for sick people!" It was hilarious. He was mad about us maybe getting sick and suing him after a 10 minute ride in an air conditioned car, but he wasnt worried enough with food safety to serve properly stored, fresh fish. Despite being a paying customer, I was treated as a nuisance and then given terrible food. Everyone says Sam's is the cheapest sushi it town. I wouldn't argue that. It's also pretty inexpensive.

text: *slides soapbox over* *stands on soapbox* Any dog trainer is going to disparage a doggie daycare. I have trained dogs, as in Schutzen trained dogs. I can assure you that any trainer, anywhere is going to tell you not to go to a doggie daycare. It's not going to matter if it is Crossroads or "best daycare ever". The argument is that a trained dog should be on command 100% time it is out of its crate. We, of course, as Americans humanize our dogs and just aren't willing to do that. *etches soapbox a bit higher* All doggie daycares have "parasites" or the possibility therein. So do all dog parks because we, as humans, don't do enough to educate ourselves about our animals. Giardia is technically a parasite. It's also super common and causes diarrhea. Most people are just like "oh well... Bowser has diarrhea" and do nothing about it... and take their dog to daycare/the dog park that way. Giardia is super contagious in dogs. So thank other humans, don't blame the daycare/dog park. *slides soapbox back to its corner* I'm sorry for the person who had bad grooming experience. But, the rest of the review is nonsense (see soapbox commentary). They clearly mark dogs with known contagions and do not allow those dogs outside of the dog's own personal kennel run and separate the dogs by distance from other dogs (I saw the signs on my tour...) Personally, I don't understand the whole grooming thing but, hey, I own German Shorthaired Pointers specifically because I didn't want to even think about grooming. Although, I'd point out that dogs existed just fine as companions without grooming for centuries. The staff at Crossroads is courteous, nice, and knowledgeable (well, the Vets and Vet techs are). They are willing to give you a tour of the entire facility including boarding runs and the daycare area - that's actually more unusual than one would think and I have boarded my GSPs at a lot of places. They do half-day rates (awesome and a first I've seen), they do a second (or more) dog discount, and their prices are more on par with what I have seen in other cities (and equivalent to A Bark Above in East Nashville which I love but it's totally inconvenient for me from a distance perspective). The records are computerized, which is done so they can remind you about vaccinations. And, there is an onsite veterinarian because it's a veterinary hospital as well as doggie daycare/boarding facility. My dislikes: It's off the ever-dreaded Mallory Lane in Cool Springs. Traffic = nightmare on that road. I pray that one day I figure out some backroads to weave my way in and out of there without ever seeing Mallory Lane... oh, plague on humanity...

text: I'd been here twice before and I dig their happy hour (except that they admittedly water down their margaritas. grrr), but lunch today was frustrating. Here's what their lunch menu insert looks like: "Served with beans, rice, and guacamole -Chile relleno -2 taquitos -Camarones empanizados -Enchiladas Served with rice and tortillas -4 -other -things -here Served with something somethign and vegetables -4 -other -things -here" I saw this menu and saw the first column of stuff and went YES. I didn't even care, I was more interested in the "beans, rice and guacamole" the menu said came with it. AWESOME. My boyfriend ordered from the same column, the taquitos. When we ordered, I proudly declared I wanted the shrimp, and that I wanted the green rice (they have red too. Just clarifying for the waitress). She nodded and took my boyfriend's order and then came back to me to ask "mumblemumble rice?" "Green rice!" I said back, all excited for this carb-fest I was about to get. And then it came. With just rice. 4 breaded shrimp and no beans, no guacamole. My boyfriend's taquitos (from the same 'served with' heading) DID come with beans and guacamole and a bunch of sour cream and 2 kinds of cheese that the menu didn't mention, which sucks for him because he hates cheese and sour cream. I went 'wait wait doesn't this come with beans and guacamole?' Waitress: "I asked if you wanted beans or rice and you said 'green rice' ". Me: "The menu said it comes with both." Waitress: "No. Just rice." She left and I felt like I couldn't argue, because she had kinda looked at me like I was a snotty bitch, but my friend ran and grabbed a menu to prove to me that I was right and I should argue. Then she came back and we showed her the menu and she just responded with "Do you want guacamole?" YES SILLY I WANT GUACAMOLE AND BEANS LIKE ON THE MENU. She did bring me some guacamole, but no beans, so I ate my boyfriend's because they were covered with cheese. Then he was still hungry so I gave him my shrimp. Here's the run-down basically: Either the menu is inaccurate or the waitress was really dumb The portions were less than fair for being in the $9 range. If you don't like cheese/crema or you're allergic or something, you should ask about it. The menu will simultaneously lie about what it will give you (cheese and sour cream) and what it won't (beans and guacamole). And I don't think it was a language barrier either, because in Spanish "incluye frijoles, arroz y guacamole" would still mean it came with all 3. I'm mad at you, Palapa.

And the happy hour, took a turn for mediocre hour. I could see how 13th St. B&G might be fun if you lived around the block, you knew your bartender and they hooked you up with big, fat, stiff drinks on the down low, or if it's closer to stumble home to than the Bittercreek, but for me, my bike is not headed in that direction.

text: The first time we went here, it was great. Not excellent, but still above good. They had a half price special for sushi and tempura, and we took advantage of it like no one's business. The maki were good but the nigiri were dried out and tasteless for the most part. We ordered tempura and whoo-hoo! It was fantastic! For what it was, it was a good meal at a great price, within walking distance of home. The atmosphere was avante garde, but it wasn't gauche. The only thing I would really complain about ambiance-wise was the music. Hellllo, the nineties called, they want Enigma back..... Our second round was a nightmare. Every single roll had turned into the infamous inside-out roll- the roll created by the Japanese to quell the weak stomachs of Americans who are afraid to eat seaweed. Oh, how nasty it was! I loath inside-out rolls, and they're made even more loathsome when the rice is mushy and under-seasoned. Blerg indeed! The rolls had also shrunk in size. Their futomaki were now the size of regular rolls and their sushi maki had diminished into hosomaki. The shame! We always knew this wasn't haute sushi, far from it, but bad sushi is really foul. We forced ourselves to eat the unraveling slices of poorly formed sushi, knowing we would hate ourselves for it. I've known youngsters who could roll a tighter, more shapely roll. I was embarrassed for the waitress who served us that night. Surely she knew how bad this was. I know I'd want to commit seppuku after knowingly serving up food that nasty.
label: NEG

text: Wow. It appears that I'm the only one that has had multiple 'meh' expeirences here. I came here once, when it first opened- and almost threw up into my plate. No joke. But I digress... After sitting myself, I had to hunt down a waitress- who did not speak english- and I had to keep repeating 'water please' until she understood me. I actually had to gesture with my hands that I wanted a drink. She returned with a glass of tepid water that was only half full, with literally 3 little peices of ice and no straw. UGH. I ordered a Crystal Shrimp long roll (no avocado) with cream cheese. It's my 'test' order, if you will. Yea, they failed in my opinion. Big time. The rice was notably dry and unimpressive. The breading on the shrimp was not good. It tasted like it had been either overcooked or fried in old oil. Bleh. I'd eaten only a couple pieces of the roll when I looked at the roll and noticed that the shrimp wasn't deveined! EW! In every piece of the roll you could see little black lines of shrimp shit. I almost hurled in my plate. I waved the waitress over, but of course she couldn't understand a word I was saying. I tried explaining it to the sushi chef behind the counter but again, no clue what I was saying. Needless to say, I paid & left. I would have refused to pay for my shit filled shrimp roll, but they had no clue what I was trying to tell them. I swore to myself I'd never go back. Buuuut, it's near my house and I wanted to be SURE that they sucked before I ruled them out - they are so much closer than Ijji. I went back, and yea...still not impressed. I very specifically asked the waitress to make sure the shrimp was deveined. She seemed to understand what I was asking so that was a plus. The woman who took my order, was also the woman that made my food. I hope she washed her hands. She informed me that she cut the veins out of my shrimp. However, the shrimp was not merely overcooked- it was burnt. It had that lovely scorched taste to it and even though I asked for NO sesame seeds- there they were, in all their glory. IN ABUNDANCE. Like last time, I didn't eat more than a few pieces of the roll. It wasn't good. Too much rice and burnt shrimp-bleh. I also didn't appreciate all the sesame seeds that were in my teeth! One positive that I will say, is that even though my food was not good, the ladies were nice (even though most of them had no clue what I was saying) they were still smiling that I-have-no-idea-wtf-you-just-said smile. Will I go back? Meh. They've already got two strikes in my book- so it'll have to be pretty good next time for me to change my mind.

The looooong tables with looooud people lead me to believe people are going out with groups of like 14+.... does that really still happen? text: I don't know what more I can say about this place, other than it is awesome! What a cool idea.....gourmet popsicles. I was in town for a day and made sure to stop by Las Paletas after reading about it on Yelp. I was torn between avocado and chocolate with hot peppers. I ended up going for the chocolate, because it seemed like such a unique twist on a common idea, and also I love spicy food. It was brilliant. When you eat the popsicle, you really only taste chocolate but there are ground up bits of pepper that add a nice, subtle heat that builds up- I could feel it best at the back of my mouth. The heat did not steal any of the flavor of the chocolate. It was such a unique experience, unlike anything I've ever had before- I know it sounds weird, but I really enjoyed it. The only thing I can say negatively is the place needs to have some signs up. I didn't get lost, but I was parked right in front of it (by the salon next door) and didn't realize I was right there. It is hidden behind glass that was hard to see through. I don't think I saw a single sign for the place.

text: Well, it's that time of year again; my anniversary and restaurant week in Philly. Thus begins four days of debauchery in the city at a different restaurant every night, and the celebration begins with my favorite, Fork. This is my third time here, and I have never been disappointed, by either the wait staff or the fabulous food. My husband and I both decided to order off of the restaurant week menu. He got the pumpkin soup, which was creamy and subtle. I got the warm spinach sfumata, which was paired with wild mushrooms, wonderfully garlicky, and delicious spread on bread. The beer on tap was from local Cherry Hill brewery Flying Fish, which we both got. For our entrees, he got the pasta with beef tripe, which he found spicy and scrumptious, and I got the veggie risotto, which was perfectly prepared, sweet, and incredibly filling. My waiter recommended a German pilsner to accompany it, and it was a great match. For dessert, it was an orange ricotta cheesecake and chocolate mousse cake. We ate as much as we could, but we were stuffed! I cannot recommend Fork enough to anyone looking for a nice place to eat, not too loud, and not more hipster than thou.

text: I'll give it a 2.5- the extra half star is for the smoke free environment Went to Broad Ripple after a Pacers game last weekend, and were looking for a place that served food late, and preferably smoke-free. AMBIENCE- I'm guessing that this place has a sister location, and/or was started at the University of Wisconsin (Madison) as there was a sign posted stating Brother's Bar UW Madison. Interesting set up, there's a bar in the middle, with plenty of room surrounding it for people to mix and mingle, and tables on the outskirts of the area. They also had tvs all around, though they didn't seem to be that huge. SERVICE- the place was pretty packed, but we managed to get a table. MENU- typical bar and grill fare. Sandwiches, appetizers, and a couple entrees. I'll leave it at that. FOOD- A couple of us weren't starving, so we rocked a few appetizers- chilli cheese fries and jumbo pretzels. My one friend ended up ordering a burger and fries. Two of my friends cannot eat pork, and we were suprised to learn that the chilli cheese fries come with bacon on them. Luckily we caught the server in time to have her request to put the bacon on the side. The fries were good, but nothing earth shattering. For $9, I was expecting a mountain of fries, but instead saw a serving good for about 2-3 people. The pretzels were decent, though you only get 3. They came with a cheese dipping sauce, and a weird "white mustard." Yeah, I've never seen a white mustard. My friend seemed to enjoy his burger and fries well enough, but when you've been drinking, a lot of food can tast good that wouldn't otherwise. OVERALL- based solely on the food, I wouldn't go back. And since I don't drink, there really isn't much to get me to come back. I suppose if my friends wanted to go drinking, to save myself from smelling like smoke, I might come here, but only under those circumstances. Celebrity Rating- Creed

text: To me, the food here isn't as adventurous as some of the other Mexican places on Cherokee, but it's a quality product nestled within a cute storefront. The outdoor patio is pretty killer, and seems welcoming for groups of people, as they enjoy one of the items on Tower Taco's large (and descriptive) menu. Outdoor seating is set up on plastic picnic tables which are easy to clean and not overflowing with random condiments. The patio is also between two buildings that shields you from some of the traffic noises of Cherokee, and the table umbrellas are pretty clean. Apparently, cleanliness is a prime directive here. Like I said, the menu is pretty large. About as large as, say, Chimichanga's menu, but looks like a Mom and Pop version of the Chevy's Mexican Grill chain. But that didn't bother me; it's the food that matters. I've been to Mexican restaurants before that have such large disparities between menu items. A tamale is good, but the enchilada is despicable... So I picked #1 on the combination platter list. Number One should always be a good thing and I wasn't disappointed. I inhaled a couple of meaty enchiladas that looked a little small, but were surprisingly filling. The enchilada sauce was a little too tomato-ey but that was refreshing (but still offered a slight kick), since the meat filling was a little spicy. Next to that was a taco, that seemed to be made with the same filling as the enchilada, but was topped with lettuce, onion, tomato and some queso that tasted a little too much like Provel "cheese." I've bought Mexican queso before and it has the same consistency, so I knew what I was getting into. That part was so-so. However, I was stunned by the rice. Some places drench their Mexican rice with a ton of tomato, lack any real flavor, and remind me of grade-school cafeteria rice mush. This was the exact opposite. The flavor wasn't too overpowering, but was there. Instead of the rice being the platform of flavor, it really focused on pairing Mexican spices with the flavor of the rice itself. Throw in a few peas into the mix (I love peas) and I am a happy camper. My server seemed a little overworked with several larger tables inside the restaurant, as well as a group outside, but she was diligent and served everyone with a great smile, and genuine happiness. text: After seeing other bad reviews, I just couldn'tt keep my experience to myself. This place is Atrocious. If that's all you were looking to know, then read no more, but if you are looking to be entertained - then by all means, do read on. This place USED to give the best pedicures. and I USED to be willing to fork over the extra cash for it. No More! Here is some background to preface this review *I live in the city and I wear flip flops Every Day. So my feet get more than their fair share of abuse. *While I bathe and generally make myself presentable to society, I am not what you might consider girlie. I am a very busy woman, and to me these things are nice, but by no means a necessity to life. I am a good human being regardless of the occasionally bushy state of my eyebrows. *The Experience:* Let me now describe for you what I could only call a cursory pedicure that lasted all of 15 minutes (including polish) and that I would not have expected to pay more than $15 ($20 with tip) for; but which ended up costing me a whopping $40. And that I probably could have done my own self for free. This particular day I thought to myself, "self, you are waaaay over due for a pedicure. it would probably be a good idea to treat yourself to the good place, despite the higher price tag." So I walked into Allure, and with a hint of embarrassment, asked for a pedicure. The 10 women who were lounging around doing nothing proceeded to fight over whose turn it was. That should have been my first clue. The woman who led me to the chair seemed nice enough. As with every nail place I have ever been, I warned her that I was ticklish, but that I didn't mind if she didn't mind my hysterical bursts of laughter. All seemed to be going well, and sure enough the minute the pumice stone hit my feet I broke out into fits of loud boisterous laughter which I am known so well for. All of the girls in the salon started to point and giggle (this is totally par for the course and happens everywhere - I am used to it). At this point, the only thing that made me feel slightly uncomfortable was the fact that she kept making what I can only describe as "bedroom eyes" at me which went so far as to include a slight puckering of the lips and sucking in of the cheeks. I thought this strange and it gave me the distinct impression of being hit on (I would have been equally unnerved by had these advances been made by a man or a woman, this scenario isn't exactly primed for romance - I mean, what would you even talk about on the second date?) After 1 or 2 passes of the pumice stone, she placed my foot back in the water and I figured that having seen my feet she realized that they might require some heavy duty artillery. But then the woman did something really quite strange. She rinsed of my feet and started to drain the water. She dried my legs and feet and started to put some lotion on them. She asked me if I shave. I said that I had the day before (there was some stubble, but it wasn't any of her business - I was by no means some wildebeest covered in fur) and jokingly said I didn't feel the need to impress anyone. Her response - raised eyebrows and a guttural sound which I can only classify as chastising in nature. She continued to prep my feet for the polish. I didn't understand what was going on. I kinda tried to tilt my feet to see if I had missed something. But No, the calluses were all present and accounted for. I should have said something then and there. But i think I might have been suffering from a shock related condition. Then, to add insult to injury. She looked up at my face, stitched her brows together, raised her upper lip and asked me when i had last done my eyebrows. I said, Why yes, I am over due, but I can't do it this evening (it was around 5) or my face will be all red. (I have been doing my eyebrows for over 10 years - and owned this face for longer than that - I'd like to think I now how it reacts to things). She continued to insist that this would not happen and that I should have her do them. I chose to drop the subject rather than insult her lest she take it out on the polish she was about to apply. This continued on into an awkward 10 minutes under the dryer not unlike weird silences while on a date you would rather not be on in the first place. (Apparently there was also a shoulder massage involved - though to be honest, at that point, it was so awkward & uncomfortable, I didn't really enjoy it) So the date metaphor was even more apt. So after all this - I would have Still given this place at least 2 stars, for the entertainment value at the very least. had it not been for the fact that the paint job didn't even last 24 hours. I felt Jilted to say the least.

text: What can even be said about Olympia that will sound like I actually do not hate every restaurant in the St Louis area? Probably not much. Here goes nothing: Olympia has decent food. If you would like to re-brand yourself as a bar Olympia, I would probably still not go to you again, because even for that it is too far off of my beaten path, and I can get bar food anywhere. The menu breakdown. Appetizers. "Flaming Cheese"? Oh you mean Saganaki? At least you are using the right kind of cheese, but I am put off by this. "Hermes Hot Wings"? If I serve everything I make with a poorly made tzatziki can I name it after historic Greek figures? Main course. Burgers do not belong on a menu at a Greek restaurant. You would think that would be the end of this portion but no. There is also the chicken fingers option. Did I come to a Greek restaurant or a burger joint? I also really have no idea what was put in the moussaka or pastitsio... but when I make these in my own kitchen they taste more Greek than this. Oh wait, that might be because I have an actual recipe for these and not the Wikipedia entry. Dessert. "Baklava". I really think the quotes say it all. I understand this is a hard dish to master. But just don't put it on your menu. Or better yet, stop calling yourself a Greek food restaurant. If you are looking for a gyro, go to Delmar, Gyro House is the place for you. If you are looking for other Greek specialties, then you are going to have to bear with me, because so am I... The once yearly St Nicholas GreekFest is not enough to hold me over. And until I can find a suitable alternative I am going to keep cooking my best friend's grandmother's pastitsio recipe. If you are craving some, let me know, I will invite you over. text: Yogawood is a safe healthy active place to continue and deepen your yoga practice. The studio is intimate and beautiful, a former art gallery with smooth warm glowing floors crafted from wide slices of old growth trees and a gorgeous Moroccan inspired wall painting in soothing purples greens and cream. I am a south jersey native, transplanted and thriving in the san francisco bay area where I have a regular yoga practice (blend of iyengar with ashtanga). When i return to NJ, i miss my yoga. Well, NOT any More! Yogawood is a sanctuary. The price is right -- there are even $7 vinyasa classes a few days a week making yoga affordable to the community. You can buy a bulk yoga card to keep your costs down to less than $10 a class and a monthly unlimited pass is $120. The teachers are clearly well educated and caring. Give yogawood a try!

text: The drinks are good (although I once asked for a bellini at the indoor bar and received champagne mixed with peach schnapps-- I don't think so!), the food is consistent and tasty, but the rooftop deck has several issues that this cupcake does not love. First, the glassware. Or shall I say, plasticware. When I order a ten dollar martini, I do not want to drink it out of room temperature plastic in a martini glass shape. I'm sure the reason behind this decision is so knucklehead drunks don't go throwing things over the ledge... but at the very least, they could serve real glasses to the patrons seated at the bar or at tables having dinner, or save the plastic for after 10 p.m. Second, although there were no pools in sight, the entire deck area curiously smelled like one. Musty, chlorine-filled air combining with the scent of prepared foods was not at all appetizing. A rooftop bar in the middle of Philadelphia should not smell like low tide under the boardwalk. Please, Mr. Starr, give this place a good scrub down and replace the flooring with something that doesn't absorb spills. I'm sure this wasn't my last visit to the deck at Continental Midtown... but with more bars and restaurants opening outdoor patios and setting up street-side tables, this place won't be topping my list for drinks al fresco.

text: Azie was like a shimmery star for us locals when we found out it was opening. It wasn't bar food, it wasn't crappy chinese takeout, it seemed kind of fancy and almost slick and hip. I've never gone for dinner, but have gone several times for happy hour as a good friend worked there...but even with him in tow....the service stunk. We'd all have to cram into this tiny front seating area to qualify for the discounted apps and drinks and he'd have to get up more than once during the meal to get us a drink, food, etc...and he wasn't on the clock. If it wasn't him, it would be at least 4 different people randomly coming over greeting us. We were greeted once, that was enough. Thanks. They were going out of their way to advertise these specials...but we got treated like we were trying to trick them out of money. Really though, we were just poor 20 somethings attempting to get some sushi at a reasonable price and perhaps get a little tipsy in the process. We weren't rooting through their trashcan in hopes of an asparagus roll, so why were we treated like street urchins? Hell, we'd even dress a little nicer if we knew we were going there, so we tried. It was never enough. In the two hours you had to get your food and drinks, you'd be lucky to get 2 drinks at the discounted price....and they were watching that clock. text: Mormoto is one of those restaurants that must really piss off the nay sayers. .You either have to admit you're picking nits or simply go out of your way to judge them so much more critically than other restaurants. Either way, you're raising the jerk quotient ever so slightly. Well, maybe a little more than that. From the entrance on, Morimoto is dead on emblematic of the Japanese personality; austere, antiseptic and frugal, albeit hynotically successful, in their aesthetic effort. Morimoto, the chef entreprenaur is like his colleagues Batali and Ducasse and all the others who have parlayed tremendous talent and hardwork into global brands. And as much as some of us would like to, we can't hate them for that. Morimoto is a 5 star restaurant on their food, service, ambiance and value. He's got all the moves, polishing his own rice, grating fresh wasabi on a sharkskin grater? Come on this is good stuff. PR? Who cares? He's not exactly sticking a gun in anybody's ribs to come in. Would I say the sashimi is light years ahead of others I've tasted? The service the best ever? Not the point! The overall package is very very nice. Have not tasted the omakase yet but am looking forward to it maybe after Babbo and a weekend in SoHo.

text: I've never given a really bad review to any restaurant before, but I feel this place deserves it. I ordered a very basic item, the deluxe pho soup that contains a variety of cuts of meat, tripe, and meatballs. I've ordered this from many of the area pho restaurants and always enjoyed my noodle bowl experiences... until now. This pho soup HAS NO SOUL!!! By that, I mean the soup is really, really bland. It's basically chicken stock with no beef flavor. Usually, each restaurant flavors the soup with its own blend of spices. This one seemed to forgot to do that. The meat they use is good, don't get me wrong. The eye round steak is a little too overcooked for my liking, but the fatty meats are all very tender and quite edible. The meatballs (three halves) tasted of mostly blenderized eye round. The tripe was scant as it should be. There were onions aplenty in the soup. I like that. One place across the street charges $1 for onions. Other pho places just include onions in their soup. The accompaniment plate had scarce amounts of lime, peppers, basil leaves, but that's forgivable. What isn't forgivable is the soup... and the noodles... the noodles were the worst pho soup noodles I've ever tasted! Okay,why does every other pho place use rice noodles that are long and chewy and Le Viet uses this cheap kind of flat rice noodle that isn't chewy? I once had some instant vietnamese noodles that had this same kind of cheap flat rice noodle in it! I give the place big kudos for decor. Lovely bamboo trees decorate the doorways. A sleek, modern black interior sets the perfect mood for a date with a lovely Asian girl. It certainly caters to an American crowd that will pay for decor over taste. If you want better pho, go across the street to Pho Hoa, Nam Phuong, or down the street to Nam Son or down the road to Pho Saigon. Even Pho 75, the "Burger King" of pho restaurants, is much better and so is Viet Cong Cafe.
label: NEG

text: My husband and I stopped here on the way through Tucson, and we both had a delicious meal and were entertained by the Flamenco show. We started off with Sangria Blanca...if that's your flavor, definitely opt for the carafe or pitcher! Then we had the shrimp in bechamel sauce, chicken shish-kabobs, pork tenderloin, and a veggie stew....all in all, a wonderful dining experience. We topped it off with the tarta de santiago...almond cake. They had Paella for groups of 4+, and also dinner plates. Since it was just the 2 of us, we decided to order just a few plates of tapas. Plus they had an additional menu that they offered when the World Cup was on with some specialties. Lots to choose from, it was hard deciding on what to choose. Plus, we got an order of papas bravas for free while we perused the menu. The Flamenco show was as authentic as it gets. The guitarist did a bang up job, as did the colorful Flamenco dancer, who danced with castanets and all...plus she would pull people out of the audience to try their hand at the dance....some were better than others, but they were all good sports, and tried their hand at the gypsy dance. The atmosphere was great, they had front row seating for those who wanted to be close to the Flamenco show, but my husband and I opted to sit in the back-- we still saw the dancing, but could hear our conversation a bit better. The artwork and over ambiance of the restaurant was perfect...might as well have been in Sevilla! Great job, Casa Vicente...I hope to return soon! :D

text: This is, by far, the best place to workout in Tucson if you are A) a real person and B) get a little wet at the thought of being able to watch your own personal cable TV while you do your cardio. For $20/month, with no contracts, and a modest sign-up fee, the price can't be beaten. There are plenty of cardio machines (five rows of ellipticals, three rows of treadmills, two rows of stair machines, and two rows of bikes). Even at peak hours, it's easy to hop on a machine. About 1/3 of those machines have the aforementioned TVs. I'm convinced that being able to watch baseball games, lame VH1 reality TV, and cable news is the main reason I've been able to lose weight. The "real person" factor is another big selling point of Gold's. Sure, there's a dude with a mullet, a 1980s sweat suit, and the mien of Chuck Norris who I always see there. There are also at least a few guys who work out there that more than likely shoot bovine growth hormone directly in to their scrotums. The vast majority of the people I see at Gold's are just regular folks, though. This is no hoity-toity, huge weight-pumping, scary, judgmental gym. The people are friendly and leave you alone. The only reason Gold's doesn't get the full five stars from me is that the machines seem to break a lot and take a long time to be repaired. Plus, the place has been in a perpetual state of renovation since I joined in February of '08. Something is always out of order or being torn down and redone - never in such a way that there is ever significant inconvenience, but it's still worth noting.

The fish is NOT fresh high-quality sashimi grade one should expect from a sushi restaurant. The fire and ice hand roll (salmon and scallops) was the best offering IMO but again, not as fresh or flavorful as it should have been. text: Oh man, what a waste of money! I rarely get a Valentine's day date, but we traded babysitting my with sister and alternated nights. After dragging my feet on making a reservation, I decided on Bimini and they had a good time for that night. The rundown of our experience goes like this: -HOLY LONG WALK TO GET TO THE RESTAURANT -Random placement of the entrance to a night club INSIDE of the restaurant's reception area. Big TV's in the hallway let you watch what is going on inside the club. Klassy. -Hostess appeared to be 16 years old, and less than interested in being a hostess in a fine restaurant. +Our server was nice and funny and attentive -We joked that the buyer meant to buy 10 pendant lights for this restaurant, but instead typed an extra 0 at the end of the order, and got 100. They thought "Well, we have to use 'em all" and hung 100 pendant lights over about 35 tables. The whole place is experiencing a decor overload. -The bread came with three different butters, none of which tasted good to me and were all very difficult to spread, straight from a very cold fridge. Plain butter would be nicer. -Escargot was literally boiling in melted butter when it got to our table. Little circles of puff pastry on the top of the escargot were burnt. The escargots themselves were extremely hot, and took a good 5 minutes to cool to the point we could consider eating them, when they did cool, they were so overcooked they were inedible. +Our nice server told us "They always overcook this", then took it back, and promised to get it fixed. Which he did. -The new escargot was still overcooked, and not very flavorful. Not the usual garlic-y-mouth-party that is escargot. Again, the puff pastry was overcooked, and it's presence didn't make much culinary sense to me. -When you order a steak here, all you get is steak. If you want a side, you have to order it a la carte. -I ordered my filet rare. I did so, because the overcooked escargot gave me the sense that I could expect an overcooked steak. I like mine med rare. When it came it was medium well. My husband's prime rib was ordered medium and arrived well done. +The broccolini and asparagus were good, albeit expensive when purchase a la carte. -they brought three sauces to our table and no explanation was given, so I didn't know what they were nor did I know if I was supposed to put them on my steak or my sides. Odd. One of them was good. The other two were not. I'm not sure why we ordered dessert but . . . -the dessert wasn't good either. Overcooked cannoli stuffed with orange zest and chocolate chips was strange. I don't remember what else was on the plate, but it was okay. -Our total with tip was about $120 for the two of us. In short: Meh. I had joked earlier in the week that "Now that I'm almost 30, I don't have to eat at Texas Roadhouse for every date night, I can go out to a nice meal once in awhile." We probably should have just gone to Texas Roadhouse.

text: I think I actually need to take another day before I fully write this review. I know if I write it now, I'll say a lot of things that are not appropriate on a public forum. text: Where do I start? Every once and while my fellow Yelpers and I disagree . For the most part I've found the reviews reliable - so much so that my team has learned to use yelp as a resource and that's how they picked up on the Stockyard for a group dinner That said, I could not disagree more strongly with the other reviews on this one. The Stockyard is a classic case of a restaurant surviving purely on its historic reputation. We had a large group - so let me begin at the beginning... While I expect a high-end steakhouse to be pricey - I also expect to "get what you pay for". The wine list was not a good start. The wines I recognized were priced 4-6X retail. When we have a significant size group I try to target wines in the 50-80$ range. Thats a real challenge at the stockyard. Precious few decent wines in this range. We went with a Malbec that I know sells for about $20 a bottle retail - $80. Also got a white -- which was a bit more reasonably priced - $65 and surprisingly good. We did the "seafood" appetizer - again, family style due to group size. I was surprised that they didn't cut the fried lobster tails into bite size portions a bit awkward to share. No real complaints here, but it wasn't superb either. At this point i am still thinking "expensive but average steakhouse". But then we got to the main course - and the hustle. Our main waiter launched into a description of the available entrees to the group, including - much to my dismay the description of limited number of American "kobe" filets. In a group this size, I'd want a heads up that he was offering $90 filets BEFORE people start to order. This was followed by an offer to each table (unknown to me) of a 2lb lobster add-on for each. He later claimed he asked first on this - but he did not come to me and i was clearly acting in the capacity of host. Talk about cranking up the bill... All of this - while disconcerting and annoying - is still somewhat "forgivable" when you get a really outstanding meal and service. Nothing could be further from the truth. To a man (or woman) our group was disappointed in the quality and preparation of the entrees - including the kobe which was described as bland and a bit chewy. My porterhouse was undercooked, non-prime beef and clearly not the size stipulated on the menu. I am no steakhouse novice. I know what to expect and this was clearly far below my expectation at a third of the price -- I could have gotten better at Outback. Based on conversation, I was clearly not alone in this opinion. Additionally, a number of people had to wait extended time for entrees while others ate. Lobsters - while large, should have been pre-cracked so inexperienced diners wouldn't struggle so much (and not overcooked). Overall, our price per person was outrageous, the food average, and the approach to draining our pockets insulting. If you want a good meal in Nashville look to the west end near Vanderbilt. Some great places... but Stockyard is the kind of place that makes "overrated" seem like a compliment.
label: NEG

We chalked it up to us being "early birds," though. The meal started off well enough. A couple of us got gumbo, and it was pretty good. Then came the entrees. My boyfriend and I got the seafood au gratin which was acceptable. The seafood tasted fresh, but I thought they could have done a bit more with the sauce (scalloped potatoes aren't usually that bland!) My brother-in-law got the BBQ shrimp and while he liked the flavor, he found it odd that they served the shrimp with the heads on when they were covered with such a thick sauce. My sister got the veal and crab, which she said was okay but too salty. My sister's boss got the redfish which he said was not particularly fresh and was overdone. He does tend to catch and eat a lot of redfish so maybe he's picky, but still. For the price you're paying, things should be more than acceptable. My boyfriend and I ordered from the prix fixe menu, so ours came with dessert. My vanilla creme brulee was a highlight. My boyfriend got the brownie and liked it but said it tasted more like cake. The service here was slow and a bit uneven. Again, for the price and the reputation, I expected a little more. Definitely a disappointment.

text: On a one night stop in New Orleans, we decided to stop here for dinner... This restaurant captured the French Quarter experience for me. A historical house that's been around for hundreds of years, and converted to a restaurant in the early 1900's, Nap House has a cool charm that can overwhelm. The dining area is classy without being obnoxious or elite. Weathered walls, clever accents and antiques adorn the place. Servers wear bowties and black n' white attire. But the food and pricing is very reasonable. I tried several items... The best thing I had was the Muffaletta. It was, in my mind, nearly perfect. The boudin, jambalaya, and pates were tasty but not mind blowing. There is a lovely patio outside for a more romantic setting. Classical music plays while you eat or drink. I loved that. A cool place to check out if you're in the Big Easy.

text: Let me begin by saying...wow I can't believe I haven't reviewed this place yet. Driving down Ewing you'll see the red roofed house that is known as Hot Diggity Dogs. If you are a native of Chicago you know what a Chicago style dog is. For those who don't know...taken from Wikipedia: "A Chicago-style hot dog is a steamed or boiled, never broiled all-beef hot dog on a poppy seed bun, which originated in the city of Chicago, Illinois. The hot dog is topped with mustard, onion, sweet pickle relish (usually a dyed neon green variety called "Nuclear Relish"), a dill pickle spear, tomato slices or wedges, pickled sport peppers, and a dash of celery salt; sometimes, but not always, cucumber slices." The cornucopia of flavors and textures will win you over. Cool, crisp, hot...all having a get down. The fine ladies at Hot Diggity Dogs do Chicago justice. You really can't find a better dog in Nashville.

text: I am excited to taste truly authentic, perfectly seasoned specialities of Middle Eastern foods. This is food representing the best that can be had. You may not realize that everything on the menu and in the culture really, must be prepared fresh. Hardly anything can be made up in advance because the flavors will be affected if the parsley in the Taboulli is wilted and bland, or the garlic which was crushed this morning is stronger than garlic yesterday. The humidity affects the amount of liquid, the strength of that days' lemon- all of these variables are so significant. In a hurry? You can't rush excellent. You can't whip up a great Hummus, and you can't re-trim the lamb in your shish kebab. The prep work is enormous and takes a long time to get right. This is very very high quality in a modest, clean and cheery setting. Oh, did I mention the rice? Believe me, families' reputation is built on something as simple ( to us) as how the rice is prepared. Fish, chicken, beef, and lamb on the menu- and outstanding vegetarian offerings too. They also serve and sell the very best Khobuz arabee ( pita to you) in the Region- Soumaya Brothers of Allentown. Please stop by- I am the big guy relishing every single bite. I have eaten this food natively, and this is excellent.

text: As part of their "grand opening," my friend and I had free meal coupons. We both ordered the dinner special, which consisted of an appetizer, a soup, an entree, rice, and a dessert. Regularly priced at 7.50-11.50, depending on the entree ordered. The appetizer was one honey wanton, one crab rangoon, and one potsticker. Served with a small cup of sweet and sour sauce in a hexagon-shaped dish. It tasted like the sauce they have at Panda Express, which is a alright in my book. Each of the three items were good, and each would be good in larger portions. The soup was at least a decent size. Choices were egg drop, wanton, or hot and sour. I ordered the wanton, my friend had the hot and sour. Both were good. Mine had more cabbage floating around in it than I'm used to, but the broth and wantons were good. I was pleasantly surprised to see that lo mein could be substituted in for rice, of which, white, brown, and fried were options. The lo mein tasted healthier than at other Chinese restuarants and needless to say, I finished it all. Pretty much every beef or chicken dish is an option for the dinner entree, but my friend and I both ordered chicken. I had the sesame chicken and she had the lemon chicken. The sauces on both were tasty. The chicken was abysmal. They weren't pieces of chicken like American Chinese-food-goers are used to, they are balls of chicken covered in a bad tasting batter. I can only hope that the beef entrees aren't the same consistency. Dessert was something I completely forgot was included, but since it was, I went ahead and ate it. Choices were vanilla, chocolate, or green tea ice cream (pronounced I-cream) or tapioca pudding. One small scoop of whichever you order is all you get, but that's ok because none of them are anything special. For my drink I ordered a watermelon slush. At $2.50 it's not a bad deal. The slush, blended ice with watermelon flavor, was brought out in a water glass with a straw. This is definitely worth getting if you decide to go to this establishment. The service was friendly, and the waitress was willing to answer all my questions regarding MSG and slushes. The answers were "we don't use that" and "no you cannot combine flavors." I don't feel the need to type out which questions I asked. Overall, I wouldn't go back unless I had another free coupon.

text: I agree that the service is sweet. I agree that the decor is charming and cheerifying (i.e. makes you cheery). I agree that the prices are very reasonable. (Well, I'm not sure anyone else has actually said this, but if they had, I would have agreed with them.) I agree that it's nice to sit outside on a warm evening, even if you are right next to whizzing traffic on Charlotte Avenue and even if some guy insists on cutting through the seating area on his way to Ava's Adult Store and nearly knocking your cone out of your hand in the process. (No, hey, excuse me for sitting in your way.) OK, I'm bitter about the invasion of personal space. It's a pet peeve. But even before that, I was having major difficulties with the dipped cone. Yep, I'd gotten a Medium cone, which translates in Bobbie's Dairy Dip-speak into a small cone piled high with a towering mound of soft-serve ice cream. I'd ordered the cone dipped (on the advice of several other Yelpers), but the chocolate dip must be somewhat warm because there was melting ice cream oozing out from under the dipped shell from the moment the cone was handed to me. To be needlessly revealing, even ordinary ice cream cones are typically pretty stressful for me. I generally prefer a cup where I don't feel like I have to race against the clock to wolf down the cream before it melts all over my hand and/or clothing. But I wanted the full dipped-cone-experience. So anyway, by the time I had demolished the top half of the cone, there was like a river of ice cream running down my hand and onto a pile of napkins that the girl at the counter had generously handed to me. It's kind of horrifying to know that the ice cream on your cone is melting, but you can't do anything about it because it's hidden behind a hard shell. Oh the angst. Anyway, eventually I gave up and dumped about half the cone in the trash. I'll go back, but any future cones are going to be naked (un-dipped) and I may just have to go totally stress-free with a shake or sundae. Oh I'm definitely going to order a Small, which I assume will translate into a Large, but hopefully not ridonkulously Large. ps - Bring clean wipes. Even after using all the napkins, I was glad I had something else to wipe my hands and save the interior of my car from becoming irredeemably sticky.

text: Charlie's Jeans is a nice, clean, stylish boutique at 2nd and Market in Olde City. Their specialty, of course, is designer jeans. They've got Sevens, Joe's Jeans, and many more. They've also got some pretty cool tops and accessories, the displays are well-done, and the sales clerks are friendly and helpful. The only downside of this place is that designer jeans are very expensive. Sevens, I was told by the sales dude, run from about $140-200 each, and I can imagine that the other brands are similarly priced. Needless to say, I browsed the day I was there and didn't buy anything, but I hope to return someday when I have some cash to buy the perfect pair of jeans. Of course, I might be 40 by then and will be too old to be able to pull those cool jeans off anymore... I have one major gripe: I went in while they were having a sale. Everything was on sale EXCEPT FOR JEANS. Since they really are a jeans store, I think that sucks. I'd be more likely to buy a pair of jeans there if they were on sale because you can find the same designer jeans (although not as many styles) on sale at places like Off Fifth or Last Call Neiman Marcus. And I don't think it would kill Charlie's to knock $20 bucks off their jeans now and then. Otherwise, though, this store is really cool.

text: Met up with everyone in Philadelphia and went to Tria on Sunday night. Seriously. This place was packed and there was a 40 minute wait. It was perfect and made me really happy. I'm so used to haters going on and on about how amazing New York is because there's a busy bar or restaurant on any given night of the week. I will admit, Philly seems to like its sleep on off-nights, but last Sunday at Tria gave me faith. My friend and I were lucky enough to score 2 seats at the bar within 5 minutes of walking in. Just seconds later, the bartender (who felt more like a casual/cool sommelier) approached us with menus and questions and shared some of her picks. We ordered at various points throughout the night. Here a dish, there a dish, everywhere a dish dish. The mission figs with gorgonzola and prosciutto were really good, but probably for someone who likes figs...they just don't excite me. The warm mushroom and raclette fondue was really just a mushroom and cheese dip. I guess the word raclette confused me. Anyway, it was fantastic - especially so when paired with the malbec. My wine enthusiast friend swore by the malbec and called it her fav of the night. Then there was some duck salad action. We paired that with the pinot noir and found the clementines (from the salad) and wine combo to be a definite match. I loved the gouda cheese and ate it with just about every wine we tried. I felt like there was nothing better than the taste of gouda and wine dancing inside my mouth. The Argentinean Torrontes, however, felt too flowery for my taste. Almost like I was drinking roses. We finished off with the banana panini (divine) and paired that with the cava (a sparkling delight). I'd say Tria is the place to go if you're looking to experiment with your taste buds. I came with an open mind and found out I like white wine and duck after all. I recommend asking your server or bartender for their favorite pairings or just wing it and make up your own. Yay wine and little plates of food.

text: "Dedicated to art and free to all." I had lived in Saint Louis for over 4 years before I set aside the time to go to the Art Museum. I had spent hours in Forest Park exploring the paths and features. I finally set aside the time during the Balloon Race in 2008. A co-worker and I had gone to the St. Louis Symphony concert on Art Hill, which was a part of the race weekend events. When he learned that I had not been to the museum yet, we made plans to meet there on Sunday. Having had the fortune to live in Paris, Moscow, New York City and the Twin Cities, I did not know how well Saint Louis would fare by comparison. I was thrilled to discover that my new home town has a museum with an impressive collection of art and artifacts (from the Egyptian mummies) to a very rare painting from the 17th century female painter, Artemisia Gentileschi. Add to this discovery, my delight in their modern art collection, especially one of the rarer Van Gogh pieces from his northern paintings, and the St. Louis Art Museum is a place that I visit as often as I can. Just this past New Year, my boyfriend and I spend a lovely afternoon strolling through the galleries. He was equally impressed. I am thrilled that they have completed groundbreaking on the new wings and eagerly anticipate their opening in 2012. Until then, there are so many exhibits that I have to explore in depth. That should take me a few more visits.

text: The Boathouse (formerly the Brown Pelican) has just opened for business and is still working out the kinks. My friend (a former local) wanted to take me to the Brown Pelican for a lovely Sunday breakfast on the beach - we didn't know the restaurant had changed hands but decided to try it anyway. After putting in our name for a table, we proceeded to wait nearly an hour to be seated. We didn't have a problem with this as the restaurant appeared to be very popular like its predecessor. When we were seated at our table on the patio - it was apparent that we were in desperate need of an umbrella. They did not have enough umbrellas for the people seated at the patio - so we were forced to seek a small corner of shade from a neighboring table. Our server arrived and promptly introduced herself as "Candy" and proceeded to take our order. We ordered; a santa barbara omelet for my friend, and "traditional" eggs benedict for myself. We chat about the day and wait for our food. Forty-five minutes after placing our order with Candy, a nice young man named Mark came by to tell us the kitchen was running late and could he buy us a cocktail? We were surprised by this, but welcomed the drink. He continues to inform us that the restaurant has been "comping" all the breakfasts because of the kitchen's delay. Thirty minutes and a cigarette later, we are still patiently waiting for our food - while trying to keep a positive attitude. Vanessa comes by our table to let us know that not only will she be replacing "Candy" but the kitchen is an hour behind in getting out orders... We ask for some toast while we continue to "stick it out" as we've now been at the restaurant over two hours waiting for breakfast. Shortly after the toast arrives, our food is dumped on our plate by a busboy with a certain frustrated flare. My girlfriends omelet is not what she ordered and the potatoes are cold; while my eggs are good - but I have the same issue with the potatoes. (sigh) VERY disappointing. Finished with our meal and desperate to make the most of the rest of our day, we wait to be released from our table like hostages. Vanessa reappears only to flutter about our neighboring table - filled with her friends- chatting about how she has aspirations of being a school teacher... and if they'll let dogs come and sit with the guests on the patio. Needless to say, it was not a great experience. We left annoyed and sunburned. The restaurant has potential - but what's a restaurant without food, service and ambiance? I would've rated this 1 star, but I'm giving the place the benefit of the doubt... for Mark's sake.
